4.3
The program is the memory
A streaming model must forget, or its context grows without bound. The question is what to keep. A human crew does not remember what every camera showed a minute ago. It remembers the broadcast, the shots that actually went on air and what was said over them. DirCast keeps this. The low-resolution views of the ten cameras stay for only
W
W
seconds and then leave the context, while the high-resolution on-air views, the events and the words stay. During training this rule is an attention mask, and during streaming the expired entries are removed from the key-value cache. The model’s memory is the program it has produced. On streams longer than a training clip, every second also leaves the cache once it is older than a clip, so the cost per second stays constant over a match of any length.
4.4
Grounding the game
Video alone is a weak signal for directing. A fight that is about to start looks like two groups of heroes walking, and a kill on the far side of the map is a small change in one of ten thumbnails. The game itself knows more. The state token of each camera gives the model the hero’s health, recent damage and the enemies around it, and the event text states what happened, such as one hero killing another. We tie each event to the camera that shows it, so that the kill of a hero raises a flag on the camera of the hero who made it. The model thus reads the game in the same terms as the cameras it has to choose from.
4.5
Learning to direct from human broadcasts
DirCast is trained on human broadcasts with three objectives. A language modeling loss teaches the commentary, a binary loss on the commentary token teaches when to speak, and a directing loss teaches the gate and the pointer. The gate learns from the human cuts, and the pointer learns which camera the human chose at every cut, where a camera whose hero is visible in the broadcast shot counts as a correct answer as well.
Imitating human broadcasts directly leaves two gaps. The first gap is between training and deployment. During training the model always sees the program the human chose. At test time it sees its own program, and a single wrong cut moves it to a state it has never seen. We close this gap with on-policy program rollouts. During training, the on-air camera in the input drifts away from the human choice for a few seconds at a time, while the targets stay human. The director learns to recover from a wrong shot by cutting back, and the commentator learns to describe whatever is on air. The second gap is in the targets. A human director makes one choice among several good ones. When a kill happens on a camera that is not on air, cutting to it is a correct directing decision even if the human stayed elsewhere. We add an event-anchored target that, in the seconds around a kill, also accepts the cameras of the killer and the victim, and asks the gate to open when neither is on air. The model learns that action is worth showing, which is the part of directing that the human labels express least consistently.
4.6
Streaming decisions at a human rhythm
At inference, the model cuts when the gate exceeds a threshold and speaks when the probability of the commentary token exceeds a threshold. Fixed thresholds fail in streaming. A model that stays silent for a few seconds conditions on its own silence and becomes more likely to stay silent, and a director that has not cut for a while drifts the same way. We let both thresholds follow the model’s own behavior,

5.1
Setup
Protocol.
All results are on the test split of four unseen matches, 496 clips with 485 commented and 11,283 strict LIVE seconds. Every model runs free through every second of each clip and conditions only on its own past decisions.
Directing.
We measure how often a model agrees with the human director (Top-1, Tol-top1 with one second of slack, and Any-visible, which accepts any feed whose hero is visible on air). We compare with three rules and eight zero-shot VLMs. The random rule cuts to a random feed at the human cutting rate, and the static rule keeps one feed throughout. The action rule scores every feed by the game state of its hero, nearby enemies, recent damage, deaths and crowding, and cuts to the highest-scoring feed when it leads and the current shot has been held at least three seconds. Main Results
Directing.
Table
1
compares DirCast with rule-based and zero-shot directors. DirCast is the best director on every measure of agreement with the human crew. It reaches a Top-1 of 26.95 and an Any-visible of 41.81, against 25.43 and 36.11 for the action rule, the strongest baseline, and it has the highest precision and F1 of correct cuts. It covers 89.1 percent of kills, more than any baseline and more than the human director, who often stays with a shot when a kill happens elsewhere. Zero-shot vision language models do not direct well, whatever their size. None of the eight reaches the action rule on agreement, scale does not help within a family, and GPT-5 reaches a Top-1 of only 13.53. They also lack a sense of rhythm. Most of them cut 20 to 56 times per minute, against 7.9 for the human crew, so that most of their cuts are wrong and their cut precision stays between 6 and 9 percent. DirCast cuts 6.7 times per minute. The action rule follows fights by construction and has the highest fight coverage at 62.4. DirCast reaches 41.1, ahead of every zero-shot model and of the human director at 37.4, even though it is trained to imitate that director.

What makes a director.
Table
4
ablates the directing components. Removing the hold-or-switch pointer costs the most, dropping Top-1 from 27.00 to 21.65 (a relative loss of about 20%) and Any-vis. from 41.80 to 35.93, which confirms that an explicit hold-or-switch decision is the backbone of the director. Without it, the director must re-select a camera from scratch at every step, which likely leads to unmotivated switches. Removing state tokens or program rollouts also hurts, dropping Top-1 to 22.59 and 22.90 and Any-vis. to 37.98 and 38.01, showing that game state complements vision and that training under self-induced states matters. Program rollouts help the commentary as well: without them CC falls from 29.21 to 28.35, since a commentator that never sees its own drifted program is less prepared for the shots the director actually produces. Removing state tokens, by contrast, leaves CC unchanged at 29.21, so their benefit is confined to directing. Without event-anchored targets, Top-1 is comparable but Any-vis. rises from 41.80 to 43.06, a trade-off between matching the human director and covering every visible event on air. Since Top-1 is our primary measure of agreement with human directors, we keep event-anchored targets in the full model. Commentary metrics are otherwise stable throughout, with TimeDiff staying within 0.30–0.32, so these components mainly affect directing.

Scaling with training data.
We train DirCast on 5, 10 and 20 matches and evaluate the director on the same test split (Figure
3
). Top-1 counts a second as correct when the model airs the same feed as the human director, and Any-vis. when the chosen feed shows the event at all. Going from 5 to 10 matches gives small gains of 0.98 in Any-vis. and 0.56 in Top-1, while doubling to 20 gives 5.56 and 6.36, reaching 41.80 and 27.00. The jump suggests that the director needs to see enough fights, teams and strategies before its choices generalize to unseen matches. The curves show no sign of saturation, and new matches are cheap to collect since each needs only its camera feeds and the aired broadcast, with no manual labels, so scaling to hundreds of matches is a natural next step. Because the subsets are nested and the test split is fixed, the rising curve reflects added training variety rather than an easier evaluation.

Figure

In each case the cut gate stays below its threshold while the action is elsewhere, so DirCast holds its shot; in the second of the kill the gate rises above the threshold and DirCast cuts to the fight, often first to the victim and then to the killer as it moves. The commentary names a hero of the fight within about two seconds of the kill: Shadow Fiend as KotL takes him down off-air in (a), Rubick as Clockwerk finishes him while DirCast follows the fight in (b), Doom as he picks off Terrorblade on the kill in (c), and Terrorblade as his ultimate kills Tusk in (d). After each cut the threshold rises, so DirCast holds the new shot instead of flickering between feeds. The human crew misses all four kills, staying on an uninvolved hero such as Techies in (a), KotL in (b), Bane in (c) and Pangolier in (d); in (d) the casters call the kill although the broadcast never shows it, so the official feed shows none of the deaths as they happen.
6
Conclusion
We introduced live esports broadcast production, where a model receives every player’s camera feed and must choose the on-air shot and commentate using only past observations. DirCast addresses both tasks with a single streaming video language model. A hold-or-switch director selects the on-air shot, commentary follows its choice, and program-only context bounds the cost of long streams while enabling real-time operation on one GPU. Trained on human broadcasts with perturbed programs and event-anchored targets, DirCast outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, shows more kills on air than human crews, and wins more comparisons than eleven streaming commentators watching human broadcasts. Together, these results establish the feasibility of unified, real-time esports production with a single model.

\beginappendix
7
Dataset Construction
This section describes how the dataset is built: the director data (Section
7.1
), the commentary (Section
7.2
), and the cleaning applied to both (Section
7.3
).
7.1
Director Data
Source data.
We build a multi-camera director dataset from 27 professional
Dota 2
matches (EPL Masters and BLAST Slam qualifiers, 2026). For each match we use two public sources: the official broadcast video (VOD), which is the only record of the human director’s output and of the casters’ voices, and the official replay file (
.dem
), which contains the complete game state at 30 ticks per second. Player and hero metadata are taken from OpenDota.
Broadcast-to-replay alignment.
The broadcast and the replay share the in-game clock shown on the HUD. We OCR the HUD clock from the VOD and fit a linear mapping between VOD time and the game clock, with a residual of about 0.3 s. Because broadcasts often cover only part of a match, and some archive records point to the wrong game, we additionally OCR the hero names on the HUD and keep only VOD stretches whose hero set matches the replay. Game pauses require special care: replay ticks and the broadcast keep running during a pause while the game clock stops, so the mapping is defined on replay ticks with the paused ticks subtracted. We validate the alignment with a consistency check: heroes whose name tags are visible together in a broadcast frame must be close to each other in the replay at the mapped tick. All 27 matches pass this check at zero time offset.
Candidate camera feeds.
Candidate feeds are rendered with the Dota 2 client itself. Each replay is played back in a headless X server and recorded by ten spectator clients in parallel, one per player, each in the client’s
Hero Chase
mode following that player’s hero with the HUD hidden. Clients are driven through the console interface; capture starts and ends at fixed replay ticks and every frame is tagged with its tick, so all ten feeds are synchronized with the replay and with the broadcast. Feeds are captured at
1280
×
720
1280\times 720
and 30 fps and stored at
640
×
360
640\times 360
; training clips use one frame per second resized to
288
×
288
288\times 288
. Each match is rendered in 300 s windows covering the broadcast-aligned part of the game.
Director labels.
The label for each second is the hero the broadcast is looking at, which maps to one of the ten feeds. We obtain it from the broadcast frame itself: the spectator HUD prints a name tag above every visible hero, which we OCR and match to the match roster, and the HUD also shows the currently selected unit. The label is the selected hero if it is on screen, otherwise the visible hero nearest the frame centre, with a 2 s hysteresis on switches and up to 4 s of carry-over when no tag is readable. Every label records which of these cases produced it, which the cleaning in Section
7.3
uses. Every second also receives a broadcast state (live, replay, production, paused, no coverage) derived from the clock OCR and a gameplay cue. We additionally store the set of all heroes on screen in each second, which supports an
any-of-visible
evaluation, since several feeds can show the same scene.
7.2
Commentary
Audio and transcription.
For every rendered window we cut the broadcast audio at the same aligned VOD times as the director labels, so the commentary shares the time axis of the feeds and the labels, and resample it to 16 kHz mono. The casters’ speech is transcribed with Whisper (large-v3-turbo) in English with voice activity detection, beam size 5 and word-level timestamps. Each window is decoded without conditioning on the previous text, which avoids repetition loops over long audio, and with a vocabulary prompt that lists the heroes and players of the match, which biases the decoder towards the names the casters use. Every word is assigned to the second in which it starts, which gives the per-second commentary targets. Of the 2,096 training clips, 1,984 have broadcast audio, and about 8% of the transcribed words have an ASR confidence below 0.5.
Polishing.
Raw ASR misspells hero and player names and keeps fillers and repetitions. Such text would teach the model wrong names and would penalise correct names at evaluation. We therefore follow the data pipeline of Proact-VL
[
43
]
, which merges ASR segments into sentences and polishes them with a language model. Consecutive Whisper segments are merged into a sentence until end punctuation, a pause of more than 1 s, 30 words or 12 s. Sentences are then rewritten in batches of twelve by GPT-5-mini with a match-specific prompt. The prompt lists both teams and their players and heroes, and asks the model to correct hero, player, item and ability names, to remove fillers and repetitions, and to keep the casters’ own words, word order and meaning. Sentences that the casters leave unfinished stay unfinished, and the model may not add who did what, numbers or outcomes. Proact-VL uses DeepSeek-V3.2 for this step. We use GPT-5-mini because GPT-4o is the opponent and GPT-5 the judge of the commentary evaluation, so neither of them sees the references beforehand.
Guard and timing.
A rewrite is accepted only if its word count lies between 70% and 140% of the ASR sentence and at least half of its words appear in the ASR sentence; otherwise we keep the ASR text with fillers removed. This guard prevents the language model from inventing content. Polishing keeps the timing of speech: the polished words of a sentence take the start times of the original words in order and are bucketed into seconds by the same rule as the raw transcript. Polishing changes the text of 38% of the seconds with speech and removes 2% of the words, mostly fillers and repetitions.
Use.
The polished commentary is the training target of DirCast and of the two fine-tuned baselines, and it is the reference for every model at test time, as in the Proact-VL protocol.
7.3
Cleaning
Table
7
follows every clip-second through the cleaning steps.
Broadcast state.
Only seconds in which the broadcast shows live gameplay are director decisions. Replays, production shots such as the desk or the drafting screen, pauses and seconds without broadcast coverage are removed, which keeps 87% of the clip-seconds.
Label quality.
Labels that come from the HUD selection alone, without the selected hero on screen, are dropped, since only 52% of them agree with the hero positions in the replay. The remaining labels form the training mask.
Verification.
Carried-over labels are the noisiest, because the broadcast may cut while no name tag is readable. We verify all 15,951 carried-over seconds with a vision–language model (GPT-6 Astra). It sees the broadcast frame and four candidate feeds, the labelled feed among them, and answers which of them shows the same scene; a label is confirmed if the answer is the labelled feed. 62% are confirmed, and the rejected seconds are removed from the training mask, which gives the
verified
mask used for training. On a manually audited sample the model’s verdicts agree with the human audit in 43 of 45 cases.
Strict evaluation subset.
Evaluation uses only labels that are observed on screen in that very second, that is, the selected hero with its tag visible or the visible hero nearest the frame centre, without hysteresis or carry-over. This
strict
mask keeps 69% of the live test seconds.
Commentary.
Commentary is cleaned by the polishing and guard described above. Windows without broadcast audio keep their director labels but contribute no commentary targets.
Splits.
Matches are split as a whole into 20 training, 3 validation and 4 test matches, so no game, broadcast or caster utterance is shared between training and test. The validation matches are used to calibrate the base thresholds of the decoding rules.
7.4
Statistics
The dataset contains 15.2 hours of aligned ten-feed footage, of which 13.1 hours are live broadcast and 10.3 hours carry verified labels (7.9 hours in the strict subset). It is packaged as 2,912 clips of 36 s (stride 18 s), split as in Table
6
. Casters speak in 64% of the training clip-seconds and 72% of the test clip-seconds. The director switches feeds every few seconds, so a persistence baseline that repeats the previous label reaches about 80% per-second accuracy; we therefore report switch-second accuracy separately.

8
Additional qualitative examples
We show twenty more off-air kills that DirCast puts on air and names, ten in Figure
5
and ten in Figure
6
, drawn from the test matches and across the random seeds used in the main experiments. The examples cover a range of heroes and situations, from single-target pickoffs to crowded team fights, and each is chosen among the off-air kills where the human crew shows an uninvolved hero, so they test the director on moments it has to find on its own.
Each panel follows the format of Figure
4
. The label at the top names the kill and the seed. The top row is DirCast’s program, one on-air thumbnail per second with the words it speaks printed underneath; the middle row plots the cut gate against its threshold, with markers for the seconds it cuts and the seconds it holds; and the bottom row is the human broadcast over the same seconds. The shaded column marks the second of the kill.
Across the examples DirCast shows the behaviour described in Section
5.4
: it holds its shot while the gate stays below the threshold, cuts to the fight as the gate rises in the second around the kill, often moving from the victim to the killer as the fight develops, and names a hero of the fight within about two seconds. After the cut the threshold rises, so it holds the new shot instead of flickering between feeds. By construction the human crew is on an uninvolved hero in every panel, and it shows the kill late or not at all, so these decisive seconds never reach the official broadcast even though DirCast puts them on air and calls them.

article.lede: DirCast 用单个流式视频语言模型，从十路英雄画面每秒选镜并解说，27 场职业 Dota 2 比赛上胜过 GPT-5
article.problem: 现有的流式解说模型（LiveCC、StreamingVLM、Proact-VL 等）都假定输入是已经剪好的成品广播，选镜这一最难的环节仍由人类导演完成，模型免费继承了导演的判断。若只给十路原始英雄画面，这类模型无法使用。论文把「导播」与「解说」合并成一个任务：模型每秒决定哪路画面播出，并在自己选出的画面上即时解说，且只能使用过去的信息。
article.method: DirCast 微调 Qwen3-VL-8B，把比赛组织成每秒增长一个 chunk 的单一 token 流：chunk 先放入事件与十路低分辨率画面（各带一个编码英雄血量、近期伤害、周围敌人的状态 token），随后由「保持或切换」导演头给出切门概率与指向十路画面的指针，选中的画面再以高分辨率追加，解说在其后生成。低分辨率视图 8 秒后移出上下文，高分辨率播出画面与已说出的文字保留，即「节目就是记忆」，使任意长度流的每秒成本有界。训练时加入扰动节目 rollout（让播出画面短暂偏离人类选择而目标仍是人类）与事件锚定目标（击杀附近也接受凶手/受害者镜头），推理时切与说的阈值跟随模型自身近期决策率向人类节奏回归。
article.results: 导播方面，DirCast 与人类导演的 Top-1 一致率为 26.95、Any-visible 为 41.81，高于最强规则基线 action rule 的 25.43 与 36.11，覆盖 89.1% 的击杀（人类导演为 50.3%），每分钟切 6.7 次（人类 7.9 次）；零样本 VLM 中 GPT-5 的 Top-1 仅 13.53，且多数每分钟切 20 至 56 次。解说方面，在 Proact-VL 协议下对 GPT-4o 的胜率为 29.21%，高于最强流式解说基线 LiveCC-7B-Base 的 19.38%（p<0.001），开口时间比人类解说平均晚 0.30 秒。联合模型优于分开训练：Top-1 27.00 对 25.17，胜率 29.21% 对 24.36%，显存从 37.8 GB 降到 18.9 GB；长流测试中每秒计算 0.29 秒、缓存 6.9k token，可在单 GPU 实时运行。
article.why_it_matters: 它把通常分开研究的「选什么给观众看」和「怎么讲」耦合进一个因果模型，直接从原始多路画面产出完整直播，让区域联赛、业余比赛这类请不起导播团队的长尾赛事有可能自动化制播。
article.limitations: 数据仅来自 27 场 Dota 2 职业比赛（训练 2,096 个片段），单一游戏、单一赛事生态，能否迁移到其他项目未知；解说评判因官方 GPT-5.1 不可得而改用 GPT-5，绝对胜率 29.21% 仍不高，F1（78.22）还低于说话率 99.9% 的 Proact-VL（83.21），战斗覆盖率 41.1 也明显低于 action rule 的 62.4，且各基线看的是人类成品广播、DirCast 看自己的节目，比较并非完全同条件。
article.figure_caption_zh: 框架：每秒由低分辨率 ViT 编码十路画面及其英雄状态，导演头决定保持或切换，选中画面以高分辨率读入，解说随后生成，低分辨率视图过期而播出的节目留存。

figure.caption: Framework. Each second a low-res ViT encodes the ten feeds with their state, the director holds or cuts, the chosen feed is read at high resolution, and the commentator speaks. Low-res views expire while the program stays.

BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
Ava Pun
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Kevin Dai
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Sally Chen
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Maxwell Jones
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Ruixuan Liu
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Kangle Deng
Affiliation:
Independent Researcher
Changliu Liu
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Maneesh Agrawala
Affiliation:
Stanford University
Deva Ramanan
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Jun-Yan Zhu
Affiliation:
Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract
Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO
®
brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page:
avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright
.
Figure 1
:
BrickWright overview.
BrickWright instructs pre-trained LLM agents to generate physically feasible brick builds by writing code using a Python SDK, BrickLayer, in a plan-execute-validate loop utilizing BrickLayer’s physical validation tools (a). BrickWright accepts text or image inputs and can produce articulated and large-scale builds, all physically valid. Agents equipped with BrickWright produce higher-quality builds with fewer physical violations (b). Red outlines in insets indicate mesh intersections.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Without additional fine-tuning, commercially available agents can successfully produce articulated objects
[
58
,
45
]
, scenes
[
52
]
, and constructive solid geometry models
[
27
]
.
However, they still face challenges when building objects for the physical world. We focus on the task of creating
multi-part assemblies
: real-world objects made from a set of prefabricated parts joined by fixed connectors, such as LEGO
®
builds. Multi-part assemblies must obey multiple constraints: all parts must be drawn from a preset library, parts must not collide or float, and the joined parts typically form a single connected component.
We argue that designing a
toolkit
for multi-part assembly creation is sufficient to enable agents to create physically valid builds. This toolkit should include (1) an
assembly API
, which provides an ergonomic programmatic interface for 3D creation; and (2) a
validator
, which provides feedback on a finished build’s physical validity. The need for a toolkit is
independent of how powerful a coding agent is
. We observe that GPT-6 Astra with Codex, when asked to make brick builds, already writes scripts to generate and validate its output more than 80% of the time (
Appendix
D
). For complex physical domains, this self-validation is often not enough, resulting in builds that do not satisfy physical constraints, containing colliding, floating, or disconnected parts (
Fig.
2
). Even if an agent is powerful enough to write a perfect toolkit, separately developing a toolkit remains important to reduce token usage and avoid repeated work. Existing toolkits for agentic 3D generation
[
58
,
45
]
are usually intended for digital asset creation; as they do not consider physical constraints, they cannot be repurposed as-is to create real-world objects.
Figure 2
:
Physical violations in builds by Codex (GPT-6 Astra, high reasoning).
Red outlines in insets show mesh intersections.
We focus on the domain of LEGO
®
generation as it is a commonly available yet complex system, consisting of thousands of parts that connect in dozens of ways. Our key insight is to merge agentic code-as-3D-models with the regularity of brick parts. Parts can be modeled as geometries with localized connectors that have
programmatic rules
for assembly (e.g., studs interlock with antistuds). From this perspective, we leverage the physical production rules for snap-fit brick builds
[
6
]
to create an ergonomic assembly API. Then, given an image or text prompt, our task is to generate a program using this API that, when compiled, produces a LEGO
®
brick build in the standard LDraw format
[
21
]
. This build should include a list of library part placements, and it must be
physically feasible
, having no intersecting or floating parts and forming a connected structure if possible. While there are several specialized brick generation methods
[
50
,
10
,
11
,
19
,
37
,
48
,
36
,
53
]
, some of which consider physical constraints, they generally exhibit worse generalization and lower fidelity than commercial LLM agents on the same task. Hence, we wish to achieve this task agentically.
Toward this goal, we introduce
BrickLayer
, a Python package for assembling and validating brick builds, alongside
BrickWright
, a framework that guides LLM agents through creating validated brick builds with BrickLayer. Agents equipped with BrickWright create higher-quality builds with fewer physical violations; on a test set of 512 prompts, all agents—including lightweight models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5—achieve a 100% validity score without a significant cost increase or drop in fidelity. BrickWright is especially useful for lightweight models: it improves Luna’s performance from 9% to 100% valid builds and boosts its prompt adherence at 2% the price of frontier models. BrickWright additionally outperforms specialized brick generation models on validity and fidelity. Code is available on our project page:
avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright
.
Figure 3
:
Method overview.
(a) BrickLayer supports catalog discovery, compositional construction with typed connectors, and physical validation. (b) BrickWright prompts a pre-trained LLM agent to write and revise
build.py
, which contains brick build creation code and agent-defined tests. The
validate
tool runs fixed collision and floating checks alongside the agent’s tests, while the
render
tool provides views for visual inspection. The agent calls
finalize
once all checks pass. The agent may optionally run
explore
at any time to investigate the BrickLayer API and written brick build. Arrows summarize information flow rather than a fixed tool-call sequence.
2
Related work
Brick Build Generation.
Early work treats brick build generation as an optimization problem over a target shape. Legolization
[
34
]
voxelizes a 3D mesh, merges voxels into standard bricks, and iteratively re-merges regions identified as unstable. Subsequent work captures finer geometric detail through feature-aware shape approximation and non-rectangular bricks
[
57
,
59
]
, assembles bricks sequentially via Bayesian optimization
[
17
]
, or optimizes Technic assemblies to match annotated sketches
[
49
]
. Retrieval-based methods map images to figurines assembled from prebuilt templates
[
56
,
9
]
. These methods are limited by small brick vocabularies, explicit geometric guidance, or fixed templates.
Learning-based methods generate brick structures directly from data. These approaches adapt graph generative models
[
41
]
, predict voxel representations that are assembled into bricks algorithmically
[
24
,
4
]
, learn sequential construction policies
[
7
]
, or use diffusion
to predict labeled voxels within a single category
[
10
]
. Autoregressive methods generate bricks conditioned on text or
images. BrickGPT
[
37
]
fine-tunes an LLM to generate stable structures, but is restricted to eight rectangular brick types across 21 object categories. LEGO-Maker
[
11
]
generates builds from images, but
supports only axis-aligned orientations and two categories. LegoACE
[
50
]
and BrickNet
[
19
]
scale to open-vocabulary generation by training on
large collections of human-designed builds. However,
LegoACE learns connectivity implicitly and can produce disconnected components, while BrickNet represents assemblies as connector graphs but accumulates collisions over longer build sequences. Brick-Composer
[
30
]
instead approaches assembly from target views as sequential brick selection and pose estimation, training a multimodal LLM on simulator-generated data and feedback. Other methods improve buildability through preference optimization or reinforcement learning
[
36
,
48
]
. In contrast, BrickWright utilizes pre-trained models to build arbitrary objects without task-specific training, verifies collisions and connectivity in a feedback loop, and supports articulation. Concurrent with our work, BrickBench
[
20
]
introduces a toolkit for agentic brick build creation, focusing on benchmarking the performance of different agents.
Agentic 3D Generation.
LLM agents have been used successfully to create 3D scenes. Recent works use a plan-execute-critique loop
[
15
,
29
]
or reconstruct scenes from images through iterative code execution and visual inspection
[
52
,
13
]
. Other works fine-tune LLMs to reason directly over 3D spatial inputs
[
44
]
or to generate tool-call trajectories
[
14
]
. These methods place objects in continuous space and rely on optimization or visual judgment to resolve collisions and floating objects. In BrickWright, explicit connector rules enable deterministic checks of attachment validity.
Representing shapes as programs provides structured descriptions of geometry and part relationships
[
39
,
42
,
16
]
. Separately,
LLMs have been shown to reason more reliably when they write code and offload exact
computation to an interpreter
[
8
]
. Building on both ideas, agents have been applied to modeling individual objects as code, typically through plan-execute-critique loops. Prior work augments this loop with API retrieval
[
32
]
, domain-specific languages
[
45
]
, or procedural part-based modeling
[
27
]
, with some supporting articulation
[
45
,
27
,
58
,
23
]
. In CAD, LLMs have been
fine-tuned to generate parametric modeling code
[
47
,
12
,
18
]
, while tool-augmented agents generate and refine parts and assemblies
[
35
,
40
,
1
,
55
]
. Articraft
[
58
]
generates articulated assets using a custom SDK and a minimal harness that provides textual feedback from tools that probe the model code. Unlike these systems, where the agent generates geometry or infers inter-part relationships, BrickWright assembles fixed parts whose connectors determine how they attach and move.
Physics-Aware Generation.
To improve physical validity, prior work refines shapes or layouts after generation
[
5
,
51
,
54
,
29
,
25
]
, fine-tunes generators on simulator feedback
[
26
]
, or guides diffusion sampling with physical constraints
[
33
]
. Geometric analysis has also been used to plan LEGO assembly sequences without explicit connector information
[
2
]
. For brick structures, stability has been assessed through force-based equilibrium analysis
[
34
,
37
,
31
]
or physics simulation
[
17
,
46
]
. In contrast, BrickWright uses an executable verifier to check for collisions, floating parts, and connectivity, allowing a pre-trained agent to iteratively repair builds without task-specific training. Incorporating force-based stability analysis
[
34
,
31
]
is a natural extension.
3
BrickWright
Given a natural-language or image description, our task is to generate a
physically feasible brick build
from a fixed part catalog. A brick build is defined as an ordered sequence of
placements
. Each placement consists of an
element
or a nested brick build, together with a rigid transformation relative to the containing build. An element specifies a single
part
drawn from the catalog and a color. Elements expose typed
connectors
, such as studs, whose compatibility and relative alignment determine valid
connections
. A build is
valid
if it uses only catalog parts and contains no colliding (intersecting) or floating parts. It forms a
connected component
if one can draw a path of connections between any two elements in the build. We define a build to be
physically feasible
if it is valid and contains as few connected components as possible. More complex feasibility considerations, such as ensuring a build is stable and has an executable assembly sequence, are left to future work. Note that although having a single connected component is desirable as it makes a build less likely to break apart in the physical world, builds with multiple components are still necessary in some cases: for example, two separate vehicles in a car chase scene.
We introduce
BrickWright
(
Fig.
3
), a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds using LLM agents.
Using a lightweight harness, BrickWright guides a single agent to write Python code that produces a brick build using a custom toolkit called
BrickLayer
. If the build passes a set of predefined and agent-written tests, it is accepted; otherwise, the agent makes edits informed by the test results, following the commonly used plan-execute-validate loop.
3.1
BrickLayer
LDraw
[
21
]
, the standard text format for LEGO
®
builds, includes no physical validation and is not very
ergonomic
: it only allows users to place parts and sub-models by their absolute 3D poses. This makes it difficult to mate parts by their connectors or place them relative to others, which can lead to wasted tokens and misplaced components. To provide agents with an ergonomic interface for creating and validating brick builds, we introduce
BrickLayer
(
), a Python package that includes functions for part discovery, assembly, and validation. BrickLayer provides a unified programmatic representation for brick builds, enabling them to be easily understood and edited by humans and agents; builds can be translated from BrickLayer to LDraw and vice versa. See
Appendix
B
for BrickLayer documentation.

Discovery.
BrickLayer allows users to search the LDraw catalog
[
22
]
, which contains 17k+ parts. This search accepts keywords matched against the part’s official LDraw name. Results are ordered by their BM25 score
[
38
]
multiplied by a popularity factor that scales logarithmically with the number of official LEGO
®
sets containing the part. LDraw names are parsed into fields such as category, subcategory, and dimensions; users may target specific fields with their keyword search and filter results using exact field matches.
Assembly.
The central objects of BrickLayer are
Element
, representing a single colored part, and
LegoBuild
, representing a brick build. Both objects support a unified
LegoGeometry
interface; this interface exposes dimensions and available connectors, which can be filtered by type and position. We use BrickNet’s connector annotations
[
19
]
, which mark the local frames of the connectors on each part, along with compatible connector types and the joints they form: fixed, revolute, ball, prismatic, or cylindrical. For example, studs and antistuds join with a revolute joint. As BrickNet annotations do not differentiate between prismatic and cylindrical joints, we determine a sliding joint’s type by rotating it
15
∘
15^{\circ}
about its axis in one direction; if a collision occurs, we mark the joint prismatic.
LegoBuild
s have a recursive structure: they may contain both
Element
s and other
LegoBuild
s, allowing complex models to be built from smaller components. Placements can be made at arbitrary poses, fixed to a grid, or by mating specified connectors. Users may name placements, allowing them to place components relative to or directly target the connectors of a named component. Users may also explicitly mark movable components with articulation limits corresponding to their joint type.
For convenience, BrickLayer includes several high-level construction functions, introduced after noting repeated patterns in agent-generated code. These include
brick
,
plate
,
tile
,
slope
, and
inverted_slope
to instantiate common parts by specifying their dimensions;
minifigure
,
door
, and
window
to create common multi-component sub-builds;
mirror
to reflect a build along a given axis; and
fill_box
,
fill_slope
, and
fill_inverted_slope
to fill a cuboid or wedge in a manner guaranteed to be valid and connected if possible.
Validation.
A
LegoBuild
provides methods to list collisions, floating elements, and disconnected components. To determine whether two elements collide, we inset each mesh by 0.1 mm before checking for intersections, following BrickNet; snap connections between bricks are so tight that a naive mesh intersection check would report a false positive. The floater check first translates a build so its lowest point is at the ground plane. Then, it marks an element
floating
if it cannot reach a grounded element through mated connectors or
supporting surface contacts
. A surface contact is supporting if it has an upward component; lateral contact alone is insufficient. Two connectors form a connection if their local frames align, depending on their joint type; for example, a fixed joint requires the two frames to align exactly, while a revolute joint additionally admits a rotational degree of freedom. For builds with user-annotated articulations, a
posed
method allows an agent to create a snapshot of the build with joints set to specified articulation parameters, to validate physical feasibility under joint motion. Posing works with models whose kinematic structure forms a tree.

3.2
Building with BrickLayer
BrickWright is a framework for agentic brick build creation using BrickLayer. It provides a single agent with a set of tools and prompts it to create a build by writing and revising a single Python file in a plan-execute-validate loop, inspired by Articraft
[
58
]
. The BrickWright environment exposes the tools
validate
, which runs agent-written tests alongside fixed collision and floating checks;
render
, which renders the build into a multi-view sheet or from a single specified view; and
finalize
, which marks the build as finished.
In its system prompt, BrickWright instructs an agent to make a short internal plan, then write a Python file,
build.py
, containing two functions:
create_build()
, which returns a
LegoBuild
, and
run_tests()
, which runs a set of agent-written tests against the completed build.
After creating
build.py
, the agent is instructed to iteratively call
validate
and edit the build file until all tests pass, then call
render
; if it judges the render satisfactory, it should then call
finalize
; otherwise, it should revise
build.py
and repeat validation. Besides these instructions, BrickWright includes only the BrickLayer documentation in its system prompt, and the input text or image in a user prompt. It does not provide the agent with detailed planning advice, complete build examples, or building tips beyond the plan-execute-validate loop; the loop alone is sufficient for even lightweight agents to produce a feasible build.
BrickWright can be used alongside commercial frameworks such as Codex, which allows general file access and script execution. However, to demonstrate its utility alone, we provide the agent with only two additional tools during experiments:
read
/
write
/
insert
/
edit_build
to read and modify
build.py
, and
explore
to run a Python snippet with BrickLayer and the written
LegoBuild
in scope, returning its output as text.
4
Experiments
We compare BrickWright against two types of baselines: specially trained text-to-brick models (BrickGPT
[
37
]
and BrickNet
[
19
]
) and pre-trained agentic methods (Articraft
[
58
]
, OpenAI’s Codex, and Anthropic’s Claude Code). We evaluate the physical feasibility and prompt adherence of the output brick builds. Throughout evaluation, we use the BrickNet-512
[
19
]
dataset, which contains 512 text prompts created by VLM captioning of human-made brick builds.
Technical details.
To test agents with a range of capabilities, we run experiments with Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna (lightweight), GPT-6.1 Sol (balanced), and GPT-6 Astra (frontier). All agents use High reasoning. Figure examples use Astra unless otherwise specified. Agents are instructed to create builds with no collisions or floaters, and to ensure the build is connected if it comprises one object. Codex and Claude Code baselines may read, write, and execute arbitrary files in a workspace directory, which initially contains only the LDraw documentation
[
21
]
and the library of LDraw parts
[
22
]
, including part meshes. BrickWright agents are only allowed to read and modify the output
build.py
and execute text-output-only Python snippets; they have no access to the LDraw documentation or LDraw part library beyond the searchable parts list exposed by BrickLayer. Agentic methods have a budget of $5 per sample; for samples that reach the budget, we use the latest completed build, whether valid or invalid. Only Luna w/o assembly API (2 samples) and Astra with Codex (1 sample), Articraft (34 samples), and full BrickWright (2 samples) reached this limit.
As Articraft is intended for primitive-based 3D generation, we minimally modify it to use a library of LDraw part meshes rather than mesh primitives. Invalid operations on physical parts (e.g., scaling) are disabled, as are collision checks, which yield false positives for coupled bricks, and watertightness checks, which fail on library meshes. We adjust Articraft’s system prompt to reword phrases that do not work with brick builds, such as allowing geometry overlaps.
Metrics.
We report metrics on physical feasibility as defined in
Sec.
3
; prompt adherence as judged by VQAScore
[
28
]
, Perception Encoder
[
3
]
, and SigLIP 2
[
43
]
; average brick count per build; and average time and cost per prompt. Validity and connectivity are first evaluated using BrickLayer’s validator. Then, to independently verify the metrics’ accuracy, we flag potential false positives for review by a human experienced with LEGO
®
design. Potential false positives include collisions resolved by a tested shift of at most 0.2 mm and disconnected components containing parts without connector annotations. Human review increases collision-free rates by 0.2 percentage points for BrickNet and Claude Code (Haiku), 1.4 for Codex (Sol), and 1.0 for Codex (Astra). It reduces mean component counts by 0.13 for Codex (Sol), 0.10 for Codex (Astra), and 0.12 for Articraft; changes for the remaining methods are below 0.02 components per build. Numbers in
Tab.
1
are post-review.

4.1
Baseline comparison
Compared to vanilla agent baselines, builds produced by BrickWright-equipped agents exhibit greatly improved physical feasibility with broadly comparable token costs (
Tab.
1
). Impressively, the lightweight model Luna, which has only a 9% baseline validity rate, achieves 100% validity when used with BrickWright. This increase in physical validity is not accompanied by a significant decrease in complexity or fidelity; on average, BrickWright agents use more bricks and more unique parts than vanilla agent baselines, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight models (Haiku, Luna) and maintaining it for powerful models (Sol, Astra). These gains hold even with BrickWright’s minimal harness, whereas Codex and Claude Code can read, write, and execute arbitrary files. BrickWright-equipped agents additionally outperform specially trained text-to-brick models in overall feasibility and prompt adherence. The Articraft baseline, which is intended for digital 3D assets, yields comparable prompt adherence but worse physical validity at more than twice the cost of BrickWright. The visual results in
Fig.
6
show how BrickWright reduces physical artifacts for all agent backends and improves the coherence of builds created by lightweight agents. On average, most BrickWright agents use 2–3
validate
calls; Luna uses 4–5 (
Tab.
1
).
4.2
Ablation study
We ablate BrickLayer’s two key components: the assembly API and the validator. In our first ablation, “w/o assembly API”, agents write a program that creates an LDraw file without using BrickLayer’s assembly functions. The
LegoBuild
abstraction is removed from BrickLayer, leaving only part search and physical validation, and its documentation is replaced by LDraw documentation of similar length. In our second ablation, “w/o validator”, agents are still told to make their output physically valid but cannot use the
validate
and
render
tools or BrickLayer’s physical validation functions. They are allowed to run their own validations using
explore
. We run ablations using Haiku, Luna, and Sol; we exclude Astra due to budget constraints.
BrickLayer’s assembly API greatly reduces token usage and makes it easier to create valid builds; when forced to work in LDraw rather than using
LegoBuild
, agents spend around twice the token cost and three times as many
validate
calls (
Tab.
1
). Though stronger agents (Sol) still achieve 100% validity with no assembly API, weaker agents (Luna and Haiku) sometimes give up without finalizing the build, leading to validity scores below 100%. Without an assembly API, Luna’s prompt-similarity scores degrade significantly; it often produces simple structures (
Fig.
4
) and its average part count drops from 27.4 to 7.2. Interestingly, merely using BrickLayer’s API
without a provided validator
boosts validity by up to 44 percentage points from Codex/Claude Code baselines! The automatic grid-snapping and connector-mating functions provided by BrickLayer help agents, especially lightweight ones, produce valid builds more easily. However, the validator remains a crucial component; without it, all agents score below 79% validity (
Tab.
1
).
4.3
Extensions
BrickWright works with image conditions, indoor and outdoor scenes, large-scale builds of more than 29,000 parts, articulated objects, build editing by providing a BrickLayer script or LDraw file as input, and special requirements such as being constrained to a given set of bricks (
Fig.
5
). This functionality naturally arises from pre-trained agent capabilities, without needing to update BrickWright’s toolkit.
5
Discussion
Frontier coding agents are capable of producing aesthetically pleasing LEGO
®
brick builds from text or image prompts. However, even the most capable agents fail to produce physically feasible builds much of the time. Our framework, BrickWright, closes this gap by introducing a toolkit for brick build creation and validation. Equipped with BrickWright, even lightweight agents achieve 100% validity on 512 samples tested, while improving prompt adherence at a similar cost to agents without BrickWright. We hope this work highlights the importance of well-written construction APIs and physical validation in improving the performance of LLM agents on building tasks.
Limitations and future work.
Our definition of physical feasibility does not cover valid assembly sequences or stability analysis, which we leave to future work. Though agentic methods outperform specially trained models on brick build generation, they are generally slower and more costly. Effectively distilling the capabilities of powerful agents into smaller, faster models remains an interesting future direction.

Appendix D
Brick build generation with vanilla agents
We give a short analysis of the brick build creation process of baseline GPT-6 Astra, used with Codex. We inspect the Python programs produced and executed by the agent during generation (whether inline or from a file) and classify them as
generators
and/or
validators
by using heuristics that trace the program’s abstract syntax tree (AST). If a program calls
write_text()
or
write_bytes()
on a
model.ldr
file or
open
s the file in a mode with write access, we classify it as a generator. If a program reads
model.ldr
and includes an assertion or error involving values derived from
model.ldr
, we classify it as a validator. Out of 512 builds created using prompts from BrickNet-512, 471 (92%) use a generator and 424 (83%) use a validator.

article.headline: 积木装配工具包让 LLM 智能体告别悬空与穿模
article.lede: CMU 等提出 BrickWright：给 LLM 智能体一套积木装配工具包，512 条提示上物理可行率达 100%。
article.problem: 前沿编程智能体已能写出像样的 LEGO 模型代码，但生成的装配体经常出现零件穿模、悬空或互不相连，无法在真实世界拼装。作者认为这一瓶颈的根本原因是缺少装配用的工具，而不是模型能力不够。
article.method: 作者先构建 BrickLayer：一个 Python 积木工具包，包含可按连接器对接的装配 API（支持卡扣、铰链、球关节等）、零件检索和物理验证器，可检查碰撞、悬空与连通性；该 API 相比直接写 LDraw 可将推理成本减半。其上搭建 BrickWright 框架，让预训练 LLM 智能体在“规划—执行—验证”循环中反复编写与修改 build.py，调用 validate 和 render，直到通过固定检查与自写测试。
article.results: 在 BrickNet-512 的 512 条文本提示上，未加工具的智能体物理可行率从 9%（GPT-6 Luna）到 69%（GPT-6 Astra）不等，配备 BrickWright 后所有智能体（含 Haiku 5.5、Luna）均达到 100%，且强模型的提示一致性（VQAScore、PE、SigLIP 2）基本持平；轻量模型 Luna 的成功率从 9% 提升到 100%，成本约为前沿模型的 2%。消融显示：不用装配 API 时 token 花费约 2 倍、validate 调用约 3 倍，Luna 的平均零件数从 27.4 掉到 7.2；仅用 API 而无验证器，可行率最多提升 44 个百分点，但所有智能体都低于 79%。GPT-6.1 Sol 完整版有 81% 的构建在两次 validate 内通过，不用 API 时为 37%。成本上 Astra 完整版为每样本 $1.28（Codex 基线 $1.21），Articraft 为 $3.00。框架还支持图像条件、关节可动结构，以及超过 29,000 个零件的大规模场景。
article.why_it_matters: 这一结果表明，在需要满足物理约束的生成任务中，精心设计的构造 API 与可执行验证器，比单纯换用更强的模型更能带来性能提升；轻量模型也能借此以低得多的成本产出可用结果。这套“工具包加验证反馈”的模式可以迁移到其他多零件装配与 CAD 生成任务。
article.limitations: 论文对“物理可行”的定义只覆盖是否使用真实零件、有无碰撞与悬空、是否连通，不包含稳定性和可执行装配顺序，作者将这些检查留作后续工作。评测中的可行率由 BrickLayer 自身的验证器判定，作者虽对疑似误报做了人工复核，但仍属自评；且智能体方法比专用模型慢且贵（BrickNet 约 5 秒对完整版 143–267 秒）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 方法总览：(a) BrickLayer 提供零件检索、带类型连接器的组合式搭建与物理验证；(b) BrickWright 让预训练 LLM 智能体编写并修改含搭建代码与自写测试的 build.py，validate 执行固定的碰撞与悬空检查以及智能体自写测试，render 提供多视角渲染供目视检查，全部通过后调用 finalize。

figure.caption: {Method overview.} (a) BrickLayer supports catalog discovery, compositional construction with typed connectors, and physical validation. (b) BrickWright prompts a pre-trained LLM agent to write and revise {build.py}, which contains brick build creation code and agent-defined tests. The {validate} tool runs fixed collision and floating checks alongside the agent's tests, while the {render} tool provides views for visual inspection. The agent calls {finalize} once all checks pass. The agent may optionally run {explore} at any time to investigate the BrickLayer API and written brick build. Arrows summarize information flow rather than a fixed tool-call sequence.

Abstract
Energy-Based Models (EBMs) are a flexible class of generative models that decouple probabilistic modeling from the generation process. This decoupling directly enables compositional generation and inference-time scaling, where sample quality can be refined simply by increasing sampling steps. However, severe challenges in high-dimensional sampling and training instabilities with deep architectures have restricted EBMs to low-dimensional regimes. To resolve these bottlenecks, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), a scalable transformer energy function operating entirely within a latent space. On top of this backbone, we extract energies at multiple layers and sum them, composing complementary constraints from local texture to global semantics. Furthermore, two components make this high-quality at scale: Positive Representation Alignment (PRA), which supervises TEM’s intermediate representations with a vision foundation model, and advanced sampling strategies that improve sample quality at inference. TEM-XL achieves an FID-50K of 3.82 on class-conditional ImageNet 256
×
\times
256 without classifier-free guidance, showing that a contrastive EBM can generate high-fidelity images. On ImageNet 512
×
\times
512, TEM achieves an FID-50K of 8.24, demonstrating that the approach scales to higher resolution. We further validate the core promises of EBMs: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection.
1
Introduction
Energy-Based Models (EBMs)
[
23
,
11
]
parameterize probability distributions via an energy function that assigns lower energies to more probable samples and higher energies to less probable samples.
EBMs provide a flexible and mathematically elegant framework that fundamentally separates explicit generation from probabilistic modeling. Unlike Diffusion
[
18
,
38
]
and Flow
[
24
]
models, which are mathematically constrained to pre-defined generative trajectories governed by carefully designed timestep schedules, EBMs define the data distribution solely through an energy function, entirely decoupling the model from the generative process. This decoupling of the model from the generative process yields profound advantages. First, EBMs decouple learning from inference, allowing the sampling procedure to be chosen independently of model training. This enables flexible test-time compute scaling by increasing the MCMC steps, progressively refining the samples through a deeper exploration of the learned energy landscape. Second, this flexibility enables the composition of different distributions together
[
11
,
9
]
, which can enable zero-shot generation and generalization capabilities.
However, despite their theoretical advantages and compositional properties, EBMs have struggled with widespread adoption due to several critical unresolved challenges. First, EBMs face severe vulnerability to the curse of dimensionality: MCMC sampling suffers from poor mixing in high-dimensional spaces, leading to slow convergence and mode collapse. Second, EBMs scale poorly with model capacity. As network depth increases, conventional architectures exhibit severe training instability, making robust optimization exceedingly difficult
[
11
,
10
]
. Consequently, existing EBM research has been largely limited to smaller-scale benchmarks, unable to demonstrate competitive performance on challenging, high-resolution datasets.

trained contrastively, with negatives drawn from the model’s own MCMC
sampler, can generate high-quality

×

[
6

achieving performance competitive with strong generative models (Table

). We further validate the core theoretical promises of EBMs by demonstrating compositional generalization as well as flexible inference-time control. Our work addresses the long-standing scalability bottleneck of contrastive EBMs, reestablishing them as a viable contender for high-fidelity image generation.
Our key contributions are:
(1)
A scalable Vision Transformer-based EBM architecture with multiple energy heads that enables stable training at high resolution.
(2)
A comprehensive training framework encompassing latent space design, representation alignment, and advanced sampling strategies that together achieve state-of-the-art quality images for contrastive energy-based models.
(3)
Empirical validation of the theoretical advantages of energy-based
modeling at high resolution: compositional generation, zero-shot inpainting, and
out-of-distribution detection from a single scalar energy.

Energy-based models are naturally suited to composition, since combining distributions amounts to addition in energy space.

Inpainting.
Inpainting is particularly simple in energy-based models.
Our EBM defines a single energy over image latents,
allowing refinement from any intermediate completion.
We mask the input image before VAE encoding, preventing access to
ground-truth content in the missing region.
We then apply sampling updates to the missing latent region,
restoring the observed-region latents to their initial encoded
values after each step.

5
Related Work
Foundations of Energy-Based Models.
Energy-based models assign an unnormalized scalar energy to each input and define a Gibbs distribution over the data space, an idea with deep roots in statistical physics and undirected graphical models
[
17
,
23
]
.
Classical instantiations such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines relied on tractable architectures to make learning feasible, which in turn limited their representational capacity.
Du and Mordatch [11]
showed that short-run Langevin MCMC combined with a replay buffer yields a practical training loop, producing coherent samples on CIFAR-10.
Follow-up work refined the training recipe through improved MCMC initialization, sampler matching terms, and regularization strategies
[
10
,
30
,
29
]
, yet these methods operated at resolutions of 32
×
\times
32 or less diverse dataset, leaving the scalability of the paradigm unresolved.
Latent-Space Energy-Based Models.
Pang et al. [32]
proposed training an EBM as a prior over the latent codes of a variational autoencoder, while
Hill et al. [16]
explored energy-based priors for hierarchical latent variable models.
Nie et al. [28]
further demonstrated controllable generation by manipulating energies in a learned latent manifold.
VAEBM
[
46
]
combines a VAE with an EBM refinement in data space, reparameterizing the MCMC chain through the VAE’s latent space to make sampling practical at higher resolutions.
In contrast, we train a single scalar output Transformer energy function in the frozen latent space of a
pretrained autoencoder
[
35
]
, keeping the EBM as the sole generative
component.
Scaling Energy-Based Models.
Several recent efforts have pushed EBMs toward higher resolution and stronger performance, though each introduces auxiliary mechanisms that depart from the pure energy-based formulation. EGC
[
14
]
hybridizes energy-based learning with diffusion modeling and can produce 256
×
\times
256 ImageNet samples. However, its sampling procedure relies on the full diffusion denoising trajectory.
On the adversarial side,
Grathwohl et al. [13]
reinterpret classifier
logits as energies, and
Yin et al. [47]
scale this idea to ImageNet
256
×
\times
256. However, their sampler is initialized from an auxiliary image dataset at both training and inference, and is never seeded from noise at this scale.
Trained contrastively, TEM generates high-fidelity 256
×
\times
256 images, enabling
inference-time scaling and all EBM native applications. Appendix
G
provides an extended discussion of related work.
6
Limitations and Conclusion
Limitations.
TEM’s primary limitation is the computational cost of iterative sampling during both training and inference. One promising direction is to train a feed-forward proposal model to generate candidates in low-energy regions, reducing the sampling needed to refine them. Extended sampling also introduces a fidelity–diversity trade-off: longer trajectories sharpen images but can reduce diversity and worsen FID. Adaptive noise schedules and proposals that enable movement between distinct modes could help preserve diversity while improving sample quality.
Conclusion.
In this work, we introduce the Transformer Energy-Based Model (TEM), an approach that addresses long-standing scalability issues in contrastive training of energy-based models. With a modern transformer backbone, multi-layer energy extraction, and representation-aware training, we demonstrate that a contrastively trained EBM can synthesize high-fidelity ImageNet images at 256
×
\times
256 and 512
×
\times
512, competitive with other generative models. We also show that the properties that motivate energy-based modeling in the first place, compositional generation, inpainting, and out-of-distribution detection, remain available at this resolution. We hope this work serves as a starting point for further scaling of contrastively trained EBMs.

×

×

512, which is chosen as the threshold containing over
99.99
%

of ImageNet training latents, which stabilizes sampling. A smaller threshold clips real data points, while a larger one expands the region the sampler has to search, which slightly degrades performance.
For sampling, we use a step size of 500 and noise scale of 0.05. With a small step size, the network would have to produce very large input gradients to move samples meaningfully within a limited number of steps, and we found that this destabilizes training. With an excessively large step size, however, each update is coarse, and the model struggles to learn a fine-grained energy landscape. Following prior work
[
11
,
10
,
12

, who likewise decouple the step size from the noise scale and use a step size much larger than the standard Langevin prescription, we select the step size empirically to balance these two effects. During training, 40-step sampling is employed.
The replay buffer’s replay probability is set to 0.99 and capacity is 16000. Class labels are drawn independently for every chain, including chains initialized from the buffer. Buffer states therefore serve as class independent initializations near the data manifold, which the conditional energy refines toward the requested class. Once full, each newly added sample replaces a uniformly randomly selected buffer entry. article.headline: Transformer 能量模型实现高分辨率图像生
article.lede: MIT 等机构提出 TEM，在潜空间用 Transformer 参数化能量，ImageNet 256 无引导 FID 3
article.problem: 能量模型把概率建模与生成过程解耦，理论上支持组合生成，也支持靠增加采样步数在推理时扩展计算。但高维 MCMC 混合差和深层网络训练不稳定，长期把对比式能量模型限制在 CIFAR 级别的小规模、低分辨率场景。
article.method: TEM 用 ViT 作为能量函数，但完全工作在 Stable Diffusion VAE 的冻结潜空间中，并采用旋转位置编码、query-key 归一化与 AdaLN 条件注入。模型在多个中间层接出能量头并把各自的标量能量相加，使早期层管局部纹理、深层管全局语义。训练使用对比能量目标加采样匹配损失，并提出 Positive Representation Alignment，只用数据正样本把内部特征对齐到冻结的 DINOv2-large，MCMC 负样本不参与对齐。
article.results: TEM-XL（609M）在 ImageNet 256×256 上不用 classifier-free guidance，60 步采样取得 FID-50K 3.82，TEM-L 为 4.74；512×512 上 FID-50K 为 8.24。TEM-B 的消融显示，PRA 把 50K 步的 FID 从无对齐的 42.8 降到 19.9，而同时对齐正负样本只到 36.6；三个能量头为 19.86，优于单头 20.95 与双头 20.50。四个 OOD 基准平均 AUROC 为 0.717（DiT 0.598、SiT 0.573、SiT+REPA 0.549）；CLEVR 256×256 组合生成中 1/2/3 物体检测成功率为 0.956/0.766/0.274，Composable Diffusion 为 0.863/0.598/0.262。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明只靠自身 MCMC 负样本、不依赖扩散轨迹或辅助图像初始化的纯对比式能量模型，也能扩展到 ImageNet 256×256 和 512×512 的高保真生成；同时，组合生成、零样本 inpainting、OOD 检测这些能量模型原生能力在该分辨率下依然可用。
article.limitations: 训练和推理都需要迭代采样，计算成本是主要瓶颈：论文报告训练 TEM-XL 50K 步约需 4 张 H200 跑 6 天，512×512 的训练与推理耗时再增 3–4 倍。推理时延长采样还有保真度—多样性权衡：步数从 40 增到 80，FID 先从 7.63 降到 60 步的 3.82 再回升到 4.72，IS 从 106.0 升到 221.1，而 recall 从 0.65 降到 0.51。
article.figure_caption_zh: TEM 架构与训练策略：左侧 Transformer 能量模型处理 VAE 编码的潜变量 token，多层能量头输出标量能量并求和；右侧对比训练压低数据样本 x⁺ 的能量、抬高 MCMC 负样本 x⁻ 的能量，同时用 PRA 把内部特征对齐到冻结的视觉基础模型。

figure.caption: {Proposed Architecture and Training Strategy.} {Left}: the Transformer Energy-Based Model processes VAE-encoded latent tokens through a stack of TEM blocks. Energy heads at multiple intermediate layers produce scalar energies whose sum defines the total energy. {Right}: contrastive training pushes down the energy of data samples~$x^+$ and pushes up the energy of MCMC negatives~$x^-$, while Positive Representation Alignment (PRA) aligns the model's internal features with a frozen VFM.

page_papers.title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
page_papers.abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker
page_papers.content:
Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
Zijian Liu
Chaoyou Fu
Yan Yang
Caifeng Shan
and Ran He
†
†
thanks:
Zijian Liu, Chaoyou Fu, Yan Yang, and Caifeng Shan are with the School of
Intelligence Science and Technology, Nanjing University, Suzhou 215163, China.
†
†
thanks:
Ran He is with the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing
100049, China.
†
†
thanks:
Corresponding author: Chaoyou Fu (E-mail: bradyfu24@gmail.com).
Abstract
Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations.
To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing.
Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views.
It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states.
Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding.
Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP.
Using
Qwen2.5-Omni-7B
as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67–2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks.
Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to
VideoLLaMA2-AV
, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at
https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker
Index Terms:
Audio-visual hallucination, cross-modal conflict, frozen backbone intervention, omni-modal large language models, representation editing, training-free inference.
I
Introduction
Fig. 1:
Comparison of omni-modal hallucination mitigation paradigms.
(a)
Existing output-level methods correct hallucinations after multimodal fusion. They lack direct control over the evidence-prior interactions already encoded in the fused representations.
(b)
Omni-Woodpecker (OWP) diagnoses conflicts using complementary evidence views.
It orthogonally separates grounding evidence from competing priors, and adaptively restores their balance within the fused representations before decoding.
Omni LLMs (OLLMs) extend LLMs beyond text by jointly processing language, vision, and audio
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
, enabling models to reason across complex environments. However, it introduces a reliability challenge: when different modalities provide incomplete or conflicting cues, the model struggles to appropriately balance grounding evidence against learned priors, and omni-modal hallucinations typically emerge when this balancing process fails.
As shown in Fig.
1
a, when asked “Is the dog barking?”, the model actually encodes the evidence of silence in the audio. However, a strong visual prior (seeing a dog) overpowers this audio evidence during multimodal fusion. This shows that the model does not fail to perceive the inputs. Instead, competing cross-modal cues suppress the target evidence. This critical observation drives our core hypothesis: omni-modal hallucination is not a failure of evidence encoding, but rather an issue of representation entanglement, where evidence and priors are severely imbalanced during fusion.
Current mitigation methods primarily rely on contrastive decoding
[
4
,
5
]
, modality-adaptive generation
[
6
]
, or preference optimization
[
7
,
8
]
. As illustrated in Fig.
1
a, these methods treat hallucinations as output-level anomalies. They align cross-modal cues by calibrating final decoding distributions or optimizing response preferences. However, whether applied during training or inference, they inherently operate at the output level. In early-fusion OLLMs, grounding evidence and learned priors become deeply entangled long before decoding starts. Because these methods merely manipulate the final answer without controlling internal representations, they struggle to repair the corrupted hidden states that actually cause the hallucination, leaving the underlying conflict between grounding evidence and learned priors unresolved.
To address this issue, we propose
Omni-Woodpecker (OWP)
, a training-free framework that shifts output-level hallucination mitigation to representation-level rebalancing, without modifying model parameters or the language head. As illustrated in Fig.
2
, OWP follows a three-stage pipeline. It first identifies cross-modal conflicts and determines the target evidence together with its competing source from complementary modality-specific views. OWP then separates grounding evidence from competing priors to derive representation edits that preserve faithful evidence while removing misleading interference. Finally, it adaptively rebalances the fused representations according to the detected conflict, restoring suppressed evidence and attenuating deceptive priors before decoding.
Beyond introducing a new intervention pipeline, OWP relies on a fundamental principle: hallucinations should be corrected where they originate instead of where they appear. Rather than modifying the final decoding distribution, OWP explicitly identifies cross-modal conflicts and restores the balance between grounding evidence and learned priors directly in the hidden representation (
i.e.
, restoring suppressed evidence while selectively attenuating misleading priors). As a result, the fused representation is rebalanced before decoding, leading to more reliable, evidence-driven reasoning.
In summary, our main contributions are:
•
Evidence-Prior Rebalancing Formulation.
We reformulate omni-modal hallucination as an internal imbalance between grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations, revealing that hallucinations arise from representation entanglement rather than perception failure. This shifts the mitigation focus from output-level manipulation to representation-level repair.
•
Conflict-Conditioned Representation Rebalancing.
We propose OWP, a training-free framework that diagnoses query-conditioned cross-modal conflicts and selectively rebalances fused multimodal representations through evidence-preserving interventions, restoring suppressed evidence and attenuating misleading priors without modifying any model parameter.
•
Extensive Experimental Validation.
Experiments on CMM and AVHBench show that OWP outperforms the strongest baseline by
4.9
and
7.7
points and improves the original OLLMs by up to
12.9
points on hallucination-centric metrics. OWP further generalizes across different OLLM architectures and consistently improves performance on diverse omni-modal reasoning benchmarks.
Section II reviews related work, Section III presents OWP, Section IV
reports experiments and analyses, Section V covers limitations and future
work, and Section VI concludes.
II
Related Work
II-A
Omni-Modal Models and Cross-Modal Hallucination
OLLMs connect acoustic and visual encoders
[
9
,
10
]
to a language
model. They build on audio-visual interfaces
[
11
,
12
]
and
any-to-any architectures
[
13
,
14
,
15
]
. They support
video understanding
[
16
,
17
,
18
]
, spoken
interaction
[
19
,
20
]
, and cross-modal
reasoning
[
21
,
1
,
2
,
3
,
22
]
. Early
fusion enables joint reasoning, but it also lets an irrelevant sound, image, or
language prior override the evidence that a query needs. CMM describes these
failures as language, visual, and audio dominance and as spurious cross-modal
correlations. AVHBench tests audio-driven visual hallucination, visual-driven
audio hallucination, and audio-visual matching
[
23
,
24
]
. The frozen
model often answers correctly from the query-relevant stream alone, even when
the fused input follows a competing cue (Table
V
).
This motivates edits that keep the encoded evidence rather than replace the
output.
II-B
Output-Level Hallucination Mitigation
Hallucination in vision–language models was first measured with
caption-based and object-probing benchmarks
[
25
,
26
]
. Later
diagnostic suites also cover mixed language–visual failures
[
27
,
28
]
.
One line of work treats hallucination as an error in the output distribution
and corrects it without touching the fused representation. Contrastive decoding
penalizes tokens that stay likely when the perceptual input is degraded. VCD
contrasts original and distorted visual inputs
[
4
]
. OPERA adds an
over-trust penalty and reallocates attention in hindsight
[
29
]
. DoLa
improves factuality by contrasting logits from different layers
[
30
]
.
Other variants contrast against perturbed instructions, visual grounding
states, or the model’s own signals
[
31
,
32
,
33
]
. For audio-visual
models, AVCD estimates which of the three modalities dominates and contrasts
masked and full inputs
[
5

video, or both, and weights its contrastive branches
accordingly
[
6
]

unsupported content after generation
[
34
]
. A second line changes
the model itself. Factually augmented RLHF and AI feedback improve grounding in
vision–language models
[
35
,
36

. OmniDPO and MoD-DPO use
preference learning for perceptual alignment and for robustness to irrelevant
modalities
[
7
,
8
]
. Both lines act on the decoding distribution
or on the model weights. In early-fusion OLLMs, however, evidence and priors
are already mixed before decoding starts. Neither line controls the
interaction that causes the error, and neither identifies which stream
competes with a given query.
II-C
Representation-Level Intervention
A more recent line edits internal activations directly. Model-editing methods
locate and change factual associations inside the model
[
37
,
38
]
, and
activation steering shifts behavior along chosen directions
[
39
]
.
Inference-time intervention finds truth-related directions and shifts
activations along them during generation
[
40
]
. Representation
engineering derives such directions from contrasting prompt
sets
[
41
]
. Contrastive activation addition steers a model with the
difference between two contrasting behaviors
[
42
]
.
HulluEdit
applies this idea to visual hallucination. It separates visual evidence from an
orthogonal anti-prior subspace and edits the residual state in one
pass
[
43
]
. These studies show that the factors behind
hallucination can be reached in the representation, not only in the output.
However, they assume a fixed split, usually perceptual evidence against a
language prior, and apply one direction to every input. Query-conditioned
methods such as MAD, in turn, use modality relevance only to weight output
branches. OWP instead finds, for each input, the stream that the query needs
and the stream that competes with it. It builds the edit directions from these
two streams and splits one correction budget between attention paths and the
residual state according to the diagnosed conflict.
III
Method
Fig. 2:
Overview of Omni-Woodpecker (OWP). Given a query and an audio-visual input, OWP runs four views of a frozen model to find the target modality and the competing cue. It then splits token–head responses into protected evidence, competing prior, and unchanged context. Finally, it divides one correction budget between path reweighting and residual-state restoration and writes the edited state back to the same layer. Valid context is kept, and the cue that causes the hallucination is suppressed.

Conflict-adaptive representation rebalancing
then splits one

according to the diagnosed conflict.

Runtime order and decoding
The subscripts
R
\mathrm{R}
and
P
\mathrm{P}
denote the residual branch and the
token–head path branch, not transformer layers. OWP runs only when a conflict
appears. It first runs the full view and the target view on the frozen model.
If their answers agree, there is no conflict, and OWP returns the backbone
answer. Otherwise, the non-target and text-only views give the competing
source, the edit directions, and the allocation weight, without choosing any
output token. For an identified conflict, one edited full-view pass follows.
At each selected layer, the path branch reweights token–head routes before
aggregation. The residual branch suppresses the orthogonal prior, restores the
measured deficit, and writes the result back to the same layer. This schedule
gives the same outputs as running all four views on every input. The language
head and the decoding rule are unchanged. Quantitative evaluation scores the
answer-option tokens with a finite-answer probe, and qualitative examples use
the frozen model’s own autoregressive decoder.
