Bidirectional correction
OWP improved both conflict directions and all three dominance types. It
reached 86.0% and 90.2% under CMM visual and audio dominance, and 84.9% and
85.3% on the two AVHBench directions. It also improved language dominance,
where the competing cue is the query text rather than another sensory stream
(81.3% to 82.0%). On CMM overall, OWP raised hallucination resistance (HR)
from 57.0% to 85.5% with perception accuracy (PA) at 86.7%. This reduced the
backbone’s 32.5-point gap between PA and HR to 1.2 points, whereas MAD kept a
16.9-point gap (89.7% PA, 72.8% HR). OWP thus brings perception and
hallucination resistance into near balance.
Joint audio-visual evidence
OWP kept the evidence of both streams on AV Matching, which asks whether the
audio and the video belong together. Because this task has no single target
stream, OWP treats the joint audio-visual input as the evidence source and the
text-only view as the competing prior. It builds the evidence direction from
counterfactual inputs in which the audio or the video is replaced by another
clip. OWP reached 81.1%, exceeding the backbone, MAD, and AVCD by 6.6, 13.1,
and 17.9 points. AVCD showed the opposite trade-off, with 81.2% average
directional accuracy but only 63.2% on AV Matching. OWP combined 84.9% and
85.3% directional accuracy with 81.1% matching accuracy.

The decomposition transferred to a backbone with a different audio-visual
fusion design. On
VideoLLaMA2-AV
, OWP raised CMM accuracy from 76.2% to
80.8% and AVHBench accuracy from 70.2% to 74.1%, the best overall results in
that group. It also raised HR from 65.3% to 77.7% and AV Matching from 56.6%
to 62.2%. Moreover, OWP on
Qwen2.5-Omni-7B
exceeded the newer
Qwen3-Omni under the same protocol by 4.3 and 6.2 points on CMM and AVHBench,
without any training.

The two components acted at different depths

V
Limitations and Future Work
V-A
Limitations
OWP has four limitations that follow from its scope and design. First,
omni-modal hallucination covers several types of failure, and this paper
focuses on cross-modal hallucination, where the evidence from one modality is
overridden by a cue from another modality or from the language prior. CMM and
AVHBench are built around this failure, and OWP’s diagnosis is designed for it.
Second, OWP restores evidence that the backbone encodes but fails to use during
fusion. It reads this evidence from the single-stream views of the frozen
model, so it does not add perception that the backbone lacks: when the target
modality is misperceived even on its own, there is no reliable evidence to
restore. Third, OWP edits hidden states and attention outputs, so it requires
access to model internals. Like other representation-level
methods
[
40
,
43
]
, it applies to open-weight OLLMs but not to models
that are available only through an API. Fourth, like other inference-time
methods that contrast several input views
[
5
,
6
]
, OWP requires extra
forward passes. Its conflict-triggered schedule keeps this cost at
1.71
1.71
–
1.77
×
1.77\times
the backbone latency, lower than that of MAD on both
backbones.
V-B
Future Work
The principle of OWP, which diagnoses the stream that a query needs and
rebalances evidence and priors inside the fused representation, extends
naturally to other classes of omni-modal hallucination. For temporal
hallucination, where a model misreports the order, duration, or synchrony of
audio-visual events, the diagnosis would locate when each stream provides
evidence and compare event timing across streams. For acoustic and
paralinguistic hallucination, where a model misattributes speaker identity,
emotion, prosody, or non-speech sounds, the diagnosis would separate spoken
content from acoustic attributes within the audio stream. Because OWP leaves
the weights unchanged, it can also be combined directly with training-based
methods. More broadly, our results show that cross-modal hallucination comes
from how evidence and priors interact inside the fused representation, and
correcting this internal evidence flow is a direct path toward reliable
omni-modal reasoning.
VI
Conclusion
This paper presented Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that
corrects cross-modal hallucination in OLLMs by rebalancing evidence and priors
inside the fused representation. OWP diagnoses the target and competing
streams from four views of a frozen model, separates an evidence direction from
an orthogonal prior direction, and splits one correction budget between
attention paths and the residual state. With
Qwen2.5-Omni-7B
, OWP
improved accuracy by 12.9 points on CMM and 8.6 points on AVHBench, raised CMM
hallucination resistance from 57.0% to 85.5% with perception accuracy at
86.7%, and reached 81.1% on AV Matching. It also exceeded the newer Qwen3-Omni by
4.3 and 6.2 points on the two benchmarks, and its edits made the answer follow
the queried modality, with a 41.0-point selectivity gap under stream
corruption. It transferred to
VideoLLaMA2-AV
and improved all four general omni-modal reasoning
benchmarks by up to 2.25 points. Ablations and mechanism analyses showed that
prior suppression and evidence restoration are complementary, that the residual
state is the main site of correction, and that evidence is best restored in
middle layers and priors are best suppressed in later layers. Correcting
hallucination where it forms, inside the fused representation, is thus a
practical path toward reliable omni-modal reasoning without retraining.

article.headline: OWP：在融合表示中重平衡证据与先验
article.lede: 南京大学等提出免训练框架 OWP，用四视图诊断跨模态冲突，在融合表示中抑制竞争先验、恢复被压制的证据，再解码。
article.problem: 全模态大模型在音视频联合推理中常出现跨模态幻觉；已有方法多在输出端校正解码分布或偏好。但早融合模型中，真实证据与学习先验在解码前已深度纠缠，输出层操作难以修复受损的隐状态。
article.method: OWP 是免训练框架：先用完整、音频、视频、纯文本四个视图诊断查询所需的目标模态与竞争来源；再用正交分解把隐藏状态拆成证据方向、正交冲突方向和证据亏空。最后按冲突强度把同一校正预算分配给注意力路径与残差状态，在解码前抑制误导先验并恢复被忽略证据，不改模型参数。
article.results: 在 Qwen2.5-Omni-7B 上，OWP 将 CMM 准确率提升 12.9 个百分点、AVHBench 提升 8.6 个百分点，并比最强基线 MAD 分别高 4.9 和 7.7 个百分点。CMM 幻觉抵抗率从 57.0% 升至 85.5%，感知准确率为 86.7%；在 VideoLLaMA2-AV 上两项基准分别提升 4.6 和 3.9 个百分点。四个通用全模态推理基准也提升 0.67–2.25 个百分点，推理延迟为骨干的 1.71–1.77 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 它把幻觉缓解从输出端拉回融合表示，说明不重训练、不改语言头也能通过推理时表示编辑提升可靠性。对开源权重全模态模型，这是一条低训练成本的部署路径。
article.limitations: 方法只针对跨模态幻觉，且只能恢复骨干模型已编码但未使用的证据；若目标模态本身被误感知，就没有可靠证据可恢复。它需要访问模型内部，不能用于仅提供 API 的模型，并带来 1.71–1.77 倍骨干延迟。
article.figure_caption_zh: OWP 概览：给定查询和音视频输入，它用冻结模型的四个视图定位目标模态与竞争线索，将 token–head 响应分为受保护证据、竞争先验与不变上下文，再把同一校正预算分配给路径重加权和残差状态恢复，并将编辑写回同一层。

figure.caption: Overview of Omni-Woodpecker (OWP). Given a query and an audio-visual input, OWP runs four views of a frozen model to find the target modality and the competing cue. It then splits token--head responses into protected evidence, competing prior, and unchanged context. Finally, it divides one correction budget between path reweighting and residual-state restoration and writes the edited state back to the same layer. Valid context is kept, and the cue that causes the hallucination is suppressed.

page_papers.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
page_papers.abstract: Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions. Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users' behavioral responses over long interactions. Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results. We introduce UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types. UserArena pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts. Experiments show that OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's evaluation protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.

UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
Jujia Zhao
Jiakai Tang

Abstract
Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions.
Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users’ behavioral responses over long interactions.
Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results.
We introduce
UserArena
, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types.
UserArena
pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes.
To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose
O

OPTD
), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts.

Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in language and multimodal agents create new opportunities for agentic recommendation, in which an agent pursues a shopper’s goal through a sequence of context-dependent decisions
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Shang et al., 2025
)
.
Post-training and evaluation of the underlying recommendation policy require a scalable
recommendation world model
that simulates how the shopping environment and its users respond to each policy action
(
Ie et al., 2019
)
.
An executable environment models what the policy can observe and change, while a user simulator models how shoppers respond to those changes
(
Yao et al., 2022
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2024
)
.
Together, they support offline and counterfactual evaluation as well as reinforcement-learning-based optimization, reducing reliance on costly online experiments
(
Shi et al., 2019
;
Zhao et al., 2023
)
.
Figure 1:
Overview of
UserArena
.
Left:
cross-session histories, step-aligned interaction records, production A/B validation, and dataset scale.
Right:
the five-level evaluation protocol, progressing from environment compliance (L0) to outcome fidelity (L4).
Existing resources provide rich behavioral data and interactive evaluation for such world models.
Amazon Reviews
(
Hou et al., 2026
)
contains ratings and review text, Qilin
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
adds multimodal content and app-level sessions, and OmniBehavior
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
captures longitudinal traces.
RecBench+
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
and OPeRA
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
move from offline records toward interactive evaluation.
Yet two crucial gaps remain:
At the data level,
existing datasets rarely provide long-horizon trajectories that align real-user profiles, visual observations, product context, and actions across repeated sessions.
At the evaluation level,
next-action agreement measures step-wise choices in isolation but does not assess whether simulated trajectories preserve a user’s behavioral tendencies over long horizons.
Existing benchmarks also rarely test whether simulator-based policy comparisons agree with production A/B outcomes.
These gaps limit assessment of long-horizon behavioral fidelity and the real-world validity of simulation conclusions.
To address these limitations, we introduce
UserArena
, an interactive benchmark combining a production-grounded shopping environment with real-user trajectories recorded on one of Asia’s largest e-commerce platforms (Figure
).
It contains real-user data comprising
11,010 users, 566,102 items, and 64,729 session trajectories
and covers a complete action space of 13 action types.
Each trajectory aligns user profiles, visual observations, product context, and actions at every step.
For long-horizon evaluation,
UserArena
links sessions from the same user into cross-session trajectories.
It also supports offline validation by comparing the same recommendation-policy pair in simulation with outcomes from a controlled production A/B test.
We evaluate simulators at five levels: output validity (
L0
), local behavioral fidelity (
L1
), sequential behavioral fidelity (
L2
), personalization fidelity (
L3
), and outcome fidelity (
L4
).
The protocol traces fidelity from output validity and local decisions to long-horizon behavior, personalization, and aggregate outcomes.
Beyond constructing the benchmark, we also address the challenge of learning faithful user simulators.
Simulator design has progressed from hand-crafted and log-driven models to LLM-based models
(
Ie et al., 2019
;
Shi et al., 2019
;
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2024
)
, yet reproducing user behavior over long rollouts remains difficult for three reasons.
(i) Behavioral miscalibration:
learned simulators can deviate from real user behavior
(
Zhang et al., 2024
;
Yoon et al., 2024
)
.
(ii) Sparse supervision:
exact next-action targets penalize plausible alternatives and overlook trajectory-level quality
(
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
.
(iii) Exposure bias:
teacher forcing conditions only on ground-truth prefixes, creating a mismatch with autoregressive inference
(
Dai et al., 2021
;
Chi et al., 2022
)
.
To address these challenges, we propose
O
n-
P
olicy
T
rajectory
D
istillation (
OPTD
), which distills teacher guidance on current-policy responses at real states
(
Agarwal et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
.
This on-policy supervision trains on student-generated prefixes, while trajectory-level intent guides teacher targets toward coherent long-horizon behavior.
In summary, our contributions are threefold.
(1) We introduce
UserArena
, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark pairing long-horizon user trajectories with an interactive environment and a five-level protocol spanning environment compliance, local decisions, sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes.
(2) We propose OPTD, which uses trajectory-level intent and dense teacher targets to guide student-generated rollouts toward coherent long-horizon behavior.
(3) We benchmark representative text- and GUI-based simulators for effectiveness and efficiency and characterize
UserArena
’s behavioral composition and interaction horizons.
2
The
UserArena
Benchmark
2.1
Data and Interaction Design
A credible e-commerce interactive benchmark requires a production-grounded environment that preserves what shoppers can observe and do.
Beyond this environmental foundation, two requirements are essential.
First, the benchmark should use fine-grained real-user trajectories that align user profiles, visual observations, product context, and actions while capturing behavior over long horizons.
Second, its evaluation should go beyond next-action agreement to assess complete trajectories and whether simulator-based policy comparisons agree with real-user outcomes in production.
Existing resources cover these requirements partially.
E-commerce datasets contain real preferences and interaction logs but rarely retain the visual context of each decision
(
Harper and Konstan, 2015
;
Hou et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
.
Interactive platforms enable closed-loop evaluation but depend on user dynamics whose fidelity remains insufficiently established
(
Ie et al., 2019
;
Shi et al., 2019
;
Zhao et al., 2023
)
.
Recent benchmarks improve behavioral grounding through visual shopping traces or longitudinal records
(
Wang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Tang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, yet none combines real step-level trajectories, visual context, a full shopping action space, long-horizon cross-session behavior, and production A/B validation (Table
).

Long-Horizon denotes temporally ordered user histories spanning multiple sessions. Production A/B Validation evaluates recommendation policies offline in simulation and compares their effects with outcomes observed in production A/B tests.

To bridge this gap,
UserArena
combines a production-grounded shopping environment, fine-grained real-user trajectories, and an evaluation protocol spanning trajectory fidelity and production validation.
The environment reconstructs production recommendation-feed and item-detail pages with 13 action types, from feed navigation and product inspection to add-to-cart and purchase.
It updates the visible feed by cropping the corresponding viewport from the pre-rendered full feed as the simulator scrolls.
Clicking any currently exposed item, including one not clicked by the real user, opens an interactive detail page reconstructed from that item’s pre-rendered views and recorded product content.
Following the observation–action formulation of interactive agents
(
Yao et al., 2022
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, each recorded decision aligns the shopper’s profile, visual observation, visible product context, and action.
The benchmark contains
11,010 users, 64,729 sessions, 577,670 actions, and 566,102 products
and 6 user attributes.
Across these trajectories, 73,717 item clicks span 41 product categories (Appendix Figure
).
For long-horizon evaluation,
UserArena
organizes 59,378 chronologically ordered sessions from 5,768 users into cross-session trajectories.
They average 10.29 sessions and 86.36 actions per user, testing whether simulators preserve preferences and behavioral tendencies across repeated visits.
Appendix Table
compares their interaction horizons with related benchmarks.
For production A/B validation,
UserArena
compares the same recommendation-policy pair offline in simulation with controlled production A/B outcomes.
2.2
Evaluation Protocol
As illustrated on the right side of Figure
,
UserArena
evaluates simulator fidelity at five levels of increasing scope: from whether its outputs can be parsed to whether its trajectories, personalized behavior, and session outcomes match those of real users.
We use two evaluation modes.
(1)
Replay
uses the recorded state at each step of a real session to predict the logged next action.
This isolates local next-action fidelity without accumulating simulator-induced state changes.
(2)
Rollout
lets the simulator select actions and determine subsequent states until the session ends.
It tests whether free-running simulated sessions reproduce real trajectories and aggregate outcomes.
We evaluate L0 under both modes, L1 under Replay, and L2–L4 under Rollout.
Appendix
provides the complete definitions and computation rules.
⚫
L0: Environment Compliance
asks whether the environment can parse the simulator’s outputs.
We report valid-action rates under Replay (RVA) and Rollout (OVA), which require each output to parse as an action executable in the current state.
⚫
L1: Local Behavioral Fidelity
asks whether the simulator and real user make the same next decision from the same state.
F1 measures action-type agreement, whereas accuracy also requires the target item or comment to match when applicable.
⚫
L2: Sequential Behavioral Fidelity
asks whether a free-running simulator produces realistic long-horizon dynamics.
Decision-mix Jensen–Shannon divergence (DM-JSD) compares next-decision distributions after item-page visits, capturing whether simulated and real users follow the same item-level decision patterns.
Trajectory error (TE) compares mean action count per session.
⚫
L3: Personalized Population Fidelity
asks whether the simulator reproduces behavioral heterogeneity associated with users’ interaction histories.
Population fidelity (PF) groups users by historical activity, purchase propensity, and category breadth, then compares simulated and real behavior within each group across session dynamics, action patterns, and product preferences.
⚫
L4: Outcome Fidelity
asks whether the simulator reproduces aggregate behavioral and terminal outcomes.
Count-based click-through rate error (
Δ
\Delta
CTR) compares clicks per executed feed action, count-based add-to-cart rate error (
Δ
\Delta
ACR) compares add-to-cart actions per click, and terminal-state JSD (T-JSD) compares the distributions of final session outcomes.
3
On-Policy Trajectory Distillation
Figure 2:

OPTD extracts a trajectory-level intent from each complete training trajectory and provides it as privileged context to a frozen teacher.
The intent conditions dense token-level teacher supervision throughout each student response.
A per-token trust region limits how far these targets depart from predictions based only on the student’s observable state.

The single-session block of Table

5
Related Work
Interactive recommendation benchmarks.
Recommendation benchmarks have evolved from static preference records toward richer behavioral data and interactive evaluation. MovieLens
(
Harper and Konstan, 2015
)
records movie ratings, Amazon Reviews
(
Hou et al., 2026
)
pairs product ratings with review text, Qilin
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
adds multimodal app-level sessions, and RL4RS
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
provides real-world sequential interactions. Agent-oriented benchmarks further broaden the task interface: RecBench+
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
evaluates personalized recommendation through natural-language requests, AgentRecBench
(
Shang et al., 2025
)
introduces interactive recommendation scenarios, and OPeRA
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
and OmniBehavior
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
provide richer evidence for human behavior simulation. Simulation platforms such as RecSim
(
Ie et al., 2019
)
, Virtual-Taobao
(
Shi et al., 2019
)
, and KuaiSim
(
Zhao et al., 2023
)
further support interactive evaluation across temporal scales. Yet existing resources rarely record, throughout long-horizon sessions, what real users see and how they act, or test whether simulator-based comparisons reproduce policy effects observed in production A/B tests. UserArena provides both forms of evidence through step-aligned real-world shopping trajectories and offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test.
User simulator development.
Early systems represented users through configurable or parameterized dynamics, including RecSim
(
Ie et al., 2019
)
, RecoGym
(
Rohde et al., 2018
)
, and the probabilistic RecSim NG framework
(
Mladenov et al., 2021
)
. Log-driven approaches then learned interaction dynamics from observed behavior: Virtual-Taobao
(
Shi et al., 2019
)
combines generative customer modeling with adversarial imitation, while the Generative Adversarial User Model
(
Chen et al., 2019
)
learns user dynamics and rewards for model-based policy training. IRecGAN
(
Bai et al., 2019
)
incorporates generated trajectories into adversarial user-model learning. More recent LLM-based simulators, including RecAgent
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
, Agent4Rec
(
Zhang et al., 2024
)
, and SUBER
(
Corecco et al., 2024
)
, increase the expressiveness of profile-conditioned behavior, while Customer-R1
(
Wang et al., 2025c
)
, Shop-R1
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
, and RecVerse
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
apply reinforcement learning to shopping simulation. Despite this progress, two optimization challenges remain.
(1) Sparse rewards:
most methods use exact-match rewards, treating plausible alternatives and invalid behaviors alike.
(2) Exposure bias:
teacher forcing trains only on ground-truth prefixes, leaving models unprepared for self-generated prefixes and vulnerable to compounding errors at inference. OPTD addresses both through dense distributional supervision on student-sampled responses and trajectory-level intent for long-horizon behavioral guidance.
6
Conclusion
We introduced
UserArena
, an interactive benchmark combining a production-grounded shopping environment with fine-grained, long-horizon real-user trajectories.
We also developed a five-level protocol that evaluates simulator quality from environment compliance and local decisions to sequential, personalized population, and outcome fidelity.
For this long-horizon setting, we proposed On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to guide dense teacher supervision on the student’s own rollouts.
OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity under this protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in the controlled comparison.
As future work we will develop a leaderboard platform around
UserArena
to support standardized and continuously updated evaluation of user simulators.
We will investigate stronger long-horizon simulators that preserve evolving preferences and behavioral consistency across sessions.

Product metadata contain only product titles and English top-level category labels. We removed information that could directly identify users and replaced production identifiers with non-linkable sequential identifiers.
The released interface images contain no GUI screenshots captured from real users.
We reconstruct the two-column feed and item-detail pages in an offline React environment using the de-identified sessions and item pools, and then batch-render the resulting interfaces.
The dataset is released for non-commercial research under a data use agreement.
The agreement prohibits attempts to re-identify users, linkage with external personal data, and unauthorized redistribution.

Dataset and Behavior Statistics
We provide additional analyses of
UserArena
’s behavioral composition, interaction horizons, and coverage.
Action and item composition.
Figure
(a) reports the proportion of every action type in
UserArena
.
Feed-page downward scrolling is the most frequent action at 38.34%, followed by item clicks at 12.76%, session termination at 11.21%, returns to the feed at 10.62%, and item-page downward scrolling at 10.08%.
Add-to-cart and purchase actions account for 3.90% and 1.02% of decisions, respectively.
This imbalance supports using macro-averaged local metrics and distributional trajectory metrics rather than allowing frequent navigation actions to dominate evaluation.
Figure
(b) shows that the 73,717 item clicks span 41 product categories.
Apparel accounts for 54.90% of clicks, while the remaining 45.10% covers 40 categories, including jewelry, bags, daily goods, food, cookware, beauty, furniture, electronics, and home textiles.

Figure
(a) shows that individual sessions contain a median of 14 actions in the single-session setting and 8 actions in the cross-session setting.
Cross-session user trajectories become substantially longer by linking repeated visits: each user contributes 4–15 chronologically ordered sessions, with 10.29 sessions and 86.36 actions on average (Figure

Figure
(c) shows that availability across the six user-profile fields ranges from 99.0% to 99.9%, while 92.0% of the 67,267 clicked items appear only once.

Behavioral paths.
Figure
(d) aggregates adjacent actions into six semantic groups and reports row-normalized transition probabilities.
The resulting paths expose repeated feed navigation, item exploration after item clicks, and returns to the feed after item-page decisions.
These transitions capture multi-step shopping processes that cannot be represented by isolated action frequencies.
Cross-session continuity.
The cross-session subset yields 53,610 adjacent session pairs from the same users.
As shown in Figure
(e), successive sessions span intervals from minutes to more than 12 hours, and 57.8% revisit a product category present in the preceding session.
The benchmark therefore captures both rapid returns and longer-term revisits while preserving each user’s chronological session order.

Appendix B
Experiment Setup Details
B.1
Baseline Details
We compare against eight representative user simulators while preserving each method’s observation modality, context construction, memory mechanism, and training objective.
All methods use the common
UserArena
environment, action space, source test split, and output schema.
1.
RecAgent
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
conditions an LLM agent on a user profile and hierarchical sensory, short-term, and long-term memories. The memories are updated only with interactions that have already occurred.
2.
Agent4Rec
(
Zhang et al., 2024
)
represents a user through profile, memory, and reflection modules. Retrieved memories and a compact reflection on prior interactions inform each action.
3.
SimUSER
(
Bougie and Watanabe, 2025
)
constructs a profile from pre-session history and updates category preferences from executed interactions. Our adapted version retains one profile update per session and one action prediction per decision.
4.
Shop-R1
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
is a text-based simulator trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. It receives the textual page state and interaction history but not the user profile.
5.
Customer-R1
(
Wang et al., 2025c
)
extends the Shop-R1 training recipe with the shopper profile, recent clicks and purchases, and the executed interaction history.
6.
AlignUSER
(
Bougie et al., 2026
)
augments supervised training with counterfactual actions and teacher-generated comparison rationales. Its evaluation prompt contains only the profile, past interactions, and current state.
7.
A/B Agent
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
is a GUI-based simulator that combines the current screenshot with a user profile, retrieved long-term memory, working memory, and a fatigue mechanism.
8.
STA
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
is a GUI-based simulator that predicts a rationale and structured action from the current screenshot, textual page state, and interaction history. We use its reinforcement-learning-tuned checkpoint.
B.2
Data Processing and Implementation
Data processing.
We normalize the raw interaction logs into the 13-action
UserArena
space and reconstruct the state immediately preceding each recorded decision.
The visual observation and textual page state are drawn from the same pre-action interface state.
We stratify users into training, validation, and test sets at an 8:1:1 ratio using seed 42, assigning all sessions from each user to the same split for both single- and cross-session experiments.
Training and validation examples may be resampled to balance action coverage, whereas every test trajectory is retained once and is never resampled.
Replay reconstructs each recorded state independently, while Rollout starts from the same initial context and thereafter advances only with actions accepted by the environment.
Implementation details.
To control for backbone capacity, all methods in the main comparison, including the prompting-only baselines, use Qwen3.5-2B
(
Team, 2026
)
with a maximum context length of 32k tokens.
This shared-backbone setting isolates differences in prompting, memory, observation modality, and post-training strategy from differences in model scale.
We standardize the interaction interface of every trainable baseline and OPTD.
Their base prompts use the same task instruction, action definitions, and response schema, while retaining any method-specific context described in Appendix
.
We use Qwen3.5-397B
(
Team, 2026
)
to generate a short first-person rationale for each recorded action from the corresponding user context, interaction history, and current state.
Each SFT target pairs this rationale with the recorded structured action.
The rationale encourages the model to summarize relevant evidence from the user context, interaction history, and current state before selecting an action, and using this format for every trainable method keeps the supervision interface consistent.
We cap each GUI image at 200,704 input pixels.
For OPTD, we perform an SFT warm-up on the same interaction format so that the resulting checkpoint can follow task instructions and generate a short rationale followed by a valid action from the current state.
We then freeze this checkpoint as the teacher and initialize the student from it.
We use ROLL
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
for distributed training, vLLM
(
Kwon et al., 2023
)

(

We cap Rollout at 31 executed actions for single-session evaluation and 42 for cross-session evaluation, one more than the maximum recorded action count in each setting.

article.headline: UserArena：长程购物智能体的用户模拟基准
article.lede: 团队发布真实电商交互基准 UserArena，含 64,729 条会话轨迹，并提出 OPTD 训练方法。
article.problem: 智能体推荐需要模型在很长的交互过程中连续做出依赖上下文的决策，因此开发和评测这类策略都需要一个能忠实模拟购物环境与用户响应的推荐世界模型。现有资源很少提供长程、细粒度的真实用户轨迹，也缺乏轨迹级评测，以及能和生产 A/B 结果对齐的离线验证。
article.method: UserArena 在真实电商环境中重建推荐信息流与商品详情页，覆盖 13 类动作，并把同一用户跨多次会话的记录按时间串成长程轨迹。配套的五级评测协议从输出可执行性（L0）逐级推进到局部决策、顺序行为、个性化群体与最终结果保真（L4）。作者进一步提出 On-Policy Trajectory Distillation（OPTD）：把轨迹级意图作为特权上下文交给冻结教师模型，在学生自行采样得到的 rollout 的每个 token 上提供稠密监督，再用逐 token 信任域限制意图带来的分布偏移。
article.results: UserArena 包含 11,010 名用户、64,729 条会话、577,670 次动作和 566,102 个商品；跨会话子集为 5,768 名用户的 59,378 条会话，人均 10.29 次会话、86.36 个动作。在单会话设定下，OPTD 在全部 8 项 L1–L4 指标上排名第一，F1 为 0.4178、准确率 0.3204、决策分布 JSD 为 0.0156；在跨会话设定下，它在 8 项指标中有 5 项第一，包括决策分布 JSD 0.0284、轨迹长度误差 0.72 和群体保真 PF 0.8929。在生产 A/B 对照中，OPTD 的模拟策略效应比为 0.713×、效应误差 0.287，比次优模拟器低 50.2%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把用户模拟器的评测从单步 next-action 一致性推进到长程行为，并与线上 A/B 结论直接对照；这为智能体推荐的离线策略评估提供了一个更接近生产的验收标准。
article.limitations: 跨会话设定下 OPTD 并非全面领先，其 F1 为 0.3456，低于 Shop-R1 的 0.3533 和 STA 的 0.3556，STA 在宏 F1 与 CTR 误差上更优。数据来自单一电商平台且品类失衡，服装占点击的 54.90%；生产 A/B 验证仅覆盖一对排序策略，即便是最佳的 OPTD 仍低估线上效应 28.7%。
article.figure_caption_zh: UserArena 概览：左侧为跨会话历史、逐步对齐的交互记录、生产 A/B 验证与数据规模，右侧为从环境合规（L0）到结果保真（L4）的五级评测协议。

page_papers.title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
page_papers.abstract: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.

HiSTEVE 1.0:
Harnessing Human-Interface VLA
Agents for Open-World Games
Zecong Tang
Zian Guan
Yuncheng Guo
Zhanqiu Zhang
Yiwen Guo
Bo Dai
Abstract
Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control.
As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities.
Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills.
To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness.
At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA’s capabilities.
To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion.
At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions.
To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings.
We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery.
HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.
\maintextgeometry
1
Introduction
A long-standing goal in embodied intelligence is to build virtual embodied agents
(
Fung et al., 2025
)
that can operate in open-ended games under the same interaction constraints as human players.
Achieving this goal requires two complementary capabilities: long-horizon autonomy to maintain goals and adapt plans; and reliable native-interface control to translate first-person visual observations into keyboard-and-mouse actions.
As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying these capabilities by combining partially observable, compositional tasks with diverse visuomotor interactions
(
Fan et al., 2022
;
Zheng et al., 2023
)
.
A generally capable Minecraft agent must therefore integrate long-horizon planning with native-interface execution in a closed loop, continually updating its decisions from visual feedback.
Existing Minecraft agents have primarily emphasized one of these two capabilities.
On the one hand, visuomotor policies and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models address native-interface control by directly mapping raw first-person observations to keyboard-and-mouse actions
(
Baker et al., 2022
;
Lifshitz et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2025
)
.
However, these models typically lack mechanisms for persistently tracking task state and explicitly reasoning over task dependencies, limiting their long-horizon autonomy.
On the other hand, agents driven by large language models (LLMs) or vision-language models (VLMs) support long-horizon reasoning through task decomposition planning
(
Wang et al., 2023a
;
Zhu et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2024b
;
Li et al., 2024
)
.
However, many of these methods still rely on environment APIs, predefined skills, or functional actions for low-level execution, which may be unavailable in most games.
Although recent work has begun to combine high-level planning with learned policies
(
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Park et al., 2025
)
, integrating task-state tracking, completion verification, and failure recovery remains an open challenge.
Satisfying both requirements introduces coupled challenges at the planning and action timescales.
At the planning timescale, long-horizon autonomy requires tracking the objective, progress, and execution history across subtasks, while ensuring that plans are consistent with Minecraft mechanics and remain within the lower-level policy’s capabilities
(
Wang et al., 2023b
)
.
The agent must also determine when to terminate the current subtask: terminating too early leaves the subtask unfinished, whereas terminating too late wastes actions and may even undo existing progress.
At the action timescale, native-interface control requires a single VLA policy to operate reliably across heterogeneous task distributions.
In particular, non-GUI control and GUI interaction differ in both visual distributions and mouse-action semantics: mouse movement rotates the camera in the former but displaces the cursor in the latter, making naive joint training susceptible to negative transfer
(
He et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
.
Each VLA invocation must also be reliable, since even small per-subtask failure risks accumulate over repeated invocations in long-horizon tasks.
To address these challenges, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent that combines a capability-aware harness for long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control.
At the slower planning timescale, we design the harness with a structured memory of task progress and a VLM planner that selects the next atomic subtask.
To close the planning–execution loop, we introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion.
The harness then verifies the task state and decides whether to advance, recover, or replan.
At the faster action timescale, the VLA predicts native keyboard-and-mouse actions from the subtask instruction and first-person visual observation.
To mitigate negative transfer across heterogeneous interaction regimes, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings for non-GUI and GUI tasks.
Following world knowledge injection and imitation learning, we further finetune the VLA through reinforcement learning (RL) to improve recovery when execution deviates from demonstration trajectories.
We comprehensively evaluate HiSTEVE on atomic and long-horizon benchmarks.
Compared with the strongest baseline in our main comparison, HiSTEVE improves average success by
20.0
20.0
percentage points on MineStudio Bench and
0.6
0.6
points on OpenHA, with family-level gains of up to
28.6
28.6
points on LongBench.
The largest long-horizon improvements occur in tasks requiring multi-stage resource production or the reuse of information gathered during exploration.
Ablations reveal that stronger atomic execution alone does not yield comparable gains in long-horizon performance.
With the VLA held fixed, the full harness more than doubles goal success relative to fixed-horizon handoff, highlighting the importance of organizing local execution around a persistent task state.
The learned completion detector also outperforms prompted general-purpose VLMs, providing more accurate completion judgments to support this execution loop.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
•
We present HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness, enabling HiSTEVE to maintain goals and adapt plans throughout long-horizon execution.
•
We enable reliable native-interface control through regime-specific RMSNorm branches, separate mouse-movement token embeddings, and a three-stage training strategy.
•
HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance and can complete long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like a human player.
2
Related Work
2.1
Agent Harnesses for Execution
Foundation-model agents often use an agent harness, an external orchestration layer that supports interaction across model calls
(
Sumers et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Lin et al., 2026
)
.
Early language agents connect language models to external knowledge and tools and alternate between reasoning and action
(
Nakano et al., 2021
;
Karpas et al., 2022
;
Yao et al., 2022
)
.
Later systems added memory, feedback-based reflection, and search-based evaluation, allowing the harness to retain experience and refine subsequent decisions
(
Zhou et al., 2023
;
Packer et al., 2023
;
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2024c
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
.
In long-horizon embodied tasks, agent harnesses coordinate high-level planning and low-level execution across multiple steps
(
Huang et al., 2022a
;
Wang et al., 2024a
;
Shah et al., 2025
)
.
Such harnesses use environmental observations, feasibility assessments, and execution outcomes to continually update subsequent decisions, thereby closing the planning–execution loop
(
Huang et al., 2022b
;
Guo et al., 2024
;
Zhi et al., 2025
)
.
2.2
VLA Models and Systems
VLA models map visual observations and language instructions to embodied actions
(
Ma et al., 2026
;
Brohan et al., 2023
)
.
Early language-conditioned policies learned this mapping directly from multi-task demonstrations
(
Shridhar et al., 2022
;
Jang et al., 2022
;
Brohan et al., 2022
)
.
As model capacity and robot datasets grew, these policies generalized to a broader range of tasks, environments, and robot embodiments
(
Brohan et al., 2023
;
O’Neill et al., 2024
;
Team et al., 2024
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2026
;
Pertsch et al., 2025
)
.
To support long-horizon planning, hierarchical systems use a semantic planner to generate policy-compatible subtasks for execution by a low-level policy
(
Ma et al., 2026
;
Ahn et al., 2022
;
Driess et al., 2023
;
Shi et al., 2025
)
.
More recent approaches allow intermediate reasoning or predictive representations to directly guide low-level control
(
Belkhale et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Lin et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
.
2.3
Game-Playing Agents in Virtual Worlds
Games have long served as testbeds for sequential decision making, with research progressing from search-based systems to deep RL agents
(
Campbell et al., 2002
;
Mnih et al., 2015
;
Silver et al., 2016
)
.
More recently, pretrained models have been used to build agents that follow instructions and reason over observations
(
Ma et al., 2024
;
Zhou et al., 2026
;
Tan et al., 2025
)
.
Researchers have also trained unified policies on multi-game data, but such policies often sacrifice control precision and long-horizon reliability
(
Raad et al., 2024
;
Magne et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
Alongside efforts toward cross-game generalization, Minecraft has emerged as a focused testbed for studying embodied interaction within an open world
(
Guss et al., 2019
;
Fan et al., 2022
)
.
Research in Minecraft includes visuomotor policies learned directly from interaction trajectories
(
Baker et al., 2022
;
Lifshitz et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2025
)
, as well as LLM- or VLM-based agents for autonomous exploration and skill acquisition
(
Zhu et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2023a
;
Wang et al., 2024b
)
.
3
Capability-Aware Harness for Long-Horizon Autonomy
We propose a capability-aware agent harness that coordinates a VLM planner and a VLA policy for long-horizon autonomy.
Specifically, we integrate capability-constrained planning, evidence-driven handoff and recovery, and structured memory (Appendix
8
).
3.1
Capability-Constrained Planning
Long-horizon Minecraft tasks cannot be reliably solved through a single static plan because the environment is partially observable, and local execution failures may change the feasibility of subsequent subtasks.
Planning within the harness is reference-free: no predefined subtask sequence or expert task route is provided, and the planner selects the next atomic subtask online from the final objective and current execution context.
We constrain the planner to select and instantiate a parameterized atomic subtask schema from a set restricted to the VLA’s execution capabilities.
Each schema specifies its applicability, semantic parameters, visually observable progress and completion conditions, recognizable failure conditions, and execution budget.

3.2
Evidence-Driven Handoff and Recovery
To address the handoff-timing problem between high-level planning and VLA control discussed above, we introduce an evidence-driven handoff-and-recovery protocol.
During each bounded VLA invocation, the task-completion state detector estimates a completion probability for the current instruction

When this probability exceeds a confidence threshold, the current invocation ends and returns control to the harness, and exhaustion of the execution budget triggers the same handoff.
Our mechanism differs from failure detection: the detector signals candidate completion rather than execution failure, while the harness verifies progress and completion conditions using current and recent visual observations.

Following verification, the harness advances if the completion conditions are satisfied and attempts local recovery if the subtask remains incomplete but recoverable.
The harness replans from the updated state if recovery is infeasible or repeatedly fails, the current subtask becomes inapplicable, or the visual state changes substantially.
3.3
Structured Memory
Long-horizon execution requires persistent task state, but retaining the full history increases context length and accumulates unverified intermediate information.
The harness therefore maintains a compact structured memory centered on verified state transitions.
The memory system comprises four stores with distinct roles.
Working memory corresponds to the current planning state

j

and records the active objective and atomic subtask, verified task progress, unresolved requirements, and recent failures or lack of progress.
Episodic memory records the planning states before and after each VLA invocation, together with the selected subtask, the harness-verified outcome, execution cost, and diagnostic information.
Procedural memory stores reusable dependencies among parameterized subtasks derived from verified successful executions.
World memory stores landmarks and spatial relations inferred from visual observations to support subsequent planning within the current world.
At each high-level decision step, the working memory

Action Representation.
We represent Minecraft’s native keyboard-and-mouse actions as discrete action tokens, allowing supervised action prediction to use the same next-token prediction objective as language modeling.
Following the VPT-style action space
(
Baker et al., 2022
)
, we organize each single-step action into multiple categorical action groups.
Keyboard and click inputs are represented as discrete choices within predefined action groups, while horizontal and vertical mouse displacements are
μ
\mu
-law transformed and quantized into the same number of bins.
However, mouse displacement controls camera rotation in non-GUI interactions but cursor movement in GUI interactions, so sharing a single action token set creates an ambiguity.
We therefore assign disjoint mouse-displacement token sets: the original mouse tokens are retained for non-GUI interactions, while a separate subset is allocated to GUI interactions.
We further insert an interaction-type token at the beginning of the sequence to indicate whether the current interaction is non-GUI or GUI.
Because both sets of mouse-displacement tokens decode back to the same physical action codebook, the branching occurs solely at the representation level. We refer to this regime-separated mouse-movement token representation as
Dual-Mouse
. (Appendix
9.3
)
4.2
Three-Stage Policy Training
Because per-subtask failures compound over repeated VLA invocations, reliable long-horizon execution requires high reliability. We therefore train the VLA in three stages: world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback.
Supervised Initialization.
Before reinforcement learning, we use two supervised stages to establish the semantic knowledge and control capabilities required for reliable native-interface execution.
World knowledge injection equips the policy with Minecraft concepts and their visual grounding, while imitation learning teaches it to map subtask instructions and first-person observations to native keyboard-and-mouse actions.
Further details on data sources, sample construction and curation, training objectives, and optimization settings are provided in Appendix
10

Task Completion State Detector
We introduce a novel policy-coupled task completion state detector to support the harness in determining when to pause the VLA invocation.

LongBench evaluates whether atomic native-control capabilities remain effective when they must be repeatedly composed over extended interaction.

7
Conclusion
We present HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent combining a capability-aware agent harness for long-horizon autonomy with native-interface control.
The harness enables long-horizon autonomy through capability-constrained planning, evidence-driven handoff and recovery, and structured memory.
Regime-specific representations and three-stage training enable a single VLA to reliably handle both non-GUI and GUI interactions.
HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MineStudio Bench (
85.0
%
85.0\%
) and OpenHA (
37.4
%
37.4\%
) and can craft an iron pickaxe from scratch using only human-interface.
Our work shows that regime-specific representations support reliable control across heterogeneous tasks, while reliable long-horizon execution further requires a harness that combines local control with state-aware orchestration.
These results represent a step toward virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games human players.

8.4
Structured Memory
Long-horizon execution requires persistent task state, but retaining the complete raw interaction history rapidly increases context length and preserves many transient or unverified intermediate states. HiSTEVE instead maintains a compact memory centered on verified subtask-level state transitions.
The memory system consists of four complementary stores:
•
Working memory
records the current objective, active subtask, verified progress, unresolved requirements, and recent failure or no-progress states.
•
Episodic memory
records the state transition associated with each bounded VLA invocation, together with the selected subtask, harness-verified outcome, execution cost, and diagnostic information.
•
Procedural memory
stores reusable dependencies among parameterized subtasks extracted from verified successful executions.
•
World memory
stores visually inferred landmarks and spatial relations that may support later planning within the current world.

The four families serve complementary purposes. Resource & Crafting tasks require the agent to compose multiple native-control skills into a dependency chain whose final object is unavailable at initialization. Exploration & Memory tasks require information gathered earlier in the episode to affect later decisions. Recovery tasks introduce situations in which the current execution path can no longer be continued directly and therefore require local recovery or replanning. Open-ended tasks admit multiple valid strategies and provide less structure about the sequence of intermediate objectives.

Eleven of the fourteen tasks start from an empty inventory in a natural survival world. Formal evaluation uses fixed environment seeds, while terrain, resource distribution, and naturally occurring entities remain part of the Minecraft environment.
The three Recovery tasks use controlled initial states to reproducibly instantiate low-frequency recovery scenarios involving tool breakage, alternative fuel, and missed resource pickup.
These states are instantiated only during reset; subsequent evaluation follows the same native visual and keyboard-and-mouse interface used throughout the paper.

Matched harness evaluation.
To isolate the effect of agent orchestration from lower-level policy quality, the harness ablation keeps the native-control VLA and upper-level semantic model fixed. The compared systems therefore share the same local controller and differ only in how repeated VLA invocations are organized over time.
The fixed-horizon variant returns control after a predetermined execution boundary. Full HiSTEVE instead uses state-dependent handoff followed by visual verification and planning-state update; incomplete executions may trigger local recovery or replanning.
Because the lower-level VLA is unchanged, this comparison isolates the effect of runtime orchestration from changes in policy weights.
The corresponding controlled results are reported in Table

Diagnostic failure patterns.
LongBench exposes failures that are less visible in atomic benchmarks because successful completion depends on preserving usable state over many policy invocations. We observe three recurring patterns.
First, multi-step GUI interactions can leave the environment in a partially correct state that is difficult to continue from reliably. For example, an invocation may correctly place part of a recipe but fail to retrieve the output or recover from an incorrect slot configuration. A subsequent invocation then starts from a state that differs from the demonstrations seen by the policy.
Second, exploration tasks amplify errors in spatial memory. The agent may successfully discover a relevant area but later fail to recover sufficiently precise visual or spatial context for a return objective. These cases distinguish reaching a useful location once from maintaining information that remains actionable several planning steps later.
Third, recovery itself consumes execution budget. A local failure may be recoverable, yet repeated attempts can leave insufficient budget for the remaining dependency chain. LongBench therefore measures not only whether recovery is possible, but whether recovery is efficient enough to preserve the feasibility of the overall objective.
These observations explain why diagnostic progress can substantially exceed final-goal success: HiSTEVE often completes meaningful portions of a long trajectory before a later execution or recovery failure prevents satisfaction of the terminal predicate.
12.3
Controlled Harness Evaluation
The harness ablation is designed to separate improvements in agent orchestration from changes in lower-level policy quality. Across compared variants, we hold the native-control VLA, upper-level semantic model, task definitions, and evaluation protocol fixed.
The fixed-horizon variant executes the same atomic instruction until a predetermined execution boundary before returning control to the upper level. Full HiSTEVE instead uses state-dependent completion signals followed by visual verification, structured task-state update, local recovery, and replanning.
Because the underlying VLA is fixed, differences in long-horizon performance primarily reflect how the same local controller is organized across repeated invocations. This is also why we report atomic metrics for the same comparison: large changes in long-horizon behavior accompanied by only small changes in atomic performance provide evidence that the gain arises from orchestration rather than from a stronger controller.

Discussion
HiSTEVE suggests that a central challenge in long-horizon agency is maintaining task state across planning and control decisions. The agent harness provides this continuity by preserving task state, aligning plans with executable capabilities, and using execution outcomes to make decisions.
With the lower-level VLA fixed, the complete harness changes aggregate atomic performance only modestly while substantially improving LongBench goal success. This suggests that long-horizon capability depends not only on the strength of the local controller, but also on how existing capabilities are organized across repeated invocations, with task state preserved and subsequent decisions adapted to execution outcomes.
A further design insight is to decouple control handoff from task-success verification. The completion detector provides only a candidate handoff signal, while the harness subsequently verifies completion from visual evidence, preventing individual detector errors from being directly committed to persistent task state.
The current system has two main limitations. First, its atomic subtask interfaces are manually defined, and its capabilities remain limited by the existing VLA policy; adding new atomic capabilities requires additional training data and policy updates, while neither the harness nor the VLA currently performs parametric continual learning from deployment experience. In addition, high-level planning relies on an off-the-shelf VLM, making overall system performance dependent on the capabilities of the selected VLM backend.
Future work could enable independent or joint evolution of the VLA and harness: the VLA could learn continually from failure and recovery trajectories, while the harness updates its planning constraints and recovery strategies from experience. A complementary direction is to use Minecraft as training an environment for agent intelligence, examining whether planning, memory, and recovery capabilities can transfer across games and ultimately to interactive domains beyond games.

article.headline: 分层VLA智能体兼顾Minecraft长程任务
article.lede: HiSTEVE用VLM规划器加单个VLA，在Minecraft中仅靠视觉和键鼠完成原子与长程任务。
article.problem: 现有Minecraft智能体往往只强在一边：VLA能直接用视觉到键鼠控制，但缺少持久任务状态和长程推理；LLM/VLM智能体擅长分解规划，却常依赖环境API或预定义技能。长程执行还要求判断子任务何时结束，过早或过晚交接都会损害进度。GUI与非GUI交互的视觉分布和鼠标语义不同，简单联合训练容易负迁移。
article.method: HiSTEVE把慢速VLM规划器与单个VLA组成分层系统：harness用结构化记忆跟踪进度，并只在VLA能力范围内选择原子子任务；策略耦合的完成检测器给出候选完成信号，再由harness用视觉证据核验并决定推进、恢复或重规划。底层VLA以Qwen2.5-VL-7B为初始化，仅用第一人称视觉和原生键鼠动作执行，20 Hz运行。为缓解GUI与非GUI干扰，作者引入按交互类型分支的RMSNorm和分离的鼠标位移token，并按世界知识注入、模仿学习、环境反馈强化学习三阶段训练。
article.results: 在MineStudio Bench上，HiSTEVE的平均严格pass@1为85.0%（Mine 93.3%、Kill 86.7%、Craft 66.7%、Smelt 93.3%）；OpenHA平均37.4%，较Text/CoA的36.8%仅高0.6个百分点，Embodied为46.0%（基线37.0%），但GUI 27.2%和Combat 39.0%分别低于基线的33.3%和40.0%。LongBench上四个任务族最终目标成功率为42.9%、28.6%、14.3%、14.3%，宏平均25.0%；在固定VLA的对照中，完整harness把Goal SR从10.7%提高到25.0%，诊断进度从17.9%提高到28.6%，而MineStudio All仅从81.2%到85.0%、OpenHA Avg从37.8%到37.4%。完成检测器在4,674个平衡验证样本上准确率和F1均为0.863，高于GPT-4o的0.690和GPT-5.5的0.776。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明长程自主性不只取决于底层控制器强弱，更取决于如何保存任务状态、约束规划并组织反复调用；对开放世界游戏和更一般的具身智能体都有方法学意义。
article.limitations: 原子子任务接口由人工定义，新增能力需额外数据和策略更新，系统也不做参数化持续学习，高层规划还依赖现成VLM。OpenHA的GUI/Combat仍低于基线，LongBench的Recovery和Open-ended仅14.3%，多步GUI、恢复效率和弱结构化目标仍是明显瓶颈。

page_papers.title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
page_papers.abstract: Agent-evolution methods use execution feedback to improve prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration, but their implementations often rebuild the same experimental machinery. We present RSIHub, an open-source framework for building, comparing, and extending these methods on shared infrastructure. Recipes compose reusable operators and declare mutable resources; RSIHub supplies execution, evaluation, recovery, and lineage. Researchers can focus on evolution policy while evaluation stays outside the mutable surface and results remain tied to candidates and evaluation conditions. We instantiate AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA without modifying the framework core, keeping method-specific logic in recipes and operators. We evaluate them with MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and τ^3 Banking under fixed model and evaluator configurations. The largest observed overall pass@1 gain is 13.5 percentage points, while method rankings vary across settings and optimization gains do not always transfer to held-out tasks. RSIHub provides a common protocol for comparing evolution policies, inspectable candidate histories, and reusable components for developing new methods.

Abstract
Agent-evolution methods use execution feedback to improve prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration, but their implementations often rebuild the same experimental machinery. We present RSIHub, an open-source framework for building, comparing, and extending these methods on shared infrastructure. Recipes compose reusable operators and declare mutable resources; RSIHub supplies execution, evaluation, recovery, and lineage. Researchers can focus on evolution policy while evaluation stays outside the mutable surface and results remain tied to candidates and evaluation conditions. We instantiate AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA without modifying the framework core, keeping method-specific logic in recipes and operators. We evaluate them with MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and
τ
3

Banking under fixed model and evaluator configurations. The largest observed overall pass@1 gain is 13.5 percentage points, while method rankings vary across settings and optimization gains do not always transfer to held-out tasks. RSIHub provides a common protocol for comparing evolution policies, inspectable candidate histories, and reusable components for developing new methods.
1
Introduction
Language-model agents are commonly developed through an
empirical loop: developers inspect executions, revise prompts, reusable skills,
tools, or orchestration, and reevaluate the resulting behavior
[
14
,
32
]
. Agent-evolution systems
automate parts of this loop by turning execution feedback into persistent
changes to the agent
[
14
,
1
,
42
,
39

; some also
revise parts of the improvement procedure
[
5
,
41
,
40

Program-optimization methods apply a similar feedback loop to language-model
programs and textual components
[
11
,
37
]
. Across both settings, each
iteration selects a candidate to extend, gathers evidence from its behavior,
proposes and evaluates a revision, and retains the outcome for later search.
This recurring lifecycle provides a common structure across these systems.
Agent-evolution methods vary in how they instantiate this lifecycle and in which resources they allow to change.
Much of the supporting infrastructure nevertheless recurs: isolated candidate
workspaces, task execution and evaluation, artifact retention, recovery, and lineage.
Implementations commonly bundle this infrastructure with method policy. As a
result, implementing a method can require building another end-to-end system, while
comparing methods requires reconciling runners, configurations, and evaluator
interfaces. These costs motivate common infrastructure on which researchers can test new
evolution ideas without rebuilding workspaces, execution, and evaluation.
To meet this need, we introduce RSIHub, a composable framework that separates
method policy from this recurring infrastructure. As
Figure
1
illustrates, a
recipe
binds one
implementation to each enabled operator interface, declares the mutable
surface, and specifies the run configuration: the target, evaluator, runtime,
and data splits. A framework-managed
evolution loop
invokes the selected operators
to choose a parent, gather evidence, revise a candidate, and decide what to
retain. A
protected runtime
executes and evaluates candidates under that
configuration, and the framework writes their outcomes to the verified archive.
In the
agent-driven
mode, an outer agent adapts the recipe between
iterations under the same lifecycle and evaluation boundaries.
Shared framework services provide workspace construction, artifacts, recovery,
and lineage. New operator implementations plug into these stable interfaces,
leaving the framework core unchanged. This follows the
organization used by research frameworks in
adjacent fields: stable interfaces expose research choices while shared runtime
mechanics support their execution
[
22
,
25
]
.
Figure 1
:
RSIHub separates method policy from framework-managed execution. In a
recipe-driven run, a researcher-authored recipe remains fixed across
iterations. In an agent-driven run, an outer agent uses permitted feedback
from each completed iteration to revise the recipe’s operator bindings and
policy settings for the next. At each iteration boundary, RSIHub validates and
snapshots the active recipe before running the same guarded lifecycle. The
target definition, evaluator, runtime, data splits, and mutable surface remain
fixed; surface enforcement, protected evaluation, and verified archive writes
stay under framework control.
The protected-runtime layer addresses a central attribution risk in broadly
mutable evolution systems. Method-controlled
changes to evaluation can alter measurement conditions, while changes to record
keeping can rewrite the reported evidence; either can make an apparent gain
ambiguous.
RSIHub addresses this risk by keeping evaluation and its archive under
framework control, outside the declared mutable surface. Framework services
associate each result with the committed candidate and evaluation conditions
that produced it; a separate Gate operator decides whether the evaluated
candidate is eligible to become a parent.
Our evaluation compares recipes for four methods across two seed agents and two
benchmarks under fixed model and evaluator configurations. It examines
effectiveness and held-out transfer, execution fidelity, integrity through
interruption recovery and boundary enforcement, and runtime and implementation
cost.
Concretely, this paper makes three contributions:
•
Composable recipes.
We introduce a recipe abstraction that
specifies method policy through reusable lifecycle operators and
declares the resources that may be revised. We express AHE,
Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA as recipes over the same operators.
•
Shared experimental infrastructure.
We provide a common
lifecycle for candidate execution, recovery, artifacts, certified
evaluation records, and lineage.
•
Evaluation on common ground.
We compare the four recipes
across two seed agents and two benchmarks under fixed model and
evaluator configurations. We also test the framework itself: whether
it changes the measured capability of an unevolved agent, whether it
recovers from interruption and holds its boundaries, and what it costs
in runtime and code. Rankings among the recipes vary across agents,
benchmarks, and splits.
Open-source resources.
We release RSIHub through Simple Agent Lab under Apache-2.0, with runnable recipes, reusable operators, documentation

3
The RSIHub Framework
RSIHub separates method policy from the shared mechanics of candidate execution,
evaluation, and record keeping. This section states the principles behind that
separation, then describes how the candidate lifecycle and provenance model
realize it.
3.1
Design principles
RSIHub is built so that a researcher can assemble an evolution method from
interchangeable parts, decide what those parts may change and what they may
see, and reuse framework services for recurring mechanics.
Assemble methods from interchangeable parts.
RSIHub fixes the slots of the evolution lifecycle and leaves their contents
open. A
stage
is a slot such as
select
or
mutate
. An
operator
is one implementation of a stage. A
recipe
names the
operator it wants in each slot and configures it. When the required operator
implementations are available, a recipe can express the method-specific choices
through configuration.
Say what a method may change and see.
Two recipe declarations make this an experimental choice. The
surface
block declares the resources a candidate may change, allowing
the same operator interfaces to support prompt-only and whole-harness studies.
The
mutate
block configures how the editing agent runs and which
retained context it receives. Together, these declarations distinguish the persistent resources being evolved from the information used to propose each revision.
Provide the rest of the pipeline once.
Workspace construction, candidate snapshots, evaluation execution, artifact
retention, terminal-state classification, recovery from interrupted runs, and
lineage bookkeeping commonly recur across evolution methods. RSIHub implements
these services once and gives every recipe the same execution path. When a
study changes one operator without changing the other recipe fields, it isolates
one declared policy component while reusing the same framework mechanics.
Keep scoring out of the method’s reach.
Method policy may revise candidates and the operators that propose them.
Measurement remains a framework responsibility: framework services
own evaluation and the evidence record outside the mutable surface a recipe declares,
while parent eligibility remains a separate downstream policy choice.
Together, these principles separate method-specific choices from
framework-managed execution and measurement. The candidate lifecycle below
makes this separation operational.
3.2
Composable candidate lifecycle
The lifecycle follows the seven phases shown in
Figure
1
: Select, Rollout, Analyze, Mutate, Guardrail,
Evaluate, and Absorb. Across these phases, recipes bind five required operator
interfaces—Select, Rollout, Mutate, Gate, and Record—and may bind four
optional ones, marked with
∗
below: Analyze, Validate, Novelty, and Reflect.
RSIHub implements this lifecycle on Harbor
[
7
]
, which
provides container execution, trajectory capture, and per-task verification.
Above this substrate, RSIHub manages candidate lineage, train/gate/sealed splits,
mutable-surface enforcement, and certified evaluation records.
The lifecycle accepts either a fixed, researcher-authored recipe or one supplied
by an outer agent. In the agent-driven mode, the outer agent uses a
recipe-authoring skill to compose the initial recipe and may revise its operator
bindings and policy settings using permitted feedback after each completed
iteration. The outer agent adapts the evolution procedure, while Mutate edits
the candidate within an iteration. The target, evaluator, runtime, data splits,
and allowed mutable surface remain fixed; sealed tasks are excluded from
adaptation feedback. Our experiments evaluate fixed recipes.
Before each iteration, the framework validates and snapshots the active recipe,
resolving every binding and checking its settings against the operator’s schema.
Each operator runs in a separate process, and the framework validates its
structured output before using it.
The archive separates framework-certified fields, the evaluated candidate, its
parent, the evaluation conditions, and the outcome, from method-specific
annotations. Operators propose annotations; the framework filters and writes
them.
•
Select.
Chooses an eligible parent from the archive according
to the recipe’s search policy. The framework verifies its identity and
forks its exact recorded commit.
•
Rollout.
Runs the parent on training tasks and returns
execution evidence as a summary and retained artifact references. The
supplied Harbor rollout uses only the training split; a replay-based
rollout reuses the parent’s recorded evaluation instead of running
again.
•
Analyze
*
.
Distills rollout cases into
bounded mutation evidence, such as failure patterns or compact traces,
in the representation Mutate consumes.
•
Mutate.
Proposes edits within the declared mutable surface.
The operator is typically an agent rather than a fixed transformation:
it works over multiple turns, may run small-scale trials on training
tasks before proposing a change, and, as in Hyperagents, may edit the
evolution operators themselves when the surface allows. It reports
changed paths, notes, and usage.
•
Guardrail.
The framework checks the actual tree diff against
the mutable surface. Two optional operators may then reject the
proposal: Validate
*
applies a method-specific
pre-evaluation check, and Novelty
*
drops near-duplicates
of accepted diffs before they consume evaluation budget.
•
Evaluate.
This framework-managed phase commits the reviewed
tree, scores a clean checkout on the gate tasks, and certifies the result.
Gate tasks may coincide with training tasks; sealed tasks are reserved
for held-out reporting.
•
Absorb.
Gate decides from the certified score whether the
child becomes a parent, Record proposes method-specific annotations, and
Reflect
*
distills insights from archive history for
later generations. The framework records permitted outputs; none of
these operators can change certified evaluation fields.

procedure
When a recipe places operators inside the mutable surface, the framework must
decide which version of an operator runs. This candidate-level mechanism is
distinct from an outer agent revising recipe bindings or settings between
iterations. For each stage invocation, it loads the
implementation from the checkout supplied to that stage. Changes to already-run
stages take effect in a later generation,
while changes to Validate or Novelty may affect the current proposal. Gate and
Record subsequently load from the committed child. The certified record provides a recovery checkpoint after evaluation: it holds the committed child and its outcome before downstream finalization. Gate, Record, and Reflect may add policy outputs but cannot alter certified evaluation fields.
3.3
Provenance
A certified evaluation event ties the committed candidate, its parent, and the
active recipe snapshot to evaluator and task-set fingerprints, trials, score, costs,
artifact references, and lineage. A hash-referenced contract can also record evaluator-configuration and dataset-content digests,
split and repetition settings, model identity, retry policy, evaluator-runtime
digest, and framework version. This identity lets a study distinguish a change
in method policy from a change in recorded evaluation conditions.
From experiment records to method design.
Researchers can start from a bundled recipe and inspect candidate snapshots, lineage, task outcomes, costs, and trajectories to investigate stalled progress and revision patterns, combining artifacts with scores as in Fork-and-Flush
[
2
]
. For example, researchers can replace the parent-selection operator in a separate run while holding the seed agent, mutable surface, model, evaluator, and task splits fixed. RSIHub supplies execution, recovery, and provenance services, with command-line summaries and a read-only viewer for inspecting the resulting records (
Appendix
C
). This workflow lets researchers test new policy components while reusing the surrounding experimental infrastructure. At the evaluated commit, the four adaptations used 47–61 recipe lines and reused two operator bindings each, with no framework-source changes (
Table
6
). Method-specific operator code ranged from 216 to 1,087 lines.
4
Evaluation
In this section, we organize the evaluation around three research questions:
•
RQ1:
Can RSIHub support effective agent evolution?
•
RQ2:
Does RSIHub preserve the capabilities of the agents it executes?
•
RQ3:
Does RSIHub preserve the integrity of agent-evolution experiments?
To answer these questions, we compare evolution recipes across agents, benchmarks, and held-out splits for RQ1, use generation-zero controls against direct execution for RQ2, and conduct fault-injection and boundary-enforcement trials for RQ3.

All experiments use GPT-5.4 with high reasoning effort as the target model for both MiniSWE and Codex. Every recipe uses a Codex mutation agent backed by GPT-5.4 with xhigh reasoning effort. All recipes propose one child per generation, and evolution runs continue for at most 10 generations. Overall performance.
The results show substantial gains, with their size depending on the benchmark, seed agent, and evolution method. On Terminal Bench 2, every method improves the MiniSWE baseline by 7.8–13.5 percentage points; Hyperagents and A-Evolve reach the highest overall score of 69.7. Gains are smaller from the stronger Codex baseline: AHE reaches 71.9 (

These shifts indicate that method rankings are conditional on both the task environment and the starting agent.

The Codex results are more consistent across held-out splits: AHE improves train, gate, and sealed scores by 1.0, 3.0, and 5.1 points, while GEPA preserves train performance and improves both gate and sealed scores by 4.1 points.
Implications.
No method dominates across benchmarks, seeds, and splits. These setting-dependent outcomes motivate RSIHub’s support for changing evolution policies while retaining a common execution and evaluation pipeline. Gate regressions on Terminal Bench 2 and sealed regressions on
