Banking show why inspectable evidence matters: a higher overall score can conceal held-out losses. Split-level results tied to candidate records help researchers diagnose unsuccessful adaptations and choose which policies to investigate further. Substantial gains occur in several configurations, including on sealed tasks, but neither improvement nor transfer is uniform. These descriptive point estimates do not establish the stability of close differences without repeated runs.
4.4
Execution fidelity
Protocol.
To test the fidelity conjecture without confounding it with evolution, we compare framework-mediated execution of an unchanged seed agent with Direct execution. Direct execution denotes invoking the frozen evaluator outside RSIHub without creating or recording framework state. Direct-A and Direct-B are two independent direct executions placed before and after the RSIHub execution, respectively. For each condition, we conduct three repetitions, each running the same unchanged seed agent in the fixed order Direct-A, RSIHub generation zero, and Direct-B under identical model, task, evaluator, and runtime settings. We report Avg@3 as the mean pass@1 across the three repetitions. Within each repetition, the Direct score is the mean of Direct-A and Direct-B. D–D agreement measures agreement between Direct-A and Direct-B. D–R agreement is the mean of the Direct-A–RSIHub and Direct-B–RSIHub task-level agreements, and excess disagreement is the mean cross-mode disagreement rate minus the D–D disagreement rate.

4.5
Recovery and integrity
Protocol.
We test the integrity conjecture by terminating runs during mutation or evaluation and after writing an evaluation receipt, then resuming and comparing the recovered state with an uninterrupted control. We also attempt evaluator mutation, writes outside the declared mutable surface, access to gate, sealed, and anchor evidence, and forged archive outcomes. We run 30 independent trials per scenario in each benchmark campaign. A trial passes only if the workspace reaches a valid and attributable state, unauthorized changes cannot affect an accepted result, and the champion remains reproducible from framework evidence.

5
Conclusion
RSIHub provides open, reusable infrastructure for agent evolution. All four evaluated adaptations reuse framework services without framework source changes. Gains and held-out transfer vary across settings, motivating shared protocols and inspectable evidence for policy comparison. We invite researchers to build on the released recipes, compare new policy components, and contribute operators that others can reuse.
The agent-driven path extends this separation to adaptive recipe revision: an outer agent may revise operator bindings and settings between iterations, while the evaluator, sealed split, and certified record remain protected. Together, these interfaces provide a shared foundation for studying agent self-improvement.
6
Limitations
RSIHub’s evidence guarantees rely on trusted framework services, host and
filesystem protections, Git and digest operations, configured external
services, and valid evaluators. Our results apply to the workloads, hosts, and
lifecycle boundaries tested in this study, and the capability-preservation
measurements assess task-level agreement rather than full behavioral
equivalence. Runtime fingerprints do
not replace host or service attestation, and RSIHub does not contain hostile
code, so stronger deployments require independent attestation, isolation, and
containment.
The reported results characterize fixed, recipe-driven runs rather
than adaptive recipe revision by an outer agent.
7
Responsible Use Statement
RSIHub can enable unsafe capability growth, reward gaming, or exposure of
sensitive traces. Higher pass@1 does not establish safe deployment or exclude
harmful intermediate actions; banking-benchmark success does not establish
suitability for financial decisions. RSIHub supports auditing and rollback,
not containment: editable operators and candidate adapters may execute on the
host, beyond task-container isolation and feedback filtering.
Deployers should restrict filesystem and network access, exclude production
credentials, and require held-out safety evaluation and human review before
promotion. Resource budgets and halt and rollback controls are needed, although
rollback cannot undo external actions or disclosures. Trajectories and archives
need access controls, retention limits, and redaction before sharing.

B.2
Runtime Overhead
Protocol.
We measured the cost of the services shared across recipes on both benchmark workloads by instrumenting workspace initialization, candidate snapshotting, mutable-surface validation, evaluation recording, integrity verification, and recovery separately from model inference, benchmark execution, and mutation. For Terminal Bench 2, initialization uses 50 microbenchmark repetitions, recovery uses 30 replay trials, and the four regular-operation rows and end-to-end shares use 20 complete Gen-1 runs, five per method. Each regular-operation sample sums the relevant exclusive spans within one generation, and we compute the median and P95 over the 20 per-generation totals. The reported generation share uses the union of the framework’s exclusive spans rather than summing nested durations. article.headline: RSIHub：把agent进化方法拆成可复用配方
article.lede: 开源框架RSIHub将agent进化方法的策略与执行、评估基础设施分离，四个方法无需改核心即可复现和对比。
article.problem: Agent进化方法利用执行反馈持续修改提示、技能、工具和编排，但每个实现往往重建同一套候选工作区、执行、评估、恢复与谱系设施。方法策略与基础设施捆绑后，复现一个方法要另建端到端系统，比较方法还要对齐runner、配置与评估器接口。
article.method: RSIHub把方法策略写成recipe，绑定可复用operator并声明可变资源；框架提供执行、评估、恢复和谱系，评估与存档位于可变面之外。生命周期分为Select、Rollout、Analyze、Mutate、Guardrail、Evaluate、Absorb七个阶段，固定recipe与agent驱动模式共用同一受保护流程。AHE、Hyperagents、A-Evolve、GEPA作为recipe实现，无需修改框架核心。
article.results: 在固定模型和评估器下，最大总体pass@1提升为13.5个百分点（MiniSWE在Terminal Bench 2上从56.2到69.7）；但方法排名随agent、基准和数据划分变化。四个适配各用47–61行recipe、复用2个operator绑定、框架源文件改动为0，方法特定operator代码为216–1,087行；420次故障注入与边界试验全部达到要求，且未接纳损坏状态。
article.why_it_matters: 共享协议和可检查的候选历史降低了方法间比较成本，并把结果与评估条件绑定，帮助研究者区分策略变化与测量条件变化。
article.limitations: 证据保证依赖可信框架服务、主机与文件系统保护、Git和摘要操作、外部服务及有效评估器；结果仅覆盖所测工作负载与生命周期边界，能力保持测的是任务级一致性而非完整行为等价。实验评价的是固定recipe驱动运行，而非外层agent自适应修订；单次运行点估计也不能确定接近差异的稳定性。
article.figure_caption_zh: RSIHub将方法策略与框架管理的执行分离：recipe驱动运行中配方固定，agent驱动运行中外层agent可依据每轮反馈修改配方，但目标、评估器、运行时、数据划分和可变面保持固定，评估与存档由框架控制。

figure.caption: separates method policy from framework-managed execution. In a recipe-driven run, a researcher-authored recipe remains fixed across iterations. In an agent-driven run, an outer agent uses permitted feedback from each completed iteration to revise the recipe's operator bindings and policy settings for the next. At each iteration boundary, validates and snapshots the active recipe before running the same guarded lifecycle. The target definition, evaluator, runtime, data splits, and mutable surface remain fixed; surface enforcement, protected evaluation, and verified archive writes stay under framework control.

page_papers.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
page_papers.abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience and action-conditioned predictions, while MA interaction trajectories can provide feedback for refining WMs. Assessing this potential relationship requires evidence about both components. A pilot study of one MA–WM pairing on 150 cases across ten scenarios illustrates why coupled outcomes alone are insufficient for diagnosing failure. We introduce Dual Exam, a framework that evaluates MAs under a fixed environment response mechanism and WMs under fixed action interventions. The Agent evaluation compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The World Model evaluation comprises 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario; 15 of 16 configurations cover all eight scenarios, and one covers six. GPT 6 Astra attains the highest Agent Index of 31.3 under the selected case-count weights, while GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall scores at 21.7. These track-specific scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. Agent strengths remain category-specific, and the aggregate ordering depends on the domain mixture. The evaluations characterize task-specific execution and state-transition performance. They provide a basis for studying reliable MA–WM interaction, while whether these capabilities predict coupled performance or sustained reciprocal improvement remains to be tested.
Figure 1:
Agent–World Model interaction and the scope of Dual Exam.
World Models can provide simulated observations and action-conditioned predictions, while Agent trajectories can provide interaction evidence. The four domains illustrate complementary application settings. Dual Exam evaluates the two components separately under controlled conditions; the arrows describe potential uses of their interaction rather than demonstrated gains from joint training. The task labels in this overview are illustrative; the evaluated Agent categories and counts are specified in Table
5
.
1

Introduction
World Models (WMs) and Multimodal Agents (MAs) can improve each other in complementary ways. WMs support MAs through simulated experience and action-conditioned predictions
(
Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018
;
Hafner et al., 2025
;
Gu et al., 2025
)
, while MA interaction trajectories provide feedback for refining WMs
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Yu et al., 2026
)
. Recent work has coupled the two in specific settings
(
Fang et al., 2025
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
. For example, a web agent can use a world model to anticipate candidate clicks, while its trajectories provide data for model refinement
(
Fang et al., 2025
)
. Broader multimodal interaction requires both effective action selection and faithful responses to those actions. We assess these complementary requirements across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains
(
Chu et al., 2026
)
. Our focus is task-specific component performance; the relationship between these measurements and gains from joint training requires separate validation.
However, reciprocal improvement requires both MAs and WMs to remain reliable over repeated interaction. MAs still struggle with visual grounding, action sequencing, and sustained task completion
(
Xie et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Sun et al., 2026
)
. WMs also face challenges in memory consistency and action control
(
Ye et al., 2026b
)
. Visual fidelity or state similarity alone does not guarantee improved planning or successful task completion
(
Shang et al., 2026a
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
. These weaknesses become more apparent when MAs and WMs are coupled. The output of one repeatedly becomes the input to the other. WM-based simulation can improve planning
(
Gu et al., 2025
)
, but the planning benefits depend on behavioral coverage, environment complexity, and whether the MA can use the predicted outcomes
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Qian et al., 2026a
)
. Model bias may also accumulate over repeated rollouts
(
Janner et al., 2019
)
. End-to-end performance can show that the coupled system fails, but not why. Failures may come from MA decisions, WM responses, or their interaction. A component-level evaluation is therefore needed to characterize the capabilities that end-to-end outcomes alone cannot reveal.
Our preliminary study tests one MA–WM pairing on 150 cases across ten scenarios, with 0% task success under the stated protocol (Section
2.1
). The trajectories reveal state discrepancies and limited responses, but do not identify which component caused each failure. This motivates

Experiments

Experiments
Following the coupled pilot, we evaluate the two components separately. Table
3
compares 10 Agent configurations across 15 reporting categories and 1,088 evaluation items. The World Model evaluation uses 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario; Table
4
reports scenario scores and distinguishes full from partial coverage. Agent Index and WM Overall use different tasks, metrics, and aggregation rules and are not directly comparable. Appendices
A
and
B
provide illustrative trajectories. These examples explain particular behaviors rather than estimate failure frequencies or establish controlled comparisons between historical configurations.
3.1
Agent Results: RQ1
Execution performance varies across task settings.
The fixed-environment track measures Agent performance without variation from a candidate World Model. The highest displayed scores are 9.5 for Manipulation, 11.2 for Action Sequencing, and 5.6 for Desktop Application Interaction. Other settings yield higher maxima: 29.6 for Web Interaction, 42.9 for Mobile Application Interaction, and 47.1 for Game Environment Interaction. These contrasts describe performance under the respective task requirements and scoring rules; they do not isolate the effect of the interaction setting or establish equal difficulty across categories. The results nevertheless show that a high aggregate score can coexist with low scores on particular execution tasks.
Locally correct elements may fail to form a valid solution.
The illustrative Navigation cases distinguish valid feasibility judgments from routes containing nonexistent edges. The Action Sequencing cases similarly distinguish correct clip membership from correct ordering. In each setting, recognizing relevant elements is insufficient when their combination violates the task’s constraints. These examples motivate explicit checks of route validity, ordering, and goal satisfaction during execution. They illustrate possible failure mechanisms but do not establish their frequency in the current evaluation or their causal contribution to model rankings.
Scientific scores combine distinct evaluation units.
Across 109 Scientific items, GPT 6 Astra has the highest within-domain case-weighted score of 50.6, followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 44.0 and GPT 5.6 Sol at 42.2. The category leaders differ: Astra leads Mathematics & Computation (60.8) and Physical Sciences (52.2), Sol leads Health & Medicine (45.4), and DeepSeek leads Life Sciences (53.7). These scores combine 63 ALE tasks, 30 SWE-bench repair tasks, ten derived ToolChoice checkpoints, and six EdgeBench optimization tasks. SWE and ToolChoice contribute strict binary outcomes, while Edge contributes graded quality scores under the mapping in Appendix
A.13
, including our explicit clipping convention for Borden and DABIC. The domain mean is therefore not a uniform success rate, and the related ToolChoice checkpoints do not constitute independent full-workflow trials.
Aggregate rank depends on task composition.
GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index with 31.3, followed by GPT 5.6 Sol at 20.7 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at 20.1. Qwen 3.8 Max ranks fourth at 20.0 and Kimi K3 fifth at 19.8. Four configurations attain the highest displayed score in at least one category: GPT 6 Astra leads nine categories, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads three, GPT 5.6 Sol leads two, and Seed 2.1 Pro leads one. No configuration leads every category. Equal-domain weighting changes several positions: DeepSeek moves from sixth to second and Kimi from fifth to fourth, while GPT 6 Astra remains first (Appendix
A.2
). Physical tasks account for 48.16% of Index and Scientific tasks for 10.02%; these weights reflect the inventory rather than equal domain importance. These rankings describe the chosen aggregation rules and evaluated model–harness configurations. Small differences derived from rounded baseline means do not establish statistically significant superiority.
Table 3:
Agent leaderboard by overall Index.
10 model configurations are compared across 15 task categories and 1,088 evaluation items on a 0–100 scale.
N
N
is the number of items. Index uses case-count weights (524 Physical, 255 Digital, 200 Social, and 109 Scientific); it is not an equal-domain average. Bold and underline indicate the highest and second-highest distinct scores, including ties. Model columns are ordered by Index from highest to lowest, using the aggregates recomputed from displayed category scores before final rounding for ordering and Index highlights.

Discussion
4.1

Conclusion
Dual Exam evaluates Multimodal Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions, producing complementary performance profiles across four domains. The Agent evaluation compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories; GPT 6 Astra achieves the highest case-weighted Index of 31.3. The World Model evaluation contains 400 cases across eight scenarios, with 50 cases per scenario. GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall scores at 21.7. Configuration-specific coverage is reported separately, and the two tracks use different tasks and metrics, so their aggregate scores are not directly comparable. Scientific evaluation spans 109 items and combines strict repair and checkpoint outcomes with graded optimization scores; Astra leads its within-domain aggregate at 50.6. Category leaders differ, and equal-domain weighting changes the overall ordering below the leading configuration. The results characterize model–harness performance under the evaluated specifications and weighting choices, subject to the documented evidence and precision limits. Predicting coupled success and demonstrating sustained reciprocal improvement require matched interaction and learning experiments beyond these separate assessments.

article.headline: Dual Exam：分开评测智能体与世界模型
article.lede: 论文提出 Dual Exam 框架，在固定环境响应与固定动作干预下分别评测多模态智能体与世界模型，而不只看端到端耦合结果
article.problem: 世界模型可为多模态智能体提供模拟经验与动作条件预测，智能体的交互轨迹也可反过来用于改进世界模型，但两者耦合后的端到端失败无法说明问题出在智能体决策、世界模型响应还是二者交互。作者在一项预实验中用一个智能体–世界模型组合在十个场景的150个案例上测试，按所设协议任务成功率为0%，轨迹显示出状态偏差与响应能力不足，却无法定位失败来源。
article.method: Dual Exam 把两部分拆开评测：智能体侧在固定的环境响应机制下比较10个配置，覆盖物理、数字、社交与科学四个域、15个报告类别、共1,088个评测项；世界模型侧在固定动作干预下评测400个案例、八个场景，每个场景50例，16个配置中有15个覆盖全部八个场景，1个只覆盖六个。两条评测线使用不同任务、指标与聚合规则，因此各自的汇总分数不可直接比较。
article.results: 在按案例数加权的 Agent Index 上，GPT 6 Astra 以31.3居首，GPT 5.6 Sol 为20.7、Gemini 3.6 Flash 为20.1、Qwen 3.8 Max 为20.0、Kimi K3 为19.8；没有任何配置在所有类别领先，Astra 领先九个类别、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 三个、Sol 两个、Seed 2.1 Pro 一个。科学域109个评测项中 Astra 取得最高的域内得分50.6，其次是 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的44.0和 Sol 的42.2，但分项领先者不同（Astra 在数学与计算60.8、物理科学52.2，Sol 在健康与医学45.4，DeepSeek 在生命科学53.7）。世界模型侧，GPT-Image-2 在覆盖全部八个场景的配置中以21.7的 WM Overall 领先。Index 中物理任务占48.16%、科学任务占10.02%；若改为等域加权，DeepSeek 从第六升至第二、Kimi 从第五升至第四，Astra 仍居第一。
article.why_it_matters: 把智能体执行能力与世界模型状态转移能力分开测量，为研究二者交互提供了可复现的组件级基线，也说明单一端到端分数不足以诊断耦合系统的瓶颈。
article.limitations: 智能体与世界模型两条评测线的任务、指标和聚合方式不同，作者明确表示其汇总分数不可直接比较；排名依赖案例数与域混合的加权选择，等域加权即改变多个位次，且由取整后的均值造成的小差距不足以证明统计显著优势。这些测量能否预测耦合表现、以及联合训练是否带来持续互惠提升，论文并未验证。

page_papers.title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
page_papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

Introduction
Developing general robot brains
damo2026rynnbrain
,
li2026rynnbrain11capablegeneralizable
requires models that understand the physical world, anticipate interaction outcomes, and translate task intentions into action. Across interdependent operations, a robot must identify subgoals, predict scene changes, and determine how they affect subsequent decisions. These demands motivate unified embodied models that coordinate understanding, world prediction, and action generation
cosmos3
,
liang2026rxbrain
.
Existing unified multimodal models (UMMs) have made encouraging progress in jointly modeling understanding and generation
cosmos3
,
liang2026rxbrain
,
deng2025bagel
. Their coordination requires strong embodied understanding to ground task intentions, reason about physical interactions, and interpret predicted outcomes. Sustaining this interaction over long horizons remains challenging as scene changes and prediction errors accumulate, while static visual predictions can overlook intermediate dynamics. Addressing these challenges requires interleaved reasoning
hou2026interlv
that connects embodied understanding with temporally coherent video prediction.
To this end, we introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model built upon the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture
liang2025mixtureoftransformers
of Cosmos3
cosmos3
, comprising an 8B autoregressive reasoner and an 8B diffusion generator. Centered on
interleaved video-language reasoning
, RynnUnify combines strong embodied understanding with video prediction to support understanding-guided long-horizon visual planning: the reasoner guides successive video predictions, whose outcomes provide context for subsequent subtask planning. To explore generation-enhanced embodied understanding, we further post-train an additional 8B agent from RynnUnify’s reasoner through reinforcement learning with final-answer feedback. The agent dynamically chooses between direct answering and invoking the frozen RynnUnify model to generate videos, which it then interprets to answer questions about unobserved future states and interaction outcomes. To bring the UMM’s understanding and world-prediction capabilities to robot control, we also extend the full RynnUnify model to a World-Action Model (WAM) through latent planning and joint video-action training.
We perform extensive pretraining on general multimodal understanding, spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and affordance grounding, complemented by subtask planning, world-modeling descriptions, and question answering with intermediate video context. This supervision strengthens foundational embodied understanding while preparing the reasoner to formulate task-relevant visual predictions and interpret their outcomes. Generation training covers long-horizon egocentric activities, robot manipulation, and embodied reasoning videos. We introduce scene memory and self-forcing
huang2025selfforcing
to improve visual consistency and robustness during long-horizon generation.
Dedicated benchmarks remain lacking for assessing sustained visual planning and the contribution of video prediction to future-state reasoning. We therefore introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU. Rynn-VP evaluates whether visual plans remain consistent with the task and preceding operations over long horizons. Rynn-GEU focuses on action consequences, physical changes, and spatial relationships after motion or viewpoint changes, whose answers concern states not directly observable in the input. Its direct setting tests whether models can infer these states without explicit video generation, while its generation-assisted setting tests whether predicted videos improve answers to the same questions.
Extensive evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art embodied understanding among the evaluated UMMs on public benchmarks, together with strong video generation performance. RynnUnify also demonstrates sustained planning on Rynn-VP and strong direct anticipatory reasoning on Rynn-GEU, with further GEU improvements through its agentic extension. For robot control, the WAM extension achieves a 51.5% success rate on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365
robocasa365
tasks. Experiments on Astribot S1 further demonstrate effective multi-step manipulation involving body reorientation, precise object handling, and history-dependent execution.
Figure
1
summarizes RynnUnify’s capabilities and representative evaluation results.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce RynnUnify, a unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with interleaved video-language reasoning for long-horizon visual planning.
•
We post-train an agent from RynnUnify’s reasoner to explore generation-enhanced embodied understanding, demonstrating the utility of video predictions for reasoning about unobserved future states.
•
We extend the full RynnUnify UMM to a WAM through latent planning and joint video-action training, and validate its capabilities in simulated and real-robot manipulation.
•
We introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory embodied reasoning, complemented by extensive evaluations on public benchmarks that establish RynnUnify’s state-of-the-art embodied understanding among the compared UMMs.
2
Model Architecture
Figure 2
:
Overview of the RynnUnify architecture.
(a) An autoregressive reasoner and a rectified-flow video generator interact through joint attention. (b) Memory-conditioned video generation supports I2V, FL2V, and autoregressive video continuation. Scene-memory frames provide persistent visual references, while a fixed temporal prefix carries recent motion and interaction context across consecutive clips.
As shown in Figure
2
, RynnUnify adopts the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT)
liang2025mixtureoftransformers
architecture of Cosmos3
cosmos3
. The model comprises an autoregressive reasoner for multimodal understanding and language generation, and a diffusion generator for predicting continuous visual latents through rectified flow
liu2022flow
. The two branches use separate Transformer parameters and interact through joint attention, allowing the generator to attend to representations produced by the reasoner. We retain the reasoner architecture unchanged and extend the generator’s visual conditioning to incorporate cross-chunk scene memory and support first-and-last-frame-conditioned generation. These extensions provide persistent scene references and continuous interaction context for visual predictions across successive subtasks.
2.1
Reasoner
We retain the autoregressive reasoner of Cosmos3
cosmos3
without architectural modifications. The reasoner processes multimodal observations and language context to support embodied understanding, spatial grounding, and task planning. For visual planning, it takes the task goal, initial and current observations, and preceding subtask history as input, and predicts the next executable subtask together with a detailed description of its anticipated visual evolution and an estimated duration. These outputs provide the generator with structured textual conditions specifying the intended interaction and its temporal extent. During multi-step rollout, the final frame of each generated clip becomes the updated observation for subsequent reasoning, connecting subtask planning with the visual consequences of preceding predictions.
2.2
Visual tokenization and input organization.
For video generation, we encode visual inputs using a causal video VAE with spatial and temporal compression factors of 16 and 4, respectively. The resulting latents are spatially patchified into visual tokens. Both scene-memory frames and the main video follow this VAE pathway and are processed by the generator branch.
Each scene-memory frame is encoded independently, producing a group of visual tokens that represents its spatial content. Four reference frames therefore correspond to four groups of tokens, whose individual lengths depend on the frame resolutions. When scene memory is enabled, these groups are placed after the reasoner’s textual context and before the main video tokens:

2.3
Cross-chunk scene memory.
Long-horizon planning requires the model to retain visual information beyond the current observation, particularly when objects or scene regions leave the field of view. We maintain four reference frames comprising a persistent initial observation, two keyframes selected across earlier history, and a reference associated with the most recent step. This selection preserves both broader scene coverage and recent task context. When the history is insufficient, additional frames are selected from available historical clips; at the first step, the initial observation is repeated to fill the reference slots. During rollout, the initial observation remains fixed while the historical references are updated from generated videos.
We complement these sparse references with a continuous video prefix from the preceding chunk. Unlike the independently encoded memory frames, this prefix occupies the beginning of the main video’s temporal sequence. The preceding tail and the current segment form a continuous sequence, with the shared boundary frame included only once. The reference frames serve as visual anchors for scene appearance and layout, while the temporal prefix preserves recent motion and interaction context. Together, they form cross-chunk scene memory for successive visual predictions.
2.4
Generation modes and fixed conditions.
We support three generation modes through different arrangements of visual conditions within the main video sequence. In image-to-video (I2V) generation, the first latent frame is fixed to the encoded starting observation, and the model predicts the subsequent video. In first-and-last-frame-to-video (FL2V) generation, both the first and final latent frames are fixed, providing boundary conditions for generating the intervening transition. In cross-chunk video continuation, the initial latent frames are fixed to a continuous prefix from the preceding video’s tail, allowing the model to predict the next segment from recent motion and interaction context. During multi-step rollout, this prefix is extracted from the previously generated video.
Across these modes, the scene-memory latents and the conditioning latents within the main video remain fixed throughout denoising. The generator updates the remaining video positions while attending to the textual context and visual conditions. During training, only the positions to be predicted contribute to the generation loss. The same conditioning interface accommodates observed and self-generated visual inputs, supporting the self-forcing strategies used during generator fine-tuning.
2.5
Textual and temporal conditioning.
The generator receives structured textual conditions containing the subtask instruction, a detailed description of the anticipated visual evolution, and the requested duration. These conditions connect task-level reasoning with the content and temporal extent of each video prediction. We support variable-length video sequences of the VAE-compatible form

For cross-chunk continuation, the requested duration describes the new operation and excludes the historical prefix. The reasoner can therefore specify what should happen next and for how long, while the generator predicts the corresponding visual changes using the scene memory and temporal conditions.

3.1
General Understanding Data
To maintain broad embodied understanding and reasoning capabilities, we use a 10% subset of the RynnBrain pretraining corpus
li2026rynnbrain11capablegeneralizable
as the foundation of our understanding data. Reasoning about embodied tasks requires the model to interpret task intentions, recognize objects and their properties, understand spatial relationships, and track changes across successive observations. These capabilities are particularly important for long-horizon visual planning, where each subtask must be grounded in the current scene and considered in relation to subsequent operations. They also support the interaction between understanding and video generation: the model needs to identify which aspects of the scene are relevant to a task, formulate the corresponding visual prediction, and interpret the predicted changes to inform further reasoning.
The data cover general image and video understanding, visual question answering, temporal reasoning, and instruction following, together with embodied cognition tasks including object understanding, spatial reasoning, counting, and egocentric task understanding. Spatially grounded supervision further covers object, area, and affordance localization, trajectory prediction, and manipulation planning, connecting language instructions with explicit locations and interaction targets. We combine this foundational supervision with our visual planning and embodied perception and reasoning data to develop interleaved video–language reasoning while retaining a broad range of understanding capabilities. This combination is intended to support both direct responses to embodied questions and the interpretation of visual evidence produced during task-oriented video prediction.

article.headline: 达摩院推出16B统一具身模型
article.lede: 阿里达摩院RynnUnify把具身理解、长程视频规划与机器人动作整合进一个16B模型，并给出仿真与真机评测。
article.problem: 现有统一多模态模型虽能同时做理解与生成，但在长程任务中场景变化与预测误差会逐步累积，静态视觉预测也容易忽略中间动态。机器人需要在一个模型里连贯地识别子目标、预测场景演化并把任务意图转成动作。论文认为，这要求把具身理解与时间上连贯的视频预测通过交替式推理连接起来。
article.method: RynnUnify沿用Cosmos3的Mixture-of-Transformers架构，由8B自回归推理器和8B扩散生成器组成，二者通过联合注意力交互；生成器引入跨视频片段场景记忆、首尾帧条件与视频续写。作者还用强化学习从推理器后训练出8B智能体，让它自行选择直接回答或调用冻结的RynnUnify生成视频再解读；并把完整模型扩展为世界-动作模型，通过潜在规划与视频-动作联合训练输出动作块。
article.results: 论文称，RynnUnify在所受评测的统一多模态模型中取得最高的平均具身理解分数；在自建Rynn-VP上总体分数比Cosmos 3 Nano高9.75分。智能体扩展使Rynn-GEU平均分比直接推理高6.0分；世界-动作扩展在20个选定的复合RoboCasa365任务上成功率为51.5%，在三个真机任务上平均成功率为46.7%。
article.why_it_matters: 它尝试用同一个基座覆盖具身理解、长程视觉规划与机器人控制，并通过视频预测辅助推理未观测状态，为“统一具身大脑”提供了一条可评测的工程路径。
article.limitations: 论文正文未给出专门的局限性讨论；评测集中在所选20个RoboCasa365复合任务和三个真机任务，Rynn-VP与Rynn-GEU又是作者新提出的基准，缺乏第三方复现。长程 rollout 中的误差累积、场景记忆失效条件以及跨机器人平台泛化仍待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: RynnUnify-VLA总览：模型处理任务指令、视觉历史与当前观测，进行子任务推理和视频预测，动作专家利用生成器的视频隐状态预测动作块；联合视频-动作训练时生成器与动作专家被优化，推理器保持冻结。

An action expert uses the generator's video hidden states to predict action chunks. During joint video-action training, the generator and action expert are optimized while the reasoner remains frozen.

page_papers.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
page_papers.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

Abstract
Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

1
Introduction
Figure 1:
A low stop signal (SS, orange) value indicates ongoing execution, where a high failure signal (FS, purple) value marks recoverable failure and guides correction. High SS with low or high FS values indicates success (top) or terminal failure (bottom) respectively.
Vision Language Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in robotic manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions
(
Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2026
)
. Reliable execution also requires recognizing whether a task is ongoing, has succeeded, or has failed to determine when to continue, stop, or intervene. Existing methods predict progress, completion, or failure signals either within VLA policies or through external monitoring models
(
Apanasevich et al., 2026
;
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
However, existing approaches face two limitations. First, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained frame-level supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs
(
Pacaud et al., 2025
;
Feng et al., 2026
;
Yan et al., 2026
;
Deng et al., 2026
)
. Second, the predicted signals are typically used only for monitoring, leaving their potential to improve action generation underexplored
(
Pacaud et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
.
We present Echo, a compact framework that jointly denoises robot actions and task status signals within a single VLA, learning the signals without frame-level progress annotations and using them to improve action generation. Echo represents task status through a stop signal (SS), indicating whether execution should terminate, and a failure signal (FS), indicating whether execution is in a failure state. Low SS indicates ongoing execution, while high SS with low FS indicates successful completion, and high SS with high FS indicates terminal failure. Within ongoing execution, elevated FS indicates a recoverable failure, as shown in Figure
1
. Echo appends SS and FS as two additional dimensions of each action chunk and denoises them together with robot actions. This formulation reuses the VLA’s visual, language, and robot-state features with little additional parameter overhead.
To learn these signals without frame-level progress annotations, Echo combines successful demonstrations, failed policy rollouts, pre-intervention failure segments, and recovery demonstrations using subtask-level prompts together with success or failure labels. Failed rollouts and pre-intervention failure segments supervise terminal and recoverable failures, respectively, while their actions are excluded from imitation. Recovery demonstrations pair similar status supervision with corrective actions at corresponding recoverable failure states, linking failure recognition to recovery behavior.
To use the learned status information during action generation, Echo controls interactions among SS, FS, and robot actions while preserving accurate and complementary signal predictions. It also introduces asynchronous denoising, denoising signal tokens faster than action tokens so that later action denoising steps condition on cleaner status estimates. When the policy recognizes a recoverable failure with low SS and elevated FS, these estimates, together with the current observations, can guide action generation toward corrective behavior learned from recovery demonstrations.
Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate accurate task-status prediction and improved performance over action-only baselines, with larger out-of-distribution gains. Component ablations, signal interventions, and failure-data scaling analyses examine how status signals influence action generation and how different data sources contribute to prediction and execution.
Our contributions are threefold: 1) We introduce a compact task status representation that incorporates stop and failure signals into VLA action chunks with little additional parameter overhead. 2) We develop a supervision scheme that learns these signals from successful, failed, and recovery data without frame-level progress annotations. 3) We design controlled interactions and asynchronous denoising to couple status prediction with action generation.
2
Related Works
Task Status Signal Modeling.
Task status signals characterize task progress, completion, and failure
(
Kim et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026c
;
Dai et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Liufu et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. Visual-language reward models learn execution quality through representation learning, temporal supervision, and trajectory comparisons
(
Ma et al., 2023
;
Alakuijala et al., 2024
;
Ayalew et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Liang et al., 2026
)
. When deployed as standalone evaluators, these models introduce additional evaluation alongside the control policy. Complementary approaches predict completion
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
or detect failures using policy features, temporal consistency, uncertainty, and visual reasoning
(
Gu et al., 2026
;
Park et al., 2026
;
Agia et al., 2024
;
Xu et al., 2025
;
Duan et al., 2024
)
. Progress can also be extracted through lightweight probes
(
Bhardwaj et al., 2026
)
. Although feature-based monitoring reduces overhead, accurate signal extraction alone does not ensure action feedback. Jointly achieving reliable task status prediction and signal-guided action adjustment with low overhead remains underexplored.
Task Status Signals for Action Improvement.
Task status feedback improves policies through several mechanisms. VLAC
(
Zhai et al., 2025
)
uses critic tokens to estimate rewards for
online reinforcement learning, while GRAPE
(
Zhang et al., 2024
)
optimizes policies using trajectory preferences; both require additional policy updates. Other methods use execution assessments to trigger backtracking, intervention, or corrective control
(
Ma et al., 2026
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2024
)
. More directly, VLA-Corrector
(
Pan et al., 2026
)
monitors visual dynamics deviations and applies gradient-guided corrective replanning, while ProgressVLA
(
Yan et al., 2026
)
propagates progress gradients through a world model to guide action denoising. These mechanisms demonstrate the utility of execution feedback, but introduce additional policy optimization, monitoring and recovery components, or inference-time gradient computation. Preserving accurate status estimates while directly improving action generation with minimal additional training and inference overhead remains an open challenge.

3.2.2
Data Construction and Supervision
We collect successful demonstrations through teleoperation and terminal failure rollouts during policy testing. During policy execution, operators intervene when recoverable failures occur, yielding pre-intervention failure segments before human takeover and recovery demonstrations afterward. Recovery demonstrations may complete a local correction or the entire instructed task. The collected data are aggregated to update the policy for subsequent collection rounds.
We construct action, SS, and FS supervision from segment types, boundaries, and positions within recovery segments, without additional frame-level progress annotations. Table

Action supervision.
Successful demonstrations and recovery demonstrations provide task-execution and corrective actions, respectively. We exclude actions from both terminal and pre-intervention failure data to avoid imitating unsuccessful behavior. Successful demonstrations receive action supervision over the entire chunk, including padding. Recovery actions are supervised only at non-padding positions: a recovery segment may end before the instructed task is complete, and learning its padded actions could cause the policy to stop prematurely.
Stop signal supervision.
Chunks without padding receive zero SS targets at all positions. For chunks containing padding, the targets depend on whether the segment boundary marks the end of execution. Successful demonstrations end upon completion, while terminal failure rollouts end after an unrecoverable failure. Both therefore use the padding mask as the SS target, with supervision over the entire chunk.
Pre-intervention segments end at operator takeover, and task execution continues through recovery. Their SS targets are therefore zero everywhere, including padding, and are fully supervised. For recovery segments, we also set the full SS target to zero but supervise only non-padding positions. Recovery may end after a local correction or upon full task completion, so its boundary does not consistently indicate whether execution should stop. Excluding padded positions avoids assigning an incorrect termination target.
Failure signal supervision.
Successful demonstrations contain successful execution without failure, so FS targets are zero over the entire chunk. For terminal and pre-intervention failure data, the segment-level labels indicate failure but do not identify its onset. We therefore omit FS supervision for chunks without padding. The segment endpoint, however, is known to be in a failure state. For chunks containing padding, we use the padding mask as the FS target and supervise the full chunk, assigning one to padded positions and zero elsewhere. This provides a boundary-based target without requiring the precise failure onset to be annotated.

We first report main results and comparisons with existing methods to evaluate the accuracy of Echo’s task status signals and their benefit to task execution. We then analyze in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance and ablate the model components. Asynchronous denoising.
Synchronous denoising uses the same flow time for actions and signals during training and inference. It causes only a modest decrease in frame-level accuracy but degrades task completion and timely outcome recognition. This supports making cleaner status estimates available earlier to guide subsequent action updates.

4.4.4
Effect of Failure Data Quantity
On Insert Flower, we vary the number of terminal-failure trajectories using nested subsets of 50, 120, 190, and 250 trajectories, with 250 used in the main experiments. The other three data types, training settings, and failure-data sampling proportion remain fixed. Thus, larger subsets provide more diverse failure examples without increasing their share of training samples.
Figure
6
shows that frame-level status prediction improves as the failure dataset grows, while task-completion scores remain broadly stable. This is consistent with the role of terminal-failure data: they supervise the distinction between terminal failure and successful completion, while their actions are excluded from imitation. Broader coverage of terminal-failure states thus enriches status supervision without directly supplying additional corrective actions.
The stable completion scores are also consistent with adjustment and recovery depending primarily on the pre-intervention and recovery data held fixed in this experiment. Pre-intervention failures supervise signals at recoverable errors, while recovery demonstrations provide corrective actions. Together, these observations support the complementary roles of terminal-failure supervision and recovery-related data.

5
Conclusions
We presented Echo, a compact framework that jointly denoises actions and task status signals within a single VLA. Echo learns from successful, failed, and recovery data without frame-level progress annotations, using controlled interactions and asynchronous denoising to guide action generation. Experiments on five real-world tasks demonstrate accurate status prediction and improved task completion, supporting the use of task status signals for both monitoring and action generation.

Appendix A
Appendix
A.1
Robot Platform and Task Details
Robot platform.
Data collection and policy deployment use a wheeled humanoid robot with two seven-degree-of-freedom arms, gripper end effectors, and a waist–leg mechanism with six degrees of freedom. The mobile base remains stationary during task execution. The policy controls a total of 20 degrees of freedom through the two arm end effectors, the grippers, and the waist–leg mechanism. Visual observations come from three RGB cameras: one on the head and one on each wrist.
Common evaluation protocol.
All tasks start from the same initial robot state. Task objects are placed at the evaluation positions described below. Each episode has a maximum duration of five minutes. An episode is classified as a failure if the task remains incomplete at the time limit, or if the robot reaches an unsafe posture indicating an imminent risk of tipping before completing the task.
Task objectives and evaluation positions.
We evaluate five tasks: Insert Flower, Capsule Toy, Insert Pen, Make Tanghulu, and Open Drawer. Table

Action-only

The baseline uses the same successful and recovery action-supervision data as Echo, with matched optimizer settings and training steps. It predicts actions without SS or FS, so status metrics are not assigned to it. During implementation, we ensured that key settings including training data, model learning rate, and optimizer were consistent with Echo. The model was trained for the same number of steps until convergence.
CycleVLA.
CycleVLA combines a progress-aware VLA with external failure prediction and subtask backtracking.
When reproducing its performance, we trained using demonstration success data and DAgger recovery data. And we adopted a learning rate of 5e-5 and the Adam optimizer for 20k training steps (aligned with the training protocol of Echo). Since its stop signal is only supervised on the final frame, and success/failure judgment mainly relies on the progress signal, we take the maximum stop signal within the model’s actually executed frames and the average of the corresponding progress signals, apply a threshold of 0.5 to both quantities, and construct frame-level and trajectory-level state prediction discrimination accordingly. As illustrated in Figure
7

VLA-Corrector.
The VLA-Corrector considered here compares predicted and observed visual feature evolution using a latent-space vision monitor. Persistent deviations trigger action-chunk truncation and corrective replanning with Online Gradient Guidance. It does not itself establish terminal failure, so status metrics are not assigned to it.
When reproducing its performance, we adopted the frozen baseline

0.5

In practical testing, we corrected the VLA action chunk via the Online Gradient Guidance approach and the cutoff-only method, then we compared their performance and reported the better-performing one.
Robometer.
Robometer is an external video-language reward model with progress and success predictions trained using trajectory-based supervision, including preference comparisons.
When reproducing its performance, we trained the officially released Robometer-4B base model via LoRA fine-tuning. We trained for 20k iterations on all data of the Insert Flower task using its officially recommended configuration and evaluated its performance offline. Since Robometer does not provide estimations for task termination, we classify all “in-progress” samples as failures during evaluation, reducing the original 3-class classification problem to binary classification. We compute the final metrics by applying a threshold of 0.5 on the success probability output by the model.

A.9
Compatibility with External Monitoring and Planning
Echo improves the VLA policy itself by allowing learned task-status information to participate in action generation. This objective is compatible with external monitoring, recovery and planning modules. SS and FS can also provide execution-status information to a higher-level controller using the signal semantics defined in the main text.
An external controller could combine these signals with broader temporal context or additional observations to verify completion, request intervention or replan. Echo supplies policy-internal status estimates and corrective action generation, while the external module adds its own decision logic. This is architectural compatibility; improved performance from a particular combined system requires a separate evaluation.

article.headline: 让VLA自己判断该停还是该救
article.lede: Echo把停止与失败信号拼进动作块一起去噪，令信号先于动作收敛，在五个真实操作任务上提升完成度。
article.problem: VLA策略在真实机器人上执行时，需要判断任务是在进行中、已成功还是已失败，才能决定继续、停止或介入恢复。现有做法要么依赖帧级进度标注、外部监控模型或复杂架构，要么只把预测出的状态信号用于监控，很少用它直接改进动作生成。
article.method: Echo用停止信号（SS）和失败信号（FS）表示任务状态，把两者作为动作块的两个附加维度，与机器人动作一起做流匹配去噪。监督来自成功演示、失败轨迹、人工介入前的失败片段和恢复演示四类数据，仅靠子任务级提示加成功或失败标签构造目标，不需要帧级进度标注。推理时屏蔽SS与FS之间的直接注意力以保持语义区分，并让信号比动作更早收敛（τ_clean=0.5），使后续动作去噪步条件于更干净的状态估计。
article.results: 在五个真实操作任务上各做30次试验，Echo的完成分均高于只用动作的π0.5基线：Insert Flower从5.67±0.92升至8.33±0.69，Capsule Toy从8.40升至8.57，Insert Pen从6.87升至8.60，Make Tanghulu从4.33升至5.33，Open Drawer从5.40升至7.90；对应帧级Macro-F1为88.01%–92.18%，轨迹级F1为90.00%–100.00%。分布外条件下增益更大：Insert Flower从2.00±1.07升至8.00±1.07，Open Drawer从2.40±1.06升至6.87±0.29（各15次试验）。在Insert Flower上与CycleVLA（3.00）、VLA-Corrector（5.67）比较均占优。LIBERO-Recovery仿真4,500次试验成功率34.76%对32.67%，帧级状态准确率89.97%；推理延迟在RTX 4090上从115 ms增至120 ms。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“该停还是该救”的判断做进策略内部，无需外部监控模型或推理期梯度计算，为VLA的低成本失败恢复提供了一条可复用路径。信号干预实验显示，强行把FS置1会诱发机械臂上抬的恢复动作，说明状态信号确实在引导动作生成，而不只是在旁观测。
article.limitations: 与现有方法的对比、全部消融和信号干预只在Insert Flower一个任务上完成；分布内增益有限，Insert Flower的分布内完成分反而从9.33降到8.67。状态判定对SS阈值较敏感，单一0.5阈值并非每个任务最优，轨迹级F1也随评估窗口长度大幅波动（如Capsule Toy在5帧窗口下仅26.7）。仿真提升只有2.09个百分点，且三个评估种子共用同一checkpoint，不构成独立训练重复。

page_papers.title: DirCast: Live Esports Directing and Commentary with a Single Streaming Video-Language Model
page_papers.abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.

Abstract
A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director’s choices and the casters’ commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.

Introduction
A live esports broadcast is produced by two people working in tight coordination. The director watches a wall of camera feeds, one per player, and decides every second which feed goes on air. The caster watches what the director puts on air and talks over it, naming the heroes, calling the fights, and filling the quiet moments with analysis. Neither job can wait for the future. When a fight breaks out on the far side of the map, the director has a few seconds to cut to it, and the caster has to describe it while it is still happening. This is why professional broadcasts need trained crews, and why the long tail of matches, from regional leagues to amateur games, is streamed with a fixed camera and no commentary.

We present DirCast, a single causal video language model that directs and commentates at once. Every second, the model reads a short chunk that contains the new game events and the ten feeds at low resolution, each paired with a token that encodes the hero’s game state. A hold-or-switch director head then decides whether to keep the current shot or to cut, and a pointer over the ten feeds chooses where to cut to. The chosen feed is appended to the stream at high resolution, and the commentary is generated after it, so the commentator always speaks over the shot the director chose. Low-resolution feed tokens leave the context after a few seconds, while the on-air views and the spoken words stay. The memory of the model is the program it has produced, which keeps the cost per second bounded and lets DirCast run in real time on a single GPU.
Three further choices make the model robust when it runs on its own. We roll out perturbed programs during training, in which the on-air feed drifts away from the human choice for a few seconds while the targets stay human, so the director learns to recover from its own mistakes and the commentator learns to speak over any shot. We ground every kill in the event stream to the feed of the hero who made it, and we accept a cut to a fight participant as a correct directing decision, which teaches the director that action is worth showing even when the human chose otherwise. At inference, the thresholds for cutting and for speaking follow the running rates of the model’s own decisions toward the rates of human crews, which keeps the program lively and the commentary present without any tuning on test data.
To study the task we build a dataset from 27 professional Dota 2 matches. We render one camera per hero from the match replays, align the renders with the official broadcast, and label every second with the feed the human director put on air and the words the casters spoke. We evaluate commentary with the protocol of Proact-VL

43
]
and direct comparison against eleven streaming commentators, and we evaluate directing by agreement with the human director and by coverage of the kills in the match. DirCast wins 29.21 percent of its comparisons against GPT-4o, while the strongest streaming commentator wins 19.38 percent, even though every baseline is given the finished human broadcast and DirCast directs its own. It starts speaking 0.30 seconds after the human casters on average. As a director, it agrees with the human crew more often than every rule-based and zero-shot director, it covers 89.1 percent of kills, and it cuts at a rate close to the human crew. The best zero-shot vision language model agrees with the human crew only two points more often than a static director that never cuts, and GPT-5 agrees less often. Trained as one model, DirCast is also better at both roles than two models trained separately, with half the memory.

•
We introduce live broadcast production, directing and commentating a live match from raw camera feeds, with a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches.

3
Dataset
Live broadcast production needs data that no existing video corpus provides. A broadcast shows one camera at a time, and the cameras the director did not choose are lost. To learn directing, a model has to see every camera the director could have chosen, together with the one the director actually put on air and the words the casters spoke over it.
Esports make this possible. A professional Dota 2 match is fully described by its replay file, so the game can be played back and filmed from any point of view after the fact. We collect 27 recent professional matches with their official broadcasts. For every match we render ten cameras from the replay with the game’s own spectator client, one following each hero. We then align the rendered timeline with the broadcast and label every second with three complementary signals. The first is the on-air camera, the hero feed that best matches what the broadcast shows at that second. The second is the state of the broadcast, which separates live gameplay from replays, overlays and breaks, so that only live seconds count as directing decisions. The third is the commentary, transcribed from the broadcast audio with word timestamps and cleaned following the Proact-VL polishing pipeline, which corrects misheard hero and player names while keeping the timing of every word. From the replay we further extract the state of every hero at every second, such as health, nearby enemies and recent damage, and the stream of game events, such as kills and destroyed buildings, each placed at the second it happens.
We cut the aligned matches into clips of 36 seconds at one frame per second, the setting used by streaming commentary benchmarks. The split is by match, with 20 matches for training, 3 for calibration and 4 for testing, so that no team, player or game of the test set is seen in training. The training set contains 2,096 clips and 21 hours of play, and the test set contains 496 clips and 5 hours. Human directors cut 7.9 times per minute on average and hold most shots for several seconds. The casters speak in about three quarters of all seconds. These two numbers describe the rhythm a model has to reproduce, and we return to them when we discuss inference.

Method
Every second, DirCast receives the ten camera frames and the new game events, decides which camera goes on air, and decides whether and what to say. It may only use the past. We build the model around one observation. A director and a commentator are not two separate systems that happen to run at the same time. The director decides what the audience sees, the commentator talks about what the audience sees, and both depend on what has been shown and said so far. We therefore use a single causal video language model for both roles, in which the commentary is generated after, and conditioned on, the directing decision. Figure

The order of the chunk follows the order in which a human crew works. The director scans all cameras at a glance, picks one, and the commentator then looks closely at the picture that went on air. A low-resolution view is enough to tell where the action is, while the commentator needs a sharper view to name heroes, items and abilities. DirCast therefore reads only the camera that goes on air at high resolution.

4.3
The program is the memory
A streaming model must forget, or its context grows without bound. The question is what to keep. A human crew does not remember what every camera showed a minute ago. It remembers the broadcast, the shots that actually went on air and what was said over them. DirCast keeps this. The low-resolution views of the ten cameras stay for only
W
W
seconds and then leave the context, while the high-resolution on-air views, the events and the words stay. During training this rule is an attention mask, and during streaming the expired entries are removed from the key-value cache. The model’s memory is the program it has produced. On streams longer than a training clip, every second also leaves the cache once it is older than a clip, so the cost per second stays constant over a match of any length.
4.4
Grounding the game
Video alone is a weak signal for directing. A fight that is about to start looks like two groups of heroes walking, and a kill on the far side of the map is a small change in one of ten thumbnails. The game itself knows more. The state token of each camera gives the model the hero’s health, recent damage and the enemies around it, and the event text states what happened, such as one hero killing another. We tie each event to the camera that shows it, so that the kill of a hero raises a flag on the camera of the hero who made it. The model thus reads the game in the same terms as the cameras it has to choose from.
4.5
Learning to direct from human broadcasts
DirCast is trained on human broadcasts with three objectives. A language modeling loss teaches the commentary, a binary loss on the commentary token teaches when to speak, and a directing loss teaches the gate and the pointer. The gate learns from the human cuts, and the pointer learns which camera the human chose at every cut, where a camera whose hero is visible in the broadcast shot counts as a correct answer as well.
Imitating human broadcasts directly leaves two gaps. The first gap is between training and deployment. During training the model always sees the program the human chose. At test time it sees its own program, and a single wrong cut moves it to a state it has never seen. We close this gap with on-policy program rollouts. During training, the on-air camera in the input drifts away from the human choice for a few seconds at a time, while the targets stay human. The director learns to recover from a wrong shot by cutting back, and the commentator learns to describe whatever is on air. The second gap is in the targets. A human director makes one choice among several good ones. When a kill happens on a camera that is not on air, cutting to it is a correct directing decision even if the human stayed elsewhere. We add an event-anchored target that, in the seconds around a kill, also accepts the cameras of the killer and the victim, and asks the gate to open when neither is on air. The model learns that action is worth showing, which is the part of directing that the human labels express least consistently.
4.6
Streaming decisions at a human rhythm
At inference, the model cuts when the gate exceeds a threshold and speaks when the probability of the commentary token exceeds a threshold. Fixed thresholds fail in streaming. A model that stays silent for a few seconds conditions on its own silence and becomes more likely to stay silent, and a director that has not cut for a while drifts the same way. We let both thresholds follow the model’s own behavior,

What makes a director.
Table
4
ablates the directing components. Removing the hold-or-switch pointer costs the most, dropping Top-1 from 27.00 to 21.65 (a relative loss of about 20%) and Any-vis. from 41.80 to 35.93, which confirms that an explicit hold-or-switch decision is the backbone of the director. Without it, the director must re-select a camera from scratch at every step, which likely leads to unmotivated switches. Removing state tokens or program rollouts also hurts, dropping Top-1 to 22.59 and 22.90 and Any-vis. to 37.98 and 38.01, showing that game state complements vision and that training under self-induced states matters. Program rollouts help the commentary as well: without them CC falls from 29.21 to 28.35, since a commentator that never sees its own drifted program is less prepared for the shots the director actually produces. Removing state tokens, by contrast, leaves CC unchanged at 29.21, so their benefit is confined to directing. Without event-anchored targets, Top-1 is comparable but Any-vis. rises from 41.80 to 43.06, a trade-off between matching the human director and covering every visible event on air. Since Top-1 is our primary measure of agreement with human directors, we keep event-anchored targets in the full model. Commentary metrics are otherwise stable throughout, with TimeDiff staying within 0.30–0.32, so these components mainly affect directing.

Keeping every feed view doubles the cache to 92.6k tokens and pushes the slowest seconds beyond real time, with a P95 cost of 1.05 seconds per video second. Program memory halves the growth to 47.6k tokens. A 72-second horizon cuts the cache further to 12.8k tokens and the P95 cost to 0.58 seconds. A horizon that drops every token older than 36 seconds, the length of a training clip, keeps the cache at 6.9k tokens, memory at 18.9 GB, and the cost per second constant at 0.29 seconds on one GPU. The shorter context does not hurt direction, as Top-1 accuracy rises from 23.7 to 25.1. The horizon also keeps the commentary alive late in the stream, where the speaking rate otherwise decays, lifting speech from 67.2 to 76.7. Scaling with training data.
We train DirCast on 5, 10 and 20 matches and evaluate the director on the same test split (Figure
3
). Top-1 counts a second as correct when the model airs the same feed as the human director, and Any-vis. when the chosen feed shows the event at all. Going from 5 to 10 matches gives small gains of 0.98 in Any-vis. and 0.56 in Top-1, while doubling to 20 gives 5.56 and 6.36, reaching 41.80 and 27.00. The jump suggests that the director needs to see enough fights, teams and strategies before its choices generalize to unseen matches. The curves show no sign of saturation, and new matches are cheap to collect since each needs only its camera feeds and the aired broadcast, with no manual labels, so scaling to hundreds of matches is a natural next step. Because the subsets are nested and the test split is fixed, the rising curve reflects added training variety rather than an easier evaluation.

Qualitative analysis.
Figure
4
shows four of the 19 off-air kills that DirCast puts on air and names, chosen among those where the human crew shows an uninvolved hero. In each case the cut gate stays below its threshold while the action is elsewhere, so DirCast holds its shot; in the second of the kill the gate rises above the threshold and DirCast cuts to the fight, often first to the victim and then to the killer as it moves. The commentary names a hero of the fight within about two seconds of the kill: Shadow Fiend as KotL takes him down off-air in (a), Rubick as Clockwerk finishes him while DirCast follows the fight in (b), Doom as he picks off Terrorblade on the kill in (c), and Terrorblade as his ultimate kills Tusk in (d). After each cut the threshold rises, so DirCast holds the new shot instead of flickering between feeds. The human crew misses all four kills, staying on an uninvolved hero such as Techies in (a), KotL in (b), Bane in (c) and Pangolier in (d); in (d) the casters call the kill although the broadcast never shows it, so the official feed shows none of the deaths as they happen.
6
Conclusion
We introduced live esports broadcast production, where a model receives every player’s camera feed and must choose the on-air shot and commentate using only past observations. DirCast addresses both tasks with a single streaming video language model. A hold-or-switch director selects the on-air shot, commentary follows its choice, and program-only context bounds the cost of long streams while enabling real-time operation on one GPU. Trained on human broadcasts with perturbed programs and event-anchored targets, DirCast outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, shows more kills on air than human crews, and wins more comparisons than eleven streaming commentators watching human broadcasts. Together, these results establish the feasibility of unified, real-time esports production with a single model.
