1
Introduction
Building on bidirectional architectures and extensive pre-training, recent diffusion models
(
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Song et al., 2020
)
deliver impressive visual quality, but at substantial computational cost for long-duration generation.
Autoregressive generation offers a natural alternative for streaming video synthesis, typically combining a sliding-window mechanism with memory routing to maintain long-range consistency and stable generation
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2025
)
. This capability is particularly important for multi-shot video generation
(
Guo et al., 2025b
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which aims to synthesize coherent, film-like narratives through frequent shot transitions accompanied by substantial viewpoint changes. Maintaining a continuous and coherent narrative flow across discrete shot boundaries naturally calls for a well-designed memory retrieval strategy, especially
when previously observed subjects, scenes, or viewpoints reappear after intervening shots.
Existing memory mechanisms for causal video generation remain generally coarse-grained. Basic sliding-window strategies are widely adopted in single-shot causal models
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, inevitably discarding distant information as autoregressive rollout proceeds. In multi-shot scenarios, some methods preserve temporally predefined anchors as persistent memory
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
, such as the first frames of individual shots.
These designs follow fixed routing patterns determined by temporal structures rather than the model’s intrinsic memory-access patterns, limiting their ability to fully exploit historical information.
More recent studies introduce retrieval-based memory strategies
(
Meng et al., 2026a
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which typically augment fixed sinks and adjacent context with frame-level routing.
The resulting routing decision is shared across all query tokens.
Although such designs allow content-aware access to historical cues, they still rely on coarse temporal grouping and overlook heterogeneous memory requirements across queries.
Consequently, long-horizon autoregressive generation remains constrained by frame-level historical conditioning, leaving much of the available memory underutilized.
In this work, we explore how an autoregressive multi-shot video model can retrieve long-term historical information under a constrained memory budget by leveraging its intrinsic memory-access patterns.
Rather than merely preserving adjacent-frame information for pixel-level continuity, memory in multi-shot scenarios should support the recovery of previously observed visual content after multiple shot transitions, a setting we refer to as revisitation.
To this end, we propose CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
By adapting memory organization and retrieval granularity to attention-based selection patterns, CineMem enables more effective access to long-term history and improves long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, as illustrated in Figure
1
.
To investigate the intrinsic memory-access patterns of autoregressive diffusion models,
we first develop a training framework that converts a bidirectional video model into a long-duration autoregressive multi-shot generator operating in a chunk-by-chunk manner, while allowing each current chunk to attend to the full generation history.
To stabilize long-horizon rollout, we further incorporate an error accumulation mitigation strategy during adaptation.
We then analyze the attention distributions between query tokens in the current chunk and all historical memory tokens. We observe a clear clustering structure among historical memory tokens and substantial variation in retrieval preferences across query tokens and attention heads.
These observations motivate our designs for online memory organization and query-adaptive retrieval.
Specifically, our framework comprises two complementary designs, as illustrated in Figure
2
. First, we apply online clustering to the KV cache to organize historical memory throughout autoregressive rollout. As generation proceeds, historical tokens are grouped according to their semantic similarity, with each cluster serving as a retrieval unit.
In contrast to conventional frame-level schemes that partition tokens by fixed frame membership regardless of content, our design forms content-aware groups, which alleviates the redundancy introduced by retrieving entire frames, while avoiding the high computational cost of treating every historical token as an individual memory unit.
Second, we introduce query-adaptive memory access in a query-wise and head-wise manner. Given their heterogeneous retrieval preferences, each query-head pair selects its most relevant clusters from memory.
Under a fixed per-query memory budget, this individualized retrieval provides broader access to the generation history, yielding a larger effective attention receptive field without increasing the retrieval cost.
Together, these designs better match intrinsic memory-access patterns while balancing
retrieval granularity, historical coverage, and computational efficiency, enabling CineMem to maintain long-range consistency across frequent shot transitions.
For evaluation, we adopt a comprehensive protocol covering video-level quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. Since conventional similarity-based metrics can assign deceptively high inter-shot consistency scores to videos that fail to perform the intended shot transition, we further introduce a VLM-assisted evaluation protocol that jointly considers transition execution and semantic preservation. This provides a more faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency in multi-shot generation. Experimental results show that CineMem achieves superior consistency compared with existing autoregressive baselines while remaining competitive with large-scale bidirectional models.
Moreover, our attention-aligned retrieval designs are effective in a plug-in setting without additional fine-tuning, demonstrating their ability to better exploit historical information during autoregressive rollout.
Overall, our work highlights the importance of fine-grained memory organization and retrieval for coherent long-horizon autoregressive multi-shot video generation.

Overview of CineMem.

3.3
Memory Selection in Attention Module
Based on the full-memory model, we analyze memory-access patterns during autoregressive rollout to guide the design of a fine-grained retrieval mechanism that best matches the model’s intrinsic selection behavior under full-memory attention. While conventional retrieval schemes typically define the retrieval unit at the chunk-to-frame level, we revisit the fundamental token-to-token memory selection process inherent in attention, which motivates our fine-grained retrieval design. For each generated chunk, memory selection is essentially the process by which current tokens, serving as queries, select relevant historical memory tokens through their keys and values.
For a query, highly attended keys receive higher attention probabilities, which mathematically correspond to larger normalized dot-product similarities. We therefore use this signal to study token-wise selection relationships and reveal the underlying memory-selection patterns.
Memory structure.
Efficient retrieval requires grouping, since treating each token as a separate group reduces retrieval to full-memory attention. Frame-level retrieval instead treats each frame as a group, implicitly assuming stronger correlations among tokens within the same frame. However, this assumption may not always hold, especially when a frame contains diverse content. To investigate this, we cluster the full-memory tokens and visualize the results in Figure
4(a)
. Clear clustering patterns emerge: highly similar tokens tend to form cross-frame clusters, while tokens within each cluster exhibit semantic consistency to some extent. We also observe stronger correlations among tokens from the first frame than among those from other frames, consistent with prior findings on the importance of the first latent sink
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
. These observations motivate grouping memory by token similarity rather than frame membership.
This is because frame-based grouping may introduce redundant information, as retrieving a group due to a few highly relevant tokens also includes many weakly related ones. Moreover, using a single centroid to represent semantically diverse tokens from the same frames can weaken their semantics and reduce retrieval precision.
Heterogeneous memory selection.
Turning to the query side, each query in attention independently computes its similarity to all keys, naturally motivating query-level retrieval.
In practice, different queries and attention heads attend to distinct memory tokens.
We visualize these selection patterns in Figure
4(b)
and observe clear heterogeneity across queries and heads. Even when each query-head pair selects only the top 30% most relevant memory tokens, their overall memory receptive field covers nearly the full memory, which indicates the necessity of query-wise and head-wise retrieval.

3.4
Online Clustered KV Cache
To enable fine-grained memory grouping, we introduce an online cluster KV cache. During autoregressive rollout, memory tokens are dynamically grouped according to their cosine similarity, such that semantically related tokens are assigned to the same cluster.
This design leverages the semantic coherence within each cluster: tokens relevant to the same query are likely to share similar semantic information, reducing redundant retrieval while improving retrieval effectiveness.
To support fine-grained query-level retrieval, clustering is performed independently for each attention head.
We retain the first and latest chunks as memory anchors.
As rollout proceeds, expired adjacent chunks are progressively incorporated into retrieval candidates through online clustering. Specifically, newly introduced tokens are assigned to existing clusters based on centroid similarity, followed by cluster refinement.
To maintain balanced and stable clusters during online updates, we introduce several balancing strategies. In particular, over-sized and under-sized clusters are handled through explicit split and merge operations, as illustrated in Figure
3
, while cluster assignment is further stabilized by incorporating load penalties and assignment consistency terms into the assignment score, which is formulated as:

Query-level Retrieval
Considering the heterogeneous memory selection patterns discussed in Section
3.3

Conventional retrieval shares a single historical memory subset across all queries, which cannot capture diverse query and head preferences, causing redundant retrieval of irrelevant tokens and missing relevant historical information.

Evaluation and Results

PTCS assigns low scores when either unchanged semantic elements are not preserved or intended changes are not correctly realized.
Metrics.
To comprehensively evaluate streaming multi-shot video generation, we construct an evaluation set of 100 prompts and establish an evaluation protocol covering video-level, intra-shot-level, and inter-shot-level metrics. Video-level metrics assess fundamental properties of generated videos, including visual aesthetics
(
LAION-AI, 2022
)
, transition control
(
Soucek and Lokoc, 2024
)
, and text alignment
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, while intra-shot metrics
(
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Fu et al., 2023
)
evaluate consistency within individual shots. More importantly, inter-shot evaluation measures semantic consistency across shot transitions.
However, existing similarity-based inter-shot metrics suffer from an inherent ambiguity: a high similarity score may indicate either strong transition consistency or simply the absence of a meaningful transition. Consequently, models with weak transition control may receive deceptively high consistency scores.
To address this issue, we introduce a VLM-based metric
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, the Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score (PTCS), as illustrated in Figure
6
. PTCS rewards transitions only when they are successfully executed while preserving the required semantic consistency.
PTCS consists of two complementary components: Prompt-conditioned Continuity Preservation (PCP) and Prompt-conditioned Transition Alignment (PTA). Given a hierarchical prompt, we first construct a semantic state graph to identify the semantic elements that should remain unchanged and those expected to change across the transition. PCP measures whether the required elements are consistently preserved before and after the transition, whereas PTA evaluates whether the intended changes, such as modifications in focal subjects or camera configurations, are correctly realized. For each transition, PTCS is computed as the geometric mean of PCP and PTA and then averaged over the evaluation set. By jointly evaluating unchanged elements and intended changes, PTCS provides a more direct and faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency.

Quantitative Results.
Table
2
reports the quantitative comparison on our evaluation set. CineMem achieves strong performance across video-level quality and intra-shot consistency metrics, demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality videos while maintaining stable shot-level content. For inter-shot evaluation, CineMem achieves the best performance on PTCS, which jointly considers unchanged elements and intended changes during shot transitions. Notably, models with high similarity-based inter-shot scores or PCP values often exhibit limited transition control, while models specifically designed for multi-shot generation may still receive relatively low scores on these metrics. This indicates that similarity-based or preservation-only metrics can overestimate inter-shot consistency when the intended transition is not properly realized. By explicitly considering both preserved and changing elements specified in the prompt, PTCS provides a more faithful evaluation of transition quality. Finally, CineMem achieves superior PTCS performance and even surpasses larger bidirectional models with substantially more parameters.
4.3
Ablation Study
To validate the effectiveness of different design choices in CineMem, we conduct ablation studies from three perspectives, with results summarized in Table
3
.
Training Strategy.
In Section
3.2
, we introduce resampled history context to simulate autoregressive error accumulation during training. Compared with the standard teacher-forcing strategy, resampling context training provides more consistent training conditions with autoregressive inference and achieves superior performance across different metrics, especially in long-horizon consistency.
Retrieval Strategy.
We analyze different retrieval strategies introduced in Sections
3.4
and
3.5
under a plug-in setting. Specifically, we compare our clustered KV cache and query-wise retrieval with frame-level grouping and shared retrieval. To isolate the effect of retrieval design, we directly apply different strategies to the adapted base model without additional training. As shown, query-wise retrieval consistently improves performance under both frame-level and clustered memory organization, demonstrating the importance of fine-grained memory access. Moreover, clustered KV cache further improves transition quality and inter-shot consistency over frame-level grouping, validating the effectiveness of semantic-based memory organization. Notably, without additional training, our retrieval strategy achieves comparable performance to full-memory attention while obtaining higher inter-shot consistency, demonstrating its effectiveness under a constrained memory budget.
Query-level Retrieval Variant.
We investigate a query grouping variant of our retrieval mechanism. Instead of performing independent retrieval for each query, this variant recursively partitions queries into groups according to their spatial and semantic similarity using an adaptive tree structure and shares retrieved memory within each group.
Although query grouping provides an effective approximation by exploiting query similarity, it remains slightly inferior to fully query-wise retrieval, further validating the importance of fine-grained query retrieval.
5
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce CineMem, a fine-grained memory retrieval framework for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Combining an online clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval, CineMem enables broader historical access and improves long-range consistency in revisitation scenarios. We develop an autoregressive adaptation framework with resampled context to analyze intrinsic memory-access patterns, revealing semantic clustering among memory tokens and heterogeneous query-head preferences that motivate our design. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
Our results highlight the importance of fine-grained memory modeling for autoregressive video generation. Rather than relying only on recent frames, autoregressive models should exploit information throughout history. Advances in memory organization and retrieval will enable scalable long-horizon video generation.

A.2
investigates the clustering behaviors before and after positional encoding, providing further evidence for our memory organization design. Finally, Section

analyzes the retrieval overlap between CineMem and full-memory attention, demonstrating that our proposed memory access mechanism can effectively approximate full-memory access patterns during autoregressive rollout.
A.1
Heterogeneous Query and Head Memory Preferences
In Figure

The memory coverage curve shows that when each query-head pair selects only the top 30% memory tokens with the highest attention probabilities, the aggregated receptive field can cover nearly all historical memory frames. In the heatmap, each row corresponds to a query-head pair, while each column represents a spatial memory unit from a historical frame. Specifically, each frame is divided into

Although the differences among highlighted regions across rows in Figure

A.2
Pre-RoPE Clustering vs. Post-RoPE Clustering
Figure 10:
Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE.
Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.
In Section
3.4
, we introduce an online clustering mechanism to organize memory tokens into semantic groups rather than predefined frame-based partitions. In practice, before entering each transformer block, token representations are augmented with positional encoding. Our clustering and retrieval operations are therefore performed before RoPE (Pre-RoPE). This design choice is motivated by the observation that positional encoding introduces strong absolute position information into token representations, which can obscure semantic similarity and weaken semantic clustering structures.
In fact, the visualization in Figure
4(a)
is obtained using token representations before positional encoding. To further investigate this effect, Figure
10
presents representative clustering results before and after applying RoPE. We observe that RoPE-transformed tokens exhibit stronger position-dependent similarity patterns, while the semantic grouping structure becomes less apparent. Therefore, performing clustering and retrieval after positional encoding may bias memory organization toward positional grouping and degrade into a behavior similar to frame-level partitioning, limiting the benefits of semantic-aware memory organization. These observations support our choice of conducting clustering and retrieval in the Pre-RoPE space.
A.3
Retrieval Alignment with Full-Memory Attention
Figure 11:
Precision (left) and recall (right) of different retrieval strategies under varying full-memory attention thresholds. For each query-head pair, full-memory attention serves as the oracle, and retrieved tokens are considered matched if they fall within the top-

Online-clustered KV cache retrieves tokens from query-specific selected clusters, while Latent-group, Frame-group, and Sliding Window perform frame-level or fixed-context retrieval. Analysis of Efficiency
In this section, we analyze the efficiency of CineMem and compare it
with two representative memory access strategies. Full-history attention is
considered as an upper bound in terms of memory availability, as it provides
access to the complete historical context without retrieval constraints.
Meanwhile, frame-group retrieval serves as an efficient coarse-grained
baseline by selecting a fixed number of historical frames with shared routing.
In contrast, CineMem performs fine-grained query-head-wise retrieval over
online-clustered memory, aiming to achieve a better balance between retrieval
granularity and computational cost.
We evaluate these strategies from both theoretical and practical perspectives.
The theoretical analysis focuses on self-attention computation and retrieval
overhead, while the practical evaluation measures actual inference efficiency.

cost by retrieving a fixed number of latent frames and sharing the retrieved
memory across queries. In contrast, online-clustered retrieval maintains
historical tokens in semantic clusters and performs query-head-wise retrieval.
In our setting, frame-group retrieval selects 20 latent frames.

substantially reduce the self-attention cost compared with full-history
attention. With the current configurations, online-clustered retrieval achieves
a slightly lower attention cost than frame-group retrieval by accessing a more
compact set of retrieved tokens. Although the online clustering process
introduces additional computation overhead, this overhead mainly comes from
cluster refinement and maintenance operations, including centroid refinement,
cluster splitting, and merging. Nevertheless, the retrieval overhead remains
small compared with the dominant self-attention computation. The overall cost

D.1
Implementation of Metrics
For video-level evaluation, we focus on fundamental properties of generated videos, including visual quality, text-video alignment, and transition controllability. We adopt widely used evaluation tools for these aspects, including LAION aesthetic score
(
LAION-AI, 2022
)
, ViCLIP-based similarity
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, and TransNetV2-based transition evaluation
(
Soucek and Lokoc, 2024
)
.
For intra-shot-level evaluation, we treat each shot as an individual video and evaluate temporal consistency within the shot. Specifically, we extract frame-level features using DINO
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
and compute consistency scores based on feature similarities between frames.
For inter-shot-level evaluation, we first adopt a conventional similarity-based metric commonly used in multi-shot video generation
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
. Similar to intra-shot evaluation, this metric measures feature similarity between frames from different shots.
In addition, we introduce a VLM-assisted metric, Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score (PTCS), which consists of two complementary components: Prompt-conditioned Continuity Preservation (PCP) and Prompt-conditioned Transition Alignment (PTA). D.2
The effectiveness of Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score
As discussed in Section
4.2
, conventional similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics evaluate transitions by measuring feature similarity between frames from different shots. However, such metrics inherently favor cases where adjacent shots exhibit limited visual changes, assigning high consistency scores even when the intended transition is not successfully realized. This limitation explains why some methods can achieve high inter-shot consistency scores while exhibiting poor transition control. These observations motivate our design of PTCS, which explicitly considers both semantic preservation and prompt-specified transition changes. Given that PTCS serves as a key metric for evaluating the effectiveness of CineMem, we further analyze its validity in this section.
We visualize several multi-shot examples with PTCS evaluations in Figure
13
. Qualitatively, PCP successfully reflects transitions where semantic consistency is violated, while PTA captures both missing transitions, where the intended shot change is not realized, and unexpected changes introduced during transitions, including inconsistencies in style, character identity, spatial relationships, or even subtle local details. By jointly considering these two complementary aspects, PTCS provides scores that better align with the desired properties of shot transitions. In contrast, similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics may produce misleading evaluations: when the visual composition remains similar, they can assign high scores despite missing or incorrect transitions, while failing to distinguish valid and invalid transitions under substantial compositional changes.
Figure 13:
Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics.
The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.
To complement the quantitative evaluation, we conduct a user study to investigate whether PTCS aligns with human perception of inter-shot consistency. Specifically, we select 30 prompts for evaluation, and participants rate each generated video on a scale from 1 to 5 from three perspectives: overall video quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. The mean opinion scores (MOS) are summarized in Table
4
.
As shown, the human evaluation results are consistent with the trends observed in PTCS. Methods with higher PTCS scores generally receive higher inter-shot consistency ratings from human participants, while models that achieve high similarity-based consistency scores but fail to perform the intended transitions receive substantially lower human scores. This agreement indicates that PTCS better captures human-perceived transition consistency by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes. Furthermore, CineMem achieves the highest MOS in inter-shot consistency and competitive overall video quality, demonstrating its ability to generate coherent multi-shot videos with controllable transitions.

E.1
Qualitative Results of Ablation Study
Figure
15
provides additional qualitative results for the ablation study. As shown, CineMem maintains long-horizon consistency after multiple shot transitions. Even under the training-free setting, our fine-grained retrieval mechanism achieves better results than approaches based on frame-level grouping or shared retrieval. The trained model further improves visual consistency and preserves finer details. For the query-group retrieval variant, we provide additional implementation details in Figure

E.2
Fine-Grained Analysis of Generation Quality
In Table
2
, we present the overall comparison between CineMem and existing baselines. In this section, we provide a more fine-grained analysis of the evaluation results by categorizing the evaluation prompts from three perspectives: content category, shot count, and revisit distance.
Figure
16
illustrates the distribution of our evaluation set across these three categories. We use these categorizations to further analyze the performance of different methods under diverse generation scenarios. Here, revisit distance denotes the maximum number of chunks between two revisited appearances within a prompt, reflecting the difficulty of maintaining long-range consistency.
Content category.
Table
5
reports the results across six content categories. Overall, CineMem exhibits consistently strong transition control and intra-shot consistency across diverse visual content, while achieving the best or second-best PTCS in five out of the six categories.
In particular, CineMem achieves the highest PTCS on
Objects and Still Life
and
Solo Activities
, and remains competitive on more complex scenarios involving conversations, multiple entities, and animals.
These results suggest that the proposed fine-grained memory retrieval is not specific to a particular type of visual content, but generalizes across substantially different generation scenarios.
Shot count.
We further group the evaluation prompts according to the number of shots, as shown in Table
6
. CineMem achieves the highest PTCS across all shot-count groups, while also consistently obtaining the strongest transition control and intra-shot consistency. Notably, its advantage is preserved for prompts containing six to seven shots, where autoregressive error accumulation and long-range dependency modeling become more challenging. This result indicates that our memory retrieval mechanism remains effective as the generation horizon increases.
Revisit distance.
Finally, Table
7
analyzes performance with respect to revisit distance, which directly reflects the temporal range over which previously generated content needs to be recalled.
CineMem maintains strong performance across all distance ranges and achieves the highest PTCS for the longest revisit range of 13-18 chunks.
It also consistently achieves the best transition control and intra-shot consistency across different revisit distances. These results further support the effectiveness of our fine-grained memory retrieval in preserving long-range historical information and maintaining consistency when previously observed content reappears after a long temporal interval.

Figure 17:
Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.
To further investigate the long-horizon generation capability of CineMem, we provide additional qualitative results on 30-second videos. As shown in Figure
17
, CineMem can continuously extend autoregressive generation while maintaining coherent visual content and long-range consistency across multiple shot transitions. These results highlight the potential of fine-grained memory retrieval for enabling more scalable autoregressive video generation over extended durations.
Appendix F
Limitation and Failure Case
Limitations.
Due to limited computational resources, our experiments are conducted on a relatively small-scale autoregressive backbone with a limited amount of training data for adapting a bidirectional model into a long-horizon autoregressive generator. Consequently, the visual quality of generated videos may lag behind that of large-scale state-of-the-art diffusion models with substantially larger model capacity and training data. Nevertheless, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed memory retrieval framework and reveal meaningful insights into memory utilization in autoregressive diffusion models. We expect that the proposed approach can further benefit from larger-scale models and datasets.
Figure 18:
A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios.
Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.
Failure Cases.
Our memory retrieval mechanism aims to approximate the intrinsic full-memory access pattern under a constrained memory budget by enabling more effective historical information retrieval. However, it still struggles in scenarios requiring complex multi-entity reasoning, as illustrated in Figure
18
. In the presented example, the generated video exhibits issues such as missing characters and inconsistent details across shot transitions.
Such failures are particularly challenging for autoregressive generation. In this case, an early chunk introduces four characters through its prompt, while a later chunk requires only three characters. The model must therefore generate a valid transition by adjusting the camera viewpoint while preserving the spatial relationships and identities established in previous shots. However, the earlier chunks are generated without knowledge of future shot requirements, making such coordinated transitions inherently difficult, especially when the initial composition does not provide sufficient flexibility.
Therefore, multi-entity scenarios with complex shot transitions remain challenging even for full-memory autoregressive generation or bidirectional models, as they require reasoning beyond historical information retrieval. While our proposed memory mechanism improves access to relevant historical content and achieves promising results on certain multi-entity scenarios (see supplementary project page), handling complex entity interactions remains an important direction for future work.
Appendix G
Future Work
Beyond the proposed online clustered KV cache and query-adaptive retrieval framework, several directions remain open for future exploration. For memory organization, more effective clustering strategies could further improve retrieval quality. Meanwhile, exploiting the shared retrieval patterns among queries may provide more efficient alternatives to fully query-wise and head-wise retrieval, as explored by the query-group variant in Section
4.3
. These directions may enable more scalable and efficient memory mechanisms for autoregressive video generation.
From the perspective of autoregressive video generation, integrating entity-aware or structure-aware memory retrieval could help address challenging multi-entity scenarios discussed in Section
F
. Furthermore, extending autoregressive generation to substantially longer horizons remains a promising direction toward more scalable long-form video synthesis.

article.headline: 细粒度记忆检索改善多镜头视频一致性
article.lede: CineMem 用在线聚类 KV cache 和查询-注意力头级检索，提升多镜头自回归视频的跨镜头一致性。
article.problem: 多镜头自回归视频生成需要在镜头切换间保持语义连续，但现有记忆检索多在帧级进行，且所有查询共享同一历史上下文。这忽略了不同查询和注意力头对历史信息需求的异质性，导致冗余检索和历史记忆利用不足。
article.method: 作者先分析全记忆注意力，发现历史 token 呈语义聚类结构，且不同查询-注意力头关注的历史区域差异明显。据此提出在线聚类 KV cache，用分裂/合并和负载惩罚维持簇平衡，并让每个查询-注意力头按簇检索历史记忆。训练时用重采样真值帧构造带噪历史，以缓解自回归误差累积。
article.results: 在 15 秒多镜头生成评测中，CineMem 的 PTCS 为 0.8242，高于 MultiShotMaster 的 0.7984、HoloCine 的 0.7385 和 ShotStream 的 0.6917；转场控制为 0.9960，镜头内主体一致性为 0.9716。理论效率上，完整历史注意力的总 FLOPs 为 932.56 TFLOPs，聚类检索为 638.82 TFLOPs，其中检索额外开销为 15.0180 TFLOPs。免训练插入实验中，聚类缓存加查询级检索的 PTCS 为 0.8007，高于聚类缓存加共享检索的 0.7442，也略高于完整记忆注意力的 0.7922。
article.why_it_matters: 它把视频生成中的记忆检索从帧级推进到 token/簇级，并给出与注意力模式对齐的设计，对长视频和流式叙事生成有参考价值。免训练插入也能改善历史信息利用，说明该设计可能迁移到已有自回归视频模型。
article.limitations: 实验基于 1.3B 的 Wan2.1 主干、45K 视频训练集和 100 条评测 prompt，作者承认视觉质量可能落后于更大规模扩散模型；复杂多实体转场仍会出现角色消失和细节不一致。
article.figure_caption_zh: CineMem 框架：推理时查询从首块、相邻块和在线聚类检索到的候选记忆中取用 KV，训练时通过重采样真值帧模拟误差累积。

figure.caption: {Our memory retrieval framework.} Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

page_papers.title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
page_papers.abstract: Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website: https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/.
page_papers.content:
RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Yu Li
Shenghe Hu
Yuhan Wang
Yaoxiang Pu
Haotong Zhang
Yuanpei Chen
Yaodong Yang
Abstract
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data.
Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation.
In this work, we propose
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
with popular generative robot policies on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that
RoboFFT
consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate
RoboFFT
into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks. Project website:
https://student-of-holmes.github.io/RoboFFT/
.
Figure 1:
We present
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policy with forward process. (a) Reverse finetuning formulates the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP, while forward finetuning aligns with the same objective as training by following the forward noising process.
(b) One framework across popular generative robot policy on simulation benchmarks.
(c) Real-world deployment with integration of real world RL.
(d) Improved performance in success rate, training stability and efficiency.

Keywords:
Diffusion RL, Generative Robot Policy, Robot Manipulation
1
Introduction
Generative robot policies, typically based on diffusion and flow-based models
[
43
,
42
,
15
,
29
]
, have become a powerful paradigm for learning visuomotor skills from demonstrations by modeling complex and multi-modal action distributions
[
12
,
56
,
53
]
, which significantly improves robot action accuracy and robustness and yields substantial performance gains in complex manipulation tasks
[
12
,
53
]
. However, policies trained purely by imitation learning remain constrained by the quality and coverage of the demonstration data. Imperfect demonstrations, covariate shift, and insufficient exposure to deployment-time states can all limit the final task performance of behavior-cloned policies
[
13
,
40
]
. Online reinforcement learning (RL) naturally presents itself as a promising paradigm to further improve generative robot policies, as it empowers the policy to directly maximize task rewards by continuously interacting with and learning from the environment.
Applying policy gradient RL methods to generative robot policies is nevertheless nontrivial. Unlike autoregressive policies, whose token likelihoods are tractable, diffusion and flow-based models typically lack a tractable exact likelihood formulation. This makes popular policy gradient objectives, such as PPO, difficult to be applied directly. Existing approaches address this issue by formulating the reverse denoising process as a multi-step MDP embedded in the high-level environment MDP, and optimizing through this two-level decision making trajectory
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
(Fig.
1
(a), left). Despite its promising results, reverse-process finetuning introduces substantial computation and memory overhead, and may suffer from gradient instability due to long denoising chains, especially in high-dimensional and long-horizon manipulation tasks.
To address these issues, we propose
RoboFFT
, a simpler yet more effective framework for online RL finetuning of generative robot manipulation policies through the
forward
noising process, inspired by recent studies from other application domains such as image generation and simple locomotion
[
52
,
59
,
34
]
. Instead of assigning credit through the reverse denoising chain,
RoboFFT
approximates the exact log-likelihood with a more computationally stable and efficient form akin to the score / flow matching loss for pretraining, yielding a principled PPO-style objective that is aligned with the imitation-learning objective while avoiding complicated likelihood computation or backpropagation through the full reverse trajectory. For flow-based policies, we further adopt SDE sampling by injecting noise into the sampling process, enabling controllable exploration during online data collection. In practice, Monte Carlo estimation, ratio-temperature calibration and further adaptations make likelihood estimation and updates robust across different policy architectures and tasks.
We evaluate
RoboFFT
on challenging robot manipulation benchmarks such as Robomimic
[
33
]
and LIBERO
[
30
]
, which pose difficulties like high-dimensional visual observation, long horizon planning and sparse reward for finetuning. Experimental results across different tasks demonstrate substantial and consistent performance improvements over pretrained diffusion and flow policies and achieve competitive or better performance compared with representative reverse and forward process finetuning baselines, while reducing optimization overhead. We further verify the applicability of our method on more complicated VLA and real world deployment settings, and study the key designs through ablations and visualizations. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) We introduce
RoboFFT
, an online reinforcement learning framework that performs policy gradient finetuning in the forward noising process for generative robot policies.
(2) We carry out practical implementation of
RoboFFT
for representative generative robot policies (flow, diffusion and VLA) on challenging long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks, showing that
RoboFFT
achieves superior performance and improved training stability and efficiency.
(3) We integrate
RoboFFT
into the real world reinforcement learning framework for practical deployment and demonstrate its effectiveness over real world tasks.
(4) We carry out a systematic ablation analysis of key design choices and conduct investigative experiments to provide empirical insights for the mechanism of
RoboFFT
.
2
Related Work
2.1
Policy Gradient for Robot Manipulation
Policy gradient and actor critic methods provide a standard framework for learning continuous-control policies from interaction data
[
50
,
45
,
28
,
41
]
. Due to the
training stability with high-dimensional action spaces, they have been widely applied to a range of robotic control problems, including dexterous manipulation, legged locomotion, and agile navigation
[
48
,
9
,
10
,
1
,
17
,
21
]
. For long-horizon manipulation, however, training from scratch remains highly exploration-intensive and is often impractical. A more practical paradigm is therefore to finetune policies initialized from demonstration data. Prior studies have shown that reinforcement learning can further improve such demonstration-initialized policies beyond behavior cloning while substantially reducing the exploration burden
[
38
,
46
,
37
]
. RoboFFT follows this finetuning paradigm, while focusing on diffusion- and flow-based robot policies whose action distributions are implicitly induced by generative sampling processes, making the likelihood ratio computation required by policy gradient methods nontrivial.
2.2
RL for Generative Models
Reinforcement learning has recently been widely applied to generative model finetuning in offline
[
3
,
35
,
16
,
49
,
14
,
36
,
7
]
, offline-to-online
[
11
,
26
]
, and online settings
[
39
,
57
,
54
,
34
,
52
,
59
]
. Online finetuning for diffusion and flow models can be broadly categorized into reverse-process and forward-process approaches. Reverse-process methods formulate the denoising or sampling trajectory as a multi-step decision process, enabling tractable per-step likelihood for policy optimization
[
5
,
39
,
57
]
. While effective, optimizing through long internal sampling chains can increase computation and memory costs and may introduce training instability. Forward-process methods instead optimize policy via constructing surrogate likelihood objectives or contrastive learning, better aligning RL finetuning with generative pretraining
[
52
,
34
,
54
,
59
]
. DiffusionNFT and AWM
[
59
,
52
]
study this idea for text-to-image generation. FPO and FPO++
[
34
,
54
]
extend it to robotic control, but mainly focus on locomotion tasks. In comparison, RoboFFT studies forward-process finetuning in more challenging robotic manipulation, and covers more extensive settings including both diffusion and flow policies, VLA finetuning, and real world deployment with practical stabilization designs.

5.4
Evaluation on Real World
To evaluate the effectiveness of
RoboFFT
on real world robotic manipulation tasks, we integrate our method into a practical real-world RL framework
[

11

. However, directly applying PPO-style online optimization to real robots is challenging due to limited interaction budgets, slow data collection, and the absence of parallel environments. Inspired by RL100
[
26
]
, we therefore adapt
RoboFFT
to an offline-to-online formulation while retaining its core components including forward noising, the matching loss surrogate ratio, and PPO-style clipping. Specifically, we first pretrain a flow-based policy using human demonstrations collected via SpaceMouse teleoperation.
We then perform multiple offline RL iterations. In each offline iteration, we perform offline PPO-style optimization on the collected rollout data, where IQL
[
25
]
is used to estimate advantages from offline trajectories. After each offline RL update, we deploy the updated policy on the real robot to collect additional trajectories, which are added to the offline dataset for the next offline RL iteration. To stabilize policy improvement and avoid drifting away from reliable human behaviors, we combine the newly collected rollout data with the original teleoperation demonstrations and conduct imitation learning to update the base policy for the next iteration.
During the online RL phase, we continue PPO-style updates initialized from the offline actor and IQL critic. We use a sparse binary

6
Limitations
Although
RoboFFT
enables stable online finetuning of generative robot policies through the forward noising process, it still has several limitations. First, the weighted score/flow matching loss is only a surrogate for the true action log-likelihood, and its scale may vary across noise schedules, action dimensions, and policy architectures. Therefore, additional calibration such as temperature scaling is still needed to ensure stable PPO-style updates. Second, our current framework relies on on-policy PPO, which has limited data efficiency and cannot fully reuse historical trajectories. This makes real-world deployment challenging, especially when data collection is restricted to a single robot. Although offline-to-online paradigms such as RL100
[
26
]
can partially alleviate this issue, they usually require iterative data collection and offline retraining, which remains time-consuming in practice. Future work may explore more sample-efficient variants that better leverage historical trajectories and human intervention data for safer and faster real world robot learning.
7
Conclusion
We present
RoboFFT
, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies. By applying forward noising to sampled actions and using the weighted score/flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio,
RoboFFT
enables PPO-style policy optimization without requiring explicit likelihood estimation. Experiments on representative simulation benchmarks show that
RoboFFT
consistently improves popular generative robot policies on long-horizon and sparse-reward manipulation tasks, while achieving better training stability and efficiency. Further integration into a real world RL framework also demonstrates its effectiveness on real robot tasks.

B.1
Robomimic Benchmark
We use Robomimic
[
33
]
as the simulated manipulation benchmark throughout our main experiments. Robomimic provides sparse-reward robot manipulation tasks collected from human demonstrations, making it a suitable testbed for evaluating whether online finetuning can improve a behavior-cloned generative policy beyond its initial demonstration-trained performance. Following the data processing and environment conventions used in DPPO and ReinFlow
[
39
,
57
]
, we evaluate four Robomimic tasks: Lift, Can, Square, and Transport. The corresponding observation and action specifications are summarized in Table
1
.
The four tasks cover different manipulation difficulties. Lift requires the robot to grasp and lift an object, while Can is a pick-and-place task where the robot must manipulate a can into the target container. Square is a more precision-sensitive assembly task in which the robot must manipulate a square nut and place it onto a positioning peg. Transport is a long-horizon bimanual manipulation task that requires coordinated control of two robot arms to move an object across the workspace. Thus, the benchmark spans both short-horizon single-arm manipulation and longer-horizon bimanual manipulation.
We consider both state-input and pixel-input variants. In the state-input setting, the policy observes low-dimensional proprioceptive and object state features. In the pixel-input setting, the policy observes RGB image(s) at
96
×
96
96\times 96
resolution together with a compact proprioceptive state. Lift, Can, and Square use a single camera view, while Transport uses two camera views. For all tasks, the action is continuous. Lift, Can, and Square use a 7-dimensional action space, whereas Transport uses a 14-dimensional action space due to its bimanual control setup.
All Robomimic tasks use sparse rewards. We report success rate as the primary evaluation metric. The maximum episode length
T
max
T_{\max}
is task-dependent: 300 decision steps for Lift and Can, 400 for Square, and 800 for Transport. In online finetuning, the policy predicts action chunks and executes the first
H

B.4
Baseline Methods and Configurations
We compare RoboFFT with representative online RL fine-tuning baselines for diffusion- and flow-based robot policies.
DPPO.
Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
[
39
]
is a representative reverse-process fine-tuning method for diffusion policies. It formulates the reverse denoising process together with the environment interaction process as a two-level MDP, and applies PPO to optimize the Gaussian likelihoods of denoising transitions. We use DPPO as the canonical diffusion-policy RL baseline for long-horizon manipulation tasks.
ReinFlow.
ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends the reverse-process policy-gradient paradigm to flow-based policies. It injects stochasticity into the deterministic flow trajectory, turns the sampler into a discrete-time Markov process with tractable Gaussian transition probabilities, and performs PPO-style optimization over the internal sampling trajectory. We use ReinFlow as the primary flow-policy baseline.
FPO.
Flow Policy Optimization
[
34
]
is a forward-process policy-gradient method that constructs a PPO-style surrogate ratio from conditional flow matching losses. We adapt FPO into our online fine-tuning codebase for Robomimic. To ensure fair comparison under the same tasks and pretrained policies, most environment and optimizer settings are shared with RoboFFT. The main algorithmic differences are that FPO does not use our SDE explorative sampling strategy and ratio-temperature calibration adopted in RoboFFT, while following the original FPO convention of using

DRWR.
DRWR is a lightweight diffusion reward-weighted regression baseline following the implementation convention in DPPO
[
39
]
. It performs forward-noise matching style updates weighted by rewards or returns, and serves as a simple forward-process reference that is architecturally close to our approach but does not use the PPO-style objective and the many critical designs introduced by our work.
For all baselines, we match the Robomimic environment wrappers, observation preprocessing, action chunking, base-policy training data, and evaluation protocol whenever applicable. The hyperparameters of DPPO, ReinFlow, and DRWR follow their original implementations unless a task-specific adaptation is necessary. Since the released ReinFlow manipulation implementation focuses on pixel-input Robomimic tasks, for state-input tasks we adapt secondary settings such as optimizer and update-batch configurations while keeping the core ReinFlow design unchanged. For fair comparison, the number of inference steps and finetuning steps are tuned on each task, so that each baseline achieves its nearly best performance. RoboFFT-F and RoboFFT-D are respectively implemented upon the ReinFlow

and DPPO

Appendix C
Additional Analyses for the Robomimic Experiments
C.1
Performance Analysis
This subsection provides additional discussion for the main Robomimic comparison in Sec.
5.1
, where the comprehensive performance of RoboFFT-F, RoboFFT-D and the baseline methods are evaluated under both state-input and pixel-input settings.
Across the easier
Lift
and
Can
tasks, RoboFFT-D and RoboFFT-F reach final success rates comparable to reverse-process baselines such as DPPO and ReinFlow. Their convergence can be slightly slower in some early-stage curves, but the final policy quality remains competitive. This suggests that the forward-process surrogate ratio preserves enough policy-gradient signal for improving already competent pretrained policies, while avoiding explicit likelihood computation through the reverse denoising chain.
The advantage of RoboFFT becomes more pronounced on the harder tasks. On
Square
and
Transport
, especially with pixel observations, RoboFFT shows a more sustained improvement trend and stronger final performance. Reverse-process methods can suffer from instability or later performance recession, likely because optimizing through a long internal sampling chain introduces a more complicated credit-assignment path and a heavier computation graph, making the gradients and parameter updates instable. In comparison, RoboFFT directly applies forward noising to the final rollout action and optimizes a matching-loss-based surrogate ratio, which keeps the optimization path closer to imitation pretraining.
The forward-process baselines, DRWR and FPO, are generally less competitive in the Robomimic manipulation setting. DRWR uses reward-weighted regression and does not include a PPO-style trust region, making it more sensitive to high-variance reward weights in sparse-reward tasks. FPO uses a forward-process PPO-style ratio, but in our implementation it lacks the manipulation-oriented stabilization designs used in RoboFFT, including controlled SDE exploration and ratio-temperature calibration. These differences help explain why simply applying a forward matching loss is not sufficient for robust online fine-tuning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

Compared with the pretrained policy, whose sampled action chunks are more diffusely distributed and contain many low- or negative-advantage samples, the finetuned policy forms a more concentrated region with noticeably higher diagnostic advantages. In particular, after fine-tuning, a dense cluster of positive-advantage actions emerges in the embedding space, indicating that RoboFFT increases the probability mass around actions that are preferred by the diagnostic critic

Together, these results suggest that RoboFFT improves the pretrained generative policy by concentrating its action distribution around more task-relevant and higher-quality action modes, rather than merely increasing random exploration. policy likelihood or the number of behavioral modes. The observed concentration therefore does not by itself establish

Appendix H
Extended Related Work
H.1
Generative Models for Robot Manipulation
Generative models have become an increasingly important policy class for robot manipulation, as they provide expressive distributions over complex and potentially multimodal action sequences. Early approaches
[
58
,
27
]
formulate imitation learning with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). More recently, diffusion-based policies have demonstrated substantially greater expressiveness for continuous control. Diffusion Policy
[
12
,
19
]
models the conditional action distribution through an iterative denoising process, enabling stable learning of high-dimensional and multimodal action distributions and motivating a broad family of diffusion-based manipulation policies. Flow-matching models provide an alternative generative formulation by learning continuous transport from a simple noise distribution to the action distribution. Methods such as ManiFlow
[
53
]
further improve sampling efficiency and policy expressiveness through consistency-based flow training, demonstrating strong performance on diverse manipulation tasks. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models have extended robot policies toward large-scale generalist control by leveraging pretrained vision-language representations and heterogeneous robot datasets. RT-2
[
6
]
and OpenVLA
[
22
]
generate discretized robot actions within large autoregressive vision-language models, while
π
0
\pi_{0}
[
4
]
and
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
[
18
]
combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert for continuous action generation.
H.2
RL for Generative Robot Policy
Reinforcement learning has been increasingly explored to improve generative policies beyond behavior cloning. Early studies mainly focus on offline RL with fixed datasets. Diffusion Q Learning
[
49
]
parameterizes the actor as a diffusion model and combines diffusion regression with Q value maximization, while IDQL
[
14
]
uses an implicit Q-function to select actions sampled from a diffusion behavior policy. This idea has also been extended to flow-based policies. Flow Q Learning (FQL)
[
36
]
learns a flow matching behavior policy together with a one-step RL policy, avoiding recursive differentiation through iterative flow generation. Although these methods exploit the expressiveness of generative policies, their improvement is constrained by the coverage of the offline dataset and the accuracy of learned value functions.
More recent work considers online or offline-to-online adaptation of pretrained generative robot policies. One direction keeps the base policy frozen and learns a lightweight steering or residual component. DSRL
[
47
]
performs RL in the latent-noise space of a pretrained diffusion or flow policy without modifying its parameters, while residual RL methods learn corrective actions on top of a frozen behavior cloning policy
[
2
,
44
,
20
]
. These approaches preserve pretrained behaviors and reduce the complexity of online optimization, but restrict policy improvement to the residual or latent space exposed by the frozen policy.
In contrast, full policy finetuning directly updates the generative model parameters. DPPO
[
39
]
formulates diffusion denoising as a multi-step MDP and applies PPO over reverse denoising transitions. ReinFlow
[
57
]
extends likelihood-based online optimization to flow policies by injecting stochasticity into deterministic flow trajectories. Forward process methods such as FPO
[
34
]
and its extensions
[
54
]
instead construct policy-gradient objectives from flow matching losses, avoiding explicit marginal likelihood computation. Reinforced finetuning has also been extended to VLA policies, with
[
11
,
51
]
combining offline value learning and online policy optimization for real-world manipulation. RoboFFT belongs to the full policy finetuning family, but performs PPO-style optimization through the forward noising process, providing a unified framework for diffusion, flow, and VLA policies.

article.headline: RoboFFT：前向加噪微调生成式机器人策略
article.lede: RoboFFT用前向加噪和匹配损失构造PPO代理比率，在线微调扩散、流与VLA机器人策略，仿真和真机均报告提升。
article.problem: 扩散和流策略能建模多模态动作，但纯模仿学习受演示质量与分布偏移限制；在线RL又因精确似然不可解而难以直接套用PPO。现有逆向去噪链微调把采样过程当多步MDP，计算与内存开销大，长链还易导致梯度不稳。
article.method: RoboFFT对rollout动作做前向加噪，用加权score/flow matching损失作为代理负对数似然，构造PPO式策略比率。对flow策略，它把确定性采样改成带噪声的SDE采样以支持探索，并用蒙特卡洛估计和比率温度校准稳定更新。
article.results: 在Robomimic的Lift、Can、Square、Transport上，论文称RoboFFT与逆向过程基线相当或更好；效率上，RoboFFT-F相对ReinFlow平均训练加速1.53×，RoboFFT-D在四个state-input任务上相对DPPO平均加速38.0×（仍用N_mc=16）。VLA实验用3.3B参数的π0在LIBERO-Object和LIBERO-Spatial上报告提升，但论文未给出具体成功率数字。真机每任务20次试验：Pick Eggplant 12/20→18/20→20/20，Peg Insertion 10/20→19/20→20/20，Pour 9/20→15/20→18/20，Cabinet Retrieval 5/20→14/20→17/20；Pick Eggplant上BC Agg.为14/20、DRWR为12/20。
article.why_it_matters: 它把RL微调的目标对齐到生成式策略预训练时的匹配损失，避开反向采样链的似然计算，为扩散、流和VLA策略提供统一的在线后训练接口。真机离线到在线结果说明该路线不只停留在仿真。
article.limitations: 匹配损失只是真实对数似然的代理，尺度随噪声调度、动作维度和架构变化，仍需温度校准；论文自己的诊断显示代理比率与参考比率的Spearman相关仅约0.2，排序一致性有限。框架依赖on-policy PPO，数据效率有限，真机部署还需离线到在线迭代采集与重训。

figure.caption: Overview of {RoboFFT}. We first collect the offline data leveraging teleoperation and pretrain the base policy with the score / flow matching loss. The pretrained policy then generates actions using an SDE sampler and receives reward feedback from the environment. Finally, we apply forward noising and reuse the matching loss as a surrogate likelihood for PPO-style policy update.

page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.

Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
Haipeng Liu
Yang Wang
†
†

Meng Wang

Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from
https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM
.

1
Introduction
Figure 2
:
(a) Comparison of the generated results, as well as the attention score map of text prompts and image references, between IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
and MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
for image customization. (b) Comparison of the generated results between InstantStyle

and StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
for style transfer. (c) Comparison of generated results guided by different frequency band of the image reference.
Personalized image generation focuses on synthesizing text-driven images conditioned on reference images, which enjoys remarkable progress, benefiting from the powerful denosing capabilities of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)
Ho et al. (2020)
;
Liu et al. (2024)
;
Liu et al. (2025a)
,
e.g.
, Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
;
Esser et al. (2024)
;
Podell et al. (2023)
;
Qian et al. (2022)
;
Qian et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024c)
. Typically, the personalized image generation involves two key subtasks,
i.e.
,
image customization
and
style transfer
. Given text prompts, image customization
Xiao et al. (2025)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Pang et al. (2024)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Kumari et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2025b)
;
Ma et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2022)
;
Cao et al. (2026)
;
Jiang et al. (2026)
aims to generate images by substituting the foreground semantics in the text prompts with the foreground extracted from the reference images, while preserving the background of the text prompts. In contrast, style transfer
Qin et al. (2025)
;
Rout et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2023)
;
Sohn et al. (2023)
;
Zhu et al. (2025)
;
Qi et al. (2024)
;
Hertz et al. (2024)
;
Lei et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Xing et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Wang et al. (2024a)
;
Jeong et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2022)
focuses on disentangling style (
background
) from reference images and aligning the foreground with the text prompt. However, prior arts have struggled to align the generated image with the text prompts within each individual subtask.
Figure 3
:
Illustration of our proposed
Dual-FDM
pipeline (a); For customization style transfer (b), we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Sec.
2.3
). For the color style transfer (c), we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Sec.
2.4
). Each of the two personalized image generation tasks are conducted in the early and late stage of the whole denoising process guided by text prompts as illustrated in Eq. (
1
).
For image customization, substantial efforts
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
aim to
emphasize dense image references of the foreground while overwhelming sparse text prompts of the background, especially for complex ones
,
e.g.
, a degraded “
flower wreath
” and the missing “
coffee
” in the IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
of Fig.
2
(a). Building on this, layout-based methods
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
exploit spatial layouts to explicitly constrain reference concepts to the foreground, while assigning background regions to text prompts.
This preserves the foreground identity, but the explicit separation of foreground and background in the layout disrupts overall consistency, leading to the misalignment with (complex / long) text prompts.
As illustrated in the MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(a), the generated spatial arrangement of “
flower wreath
” and “
coffee
” diverges from the prompt and instead resembles
“A flower wreath around a dog near a coffee”
.
When coming to style transfer, during the early stage of the denoising process with high-level noise, the foreground is reconstructed from sparse text prompts,
the dense style information intended for the background often leaks into the foreground, resulting in misalignment with the text prompts
,
e.g.
, the incorrect number of “
woman
" in the InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
of Fig.
2
(b). To resolve such issue, StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
applies style via instance normalization
Huang and Belongie (2017)
in the cross-attention layers and leverages layout to preserve foreground in the self-attention layers. Nevertheless, self-attention score maps highlight only the most salient regions, implying that the extracted layout can align only with simple text prompts (
i.e.
, “
a dog
") rather than the multi-objects (“
two pillows and one lemon
" in the StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(b)) text prompts, thereby
preventing it from handling the complex text prompts
.
So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.
2
Methodology
Central to our proposed Dual-FDM cover the following aspects: 1) how to pop up the background of the image references (Sec.
2.2
); 2) how to disentangle the mid-frequency band in customization style transfer (Sec.
2.3
); 3) how to disentangle the low-frequency band in color style transfer (Sec.
2.4
); 4) how to adaptively modulate the timesteps within the denoising process between early and late stages (Sec.
2.5
). Before shedding light on Dual-FDM, we elaborate the preliminary regarding decoupled cross-attention mechanism, which plays a pivotal role of personalized image generation.

Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.

Aiello et al. (2025)

, and

Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.
