Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

Appendix I
Limitations and Broader Impacts
Limitations.
As illustrated in Fig.
14
, for customization style transfer, when the style reference contains extremely sparse patterns (
e.g.
, line-based structures), the mid-frequency customized cues may
attenuate high-frequency style details, leading to incomplete style information
. We plan to address this issue in our future work.
Broader Impacts.
Our
Dual-FDM
can generate the personalized image according to the text prompt and reference images, our method may raise certain ethical concerns. The personalized image could potentially be misused in the creation of misleading information. We strongly advocate for the establishment of clear accountability in the use of such technologies, along with enhanced legal and technical oversight, to ensure they are applied responsibly.

Theory assumptions and proofs
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer:
[N/A]
Justification: We did not include theoretical results in our paper.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include theoretical results.
•
All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.
•
All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.
•
The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.
•
Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.
•
Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.
4.
Experimental result reproducibility
Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We have described the model details in the implementation details in Sec.
D
of the Appendix and carefully described the experimental metrics in the experimental chapter. The information we provide is sufficient and detailed for replication purposes.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
If the paper includes experiments, a
[No]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.
•
If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.
•
Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.
•
While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example
(a)
If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.
(b)
If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.
(c)
If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).
(d)
We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.
5.
Open access to data and code
Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We make a detailed description of the implementation details to ensure that they are repeatable and use publicly available personalized image generation datasets. We provide our code in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.
•
Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (
https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy
) for more details.
•
While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so
[No]
is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).
•
The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (
https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy
) for more details.
•
The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.
•
At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).
•
Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.
6.
Experimental setting/details

[Yes]

D
of the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.

7.
Experiment statistical significance
Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?
Answer:
[N/A]
.
Justification: Based on our experimental experience, the reproducibility of the experiments involved in this work is high, with results that are replicable and stable, rather than simply reporting the highest outcomes. Additionally, previous related work
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
has also not reported error bars. We thus do not run the statistical significance test.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper does not include experiments.
•
The authors should answer
[Yes]
if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.
•
The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).
•
The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)
•
The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).
•
It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.
•
It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

of the Mainbody .

Code of ethics

https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines
?

[Yes]

10.
Broader impacts
Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: The paper have conducted a discussion of broader impacts in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

If the authors answer
[N/A]
or
[No]
, they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.
•
Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.
•
The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

•
If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
11.
Safeguards

[N/A]

Ruiz et al. (2023)

Wang et al. (2024b)

Gal et al. (2022)

Peng et al. (2025)

Gao et al. (2024)

Huang et al. (2025a)
and the pretrained generation models Stable Diffusion XL, there is no relevant description we will set up safeguards when we release the code of
Dual-FDM

The answer

•
Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
•
We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.
12.
Licenses for existing assets
Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

New assets

[N/A]

Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

article.headline: 双参考频域解耦的扩散个性化生成
article.lede: Dual-FDM 用 DCT 掩码分离双参考图的中高低频，缓解文本对齐被图像参考压制的问题。
article.problem: 现有个性化扩散模型在图像定制时容易让密集前景参考压过文本提示，在风格迁移时又常把风格泄漏到前景，导致生成图与（复杂）文本提示错位。作者观察到，问题源于去噪过程中低、中、高频段相互纠缠：低频主要承载颜色，中频编码全局结构，高频对应局部纹理。尤其在高噪声的早期阶段，低中频占主导，单一图像参考内的频段会相互强化，从而压制文本引导。
article.method: 作者提出 Dual-FDM：用离散余弦变换（DCT）和掩码把参考图拆成低/中/高频段，并在解耦交叉注意力中用替换后的频段作为 key/value 重建去噪特征。定制风格迁移替换风格参考背景的中频为定制参考前景的中频；颜色风格迁移替换风格参考背景的低频为颜色参考前景与背景的低频。方法还用 SVD 构造背景矩阵，并以替换频段的信息熵比值自适应划分去噪早期与晚期。
article.results: 在定制风格迁移上，Dual-FDM_cust 取得 CLIP-T 0.3194、CLIP-TC 0.5031、CLIP-CS 0.6687、HPS×10 2.6007；在颜色风格迁移的 Color 类别上，Dual-FDM_cost 的 CLIP-TS 为 0.5015、CLIP-S 为 0.7178、DINO-S 为 0.4970。效率方面，Dual-FDM_cust 单次推理 10.26 秒、显存占用 12.48 GB，低于表中多数基线。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“双参考”冲突显式落到频段层面，为同时处理定制参考、颜色参考与风格参考提供了可复用的扩散模型改造思路。
article.limitations: 作者在附录承认，当风格参考包含极稀疏的线条结构时，中频定制线索可能削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整；论文也未报告误差棒或显著性检验。

Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion

Abstract
Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits.
To address these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion.
Specifically, we propose
Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation.
Additionally, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.
Figure 1
:
Overview of MT Forcing.
Top left: Our approach reduces artifacts after eight editing turns. Top right: turn-wise and eight-turn mean scores for SenseNova-U1.5 with and without MT Forcing. Bottom: qualitative comparisons illustrate the roles of Single-Turn DMD and Teacher-Forcing Guidance in improving visual quality and cross-turn consistency.
1  Introduction
Multi-turn image editing
[
112
,
40
,
28
,
92
,
61
]
aims to progressively modify an image through a sequence of user instructions.
With rapid advances in unified multimodal models (UMMs)
[
15
,
67
,
12
]
, this task has attracted growing attention from the research community.
Compared with conventional single-turn editing
[
3
,
68
,
30
,
36
,
57
,
10
,
100
]
, it enables users to continuously refine visual content as their creative intentions evolve, making it well suited to creative workflows requiring precise control over successive edits.
Since each edit builds on the results of prior turns, multi-turn image editing is inherently causal
[
86
,
62
]
, which naturally aligns with autoregressive (AR) diffusion
[
23
,
19
,
37
,
13
]
in UMMs.
Such a design enables later edits to draw on the accumulated interaction history while responding to new user instructions.
However, existing methods often exhibit drift after only a few editing turns (see Fig.
1
for examples), manifesting in two aspects: 1)
unstable
visual quality, with accumulating visual artifacts and progressive degradation of fine-grained textures and local structures; and 2)
inconsistent
image content, with unintended alterations to regions outside the requested edit and failures to retain prior edits that should remain unchanged. We attribute these failures to exposure bias
[
60
,
66
]
, arising from the mismatch between training and inference conditions.
During training, the model typically conditions on reference histories, whereas inference requires recursively conditioning on its own imperfect histories.
To overcome these challenges, we propose
MT Forcing
, a training paradigm for UMMs based on AR diffusion that enables stable and consistent multi-turn image editing. First, we introduce Single-Turn
D
istribution
M
atching
D
istillation (
Single-Turn DMD
) to counteract visual-quality drift across editing turns.
Our design follows two observations: 1) a single editing turn typically introduces limited degradation
[
72
]
; and 2) editing models can execute multiple actions in one turn
[
73
]
(see Fig.
4
).
These observations motivate using single-turn editing quality as the reference for every turn of a multi-turn student.
Specifically, we reorganize all instructions up to the current turn into a
bundled prompt
that expresses their cumulative editing intent as a single edit to the source image.
Conditioned on this prompt and the source image, the teacher executes the accumulated edits in one turn, providing a quality reference without cross-turn error accumulation.
The student performs autoregressive self-rollouts during training
[
29
,
1
]
, conditioning each edit on its own imperfect outputs.
At each turn, a DMD loss
[
95
,
94
,
16
,
44
]
aligns the student’s rollout output distribution with the teacher’s single-turn output distribution for the same cumulative editing intent.
This trains the student to maintain visual quality under the histories encountered during inference, mitigating exposure bias and progressive visual degradation.
However, the bundled prompt specifies cumulative editing intent without fixing the visual details established in preceding student outputs (see Fig.
4
), so per-turn distribution matching alone does not guarantee cross-turn consistency.
To improve cross-turn consistency, we introduce
Teacher-Forcing Guidance
, which trains the student with teacher forcing on consistent reference trajectories
[
27
,
31
,
99
]
.
We apply this teacher-forced supervision in two stages.
1)
Teacher-Forcing Warmup
: before Single-Turn DMD training, we perform supervised fine-tuning to teach the model to produce consistent edits conditioned on coherent reference histories.
2)
Teacher-Forcing Regularization
: during Single-Turn DMD training, we retain this supervision with a lower weight as a regularizer to preserve history-dependent behavior and cross-turn consistency during distillation
[
97
,
78
,
8
]
.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that MT Forcing achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following across successive editing turns.
To evaluate multi-turn image editing comprehensively, we build on MTEdit-Bench’s
[
6
]
assessment of instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality.
We additionally introduce
Pixel
\mathrm{Pixel}
, a metric based on image matching
[
24
]
that measures geometric alignment between successive editing outputs.
MT Forcing also achieves better alignment under this metric, providing additional evidence of improved content preservation across turns.
In summary, we 1) propose Single-Turn DMD to stabilize visual quality across editing turns by aligning student rollouts with a single-turn teacher;
2) introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance to preserve cross-turn content consistency through teacher-forced training on consistent reference trajectories; and 3) combine these complementary objectives into MT Forcing, which achieves more stable visual quality, greater content consistency, and better instruction following in extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments.
2  Related Work
Multi-Turn Image Editing
extends instruction-based image editing
[
3
,
26
,
46
,
35
,
79
,
73
,
75
,
70
]
to an interactive setting, where users progressively refine an image through a sequence of instructions.
A straightforward approach is to recursively apply a single-turn editor, conditioning each turn on the previous output and the current instruction
[
112
,
40
,
28
,
101
]
.
However, this formulation does not explicitly model the full interaction history, limiting its ability to retain earlier constraints and resolve context-dependent instructions
[
91
]
.
Recent approaches build on UMMs to incorporate previous instructions and generated images into a shared context for subsequent edits
[
12
,
92
]
.
Multi-turn Consistent Image Editing
[
112
]
uses flow-based inversion and dual-objective guidance to stabilize sampling, while FreqEdit
[
40
]
preserves high-frequency features to reduce accumulated degradation.
VINCIE
[
62
]
learns in-context editing from video-derived image-text sequences, and AnchorEdit
[
86
]
introduces causal self-rollout training and memory to preserve subject identity across turns.
MT-EditFlow
[
28
]
optimizes rewards aggregated over editing trajectories, while Edit-R2
[
92
]
reconstructs session intent and jointly optimizes reasoning and image generation. Most recently, MT-OPSD
[
101
]
constructs degraded inputs through identity rollouts and distills clean-conditioned teacher predictions into the student.
However, the mismatch between training on reference histories and inference on self-generated outputs can cause errors to accumulate, making visual quality and content consistency difficult to maintain over successive turns
[
28
,
101
]
.
Diffusion Distillation
aims to reduce iterative diffusion sampling to one or a few steps with minimal loss in generation quality.
Teacher-trajectory regression learns the teacher’s sampling dynamics through direct noise-to-image regression
[
51
,
106
]
or progressive step compression
[
63
,
58
]
, while InstaFlow
[
47
]
straightens trajectories to facilitate one-step distillation.
Consistency-based methods constrain predictions along a diffusion trajectory to share a common endpoint
[
71
,
53
,
54
]
, with extensions to interval mappings
[
33
,
107
,
25
,
77
]
and transitive or bootstrapped supervision
[
2
,
22

5  Conclusion
We presented MT Forcing, which combines learning on self-generated histories with reference supervision for stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive UMMs.
Single-Turn DMD transfers single-turn editing quality to student rollouts using a teacher that realizes cumulative editing intent directly from the source image, avoiding recursive error accumulation in its supervision.
Teacher-Forcing Guidance complements marginal distribution matching with reference-conditioned supervision during warmup and distillation, encouraging the history–output dependencies needed for content preservation.
Experiments on SenseNova-U1 and SenseNova-U1.5 demonstrate improved instruction following, content consistency, and drift robustness on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench, with increasingly pronounced benefits at later turns.

article.headline: MT Forcing 缓解多轮图像编辑漂移
article.lede: MT Forcing 结合单轮分布匹配蒸馏与教师强制引导，在八轮图像编辑基准上显著减缓质量与内容漂移。
article.problem: 多轮图像编辑会在几轮后出现漂移：视觉质量不稳定，伪影累积、细节退化；内容不一致，未请求区域被改动、先前编辑丢失。作者将失败归因于训练—推理条件不匹配造成的暴露偏差：训练时条件于参考历史，推理时却递归依赖模型自身不完美的输出。
article.method: Single-Turn DMD 把截至当前轮的指令重组为捆绑提示，让冻结的单轮教师直接从源图执行累积编辑，并用 DMD 损失把学生自 rollout 的每轮输出分布对齐到该教师分布。Teacher-Forcing Guidance 则在参考轨迹上用 flow matching 监督历史依赖的转换，先做 warmup，再以 λTF 加权作为蒸馏正则项。整体目标结合 DMD 损失与教师强制正则，以兼顾视觉质量和跨轮一致性。
article.results: 在 MTEdit-Bench 的 step-wise 子基准（100 个 session、每个 8 轮）上，Turn 8 时 SenseNova-U1 的 IF 和 CC 分别提升 7.45 和 6.82，SenseNova-U1.5 分别提升 4.65 和 4.46；SenseNova-U1.5 的 DRS 全程保持 4.20–4.35，基线从 4.09 降至 3.03；八轮平均 Pixel 从 6.34 降至 0.74，降幅 88.4%。消融中完整方法的八轮均值为 IF 9.66、CC 8.40、DRS 4.30、Pixel 0.74。
article.why_it_matters: 多轮编辑是交互式视觉创作的关键形态，而暴露偏差会让长会话质量迅速衰减；MT Forcing 不依赖能联合生成完整编辑轨迹的双向教师，为自回归扩散 UMM 的长轮稳定性提供了可复用训练思路。
article.limitations: 单轮教师的条件弱于学生，捆绑提示也不固定前序输出中的视觉细节，因此仅靠 DMD 不能保证跨轮一致；教师强制正则的权重需仔细调节，论文显示 λTF=1 或 0.5 时毛发细节变模糊，且评估仅覆盖 100 个 session 的八轮自动评分，训练与推理开销论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: MT Forcing 总览：单轮 DMD 对齐学生自 rollout 与单轮教师分布，教师强制引导在参考轨迹上监督历史依赖转换，整体训练先 warmup 后联合 DMD 与教师强制正则。

figure.caption: {Overview of MT Forcing.} (a)~Single-Turn DMD matches student rollout marginals to single-turn teacher distributions. (b)~Teacher-Forcing Guidance supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories via flow matching to encourage cross-turn consistency. (c)~Overall training: teacher-forcing warmup followed by DMD with teacher-forcing regularization.

Abstract
Activation steering provides a lightweight and flexible way to control large
language model (LLM) behavior. However, effective steering requires more than inducing the intended behavior:
it should also limit unintended changes and remain robust across inputs and training data.
Existing evaluations cover these dimensions only in fragments. As a result, the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects have not been systematically characterized.
We introduce
SteerScope
, a two-axis,
multi-dimensional evaluation suite that jointly characterizes
steering
outcomes
and
method properties
through 15 metrics. We score
target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities,
and safety and reliability, and further assess generalization and data
dependence through steering-specific metrics for sample efficiency and sample
sensitivity.
Rather than comparing methods at a single operating point, we characterize their efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.
Under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, we benchmark 23 methods spanning 4 families, including prompting, LoRA, and SFT as
baseline methods, and release the suite as an extensible codebase.
We find that current activation steering methods do not yet surpass the Prompt Steering baseline in their overall balance between steering efficacy and side effects:
across both model scales, no evaluated activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without incurring greater composite side effects.
We further uncover a
consistent coupling between steering efficacy and side effects. Under OOD
prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to become
more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and
fluency. Methods also exhibit sharply different sample-efficiency profiles.

1
Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) are deployed across diverse tasks and
applications, fine-grained control over their behavior has become increasingly
important
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
. Prompting and fine-tuning are widely used
for this purpose. However, prompting lacks an explicit mechanism for continuously
adjusting the strength of a desired behavior, while fine-tuning requires
additional training and parameter updates
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. Recently,
activation steering
has emerged as a promising approach to behavioral control. It intervenes in internal
representations, such as the residual stream, to induce or suppress specific
concepts, styles, and safety-related behaviors
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
. By keeping
the backbone parameters frozen and allowing intervention strength to be adjusted,
activation steering is more lightweight and adjustable.
However, the effects of steering are not always confined to the intended target.
Prior work has reported multi-dimensional side effects across language quality,
task capabilities, safety, and reliability. These include degraded generation
quality and task performance, as well as changes in bias, refusal, and jailbreak
susceptibility
(
Stickland et al., 2024
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Existing evidence suggests that
these side effects may arise from concept entanglement, whereby concepts
are not behaviorally independent and steering one can unintentionally alter
others
(
Durmus et al., 2024
;
Siu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026d
)
. Beyond these side effects, steering outcomes may vary across
input distributions. They may also depend on the amount and composition of the
data used to construct the intervention
(
Tan et al., 2024
;
Braun et al., 2025
;
Ding et al., 2026
)
. Together, these challenges motivate a
comprehensive evaluation framework organized around two questions:
what steering
changes
and
when those changes hold
.
Recent work has begun to establish benchmarks for evaluating LLM steering, such as
AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
,
SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
,
FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
, and
CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
. However, existing benchmarks cover the relevant dimensions only in fragments, leaving an incomplete picture of what steering changes and when its effects hold. For example, AxBench limits side-effect evaluation to instruction following and
fluency. SteeringSafety centers on safety entanglement, while CLaS-Bench
specializes in cross-lingual language control. FaithSteer-BENCH focuses on deployment-time reliability, but evaluates each
method at a single calibrated operating point and does not cover side effects
on language quality or safety.
Fig.
1
(right) illustrates these gaps in coverage.
Figure 1:
Overview of the SteerScope evaluation suite and benchmark coverage.
Left: our hierarchical evaluation taxonomy. Right: coverage matrix of existing
steering benchmarks, where rows denote taxonomy nodes and columns denote
evaluation works (last column: SteerScope). A
✓
indicates a corresponding metric,
✗
indicates none, and
△
\triangle
indicates that the dimension is considered indirectly but
not measured independently.
To bridge this gap, we introduce
SteerScope
, a comprehensive, multi-dimensional evaluation suite for LLM steering.
1.
Systematic evaluation taxonomy.
SteerScope organizes 15 metrics into a hierarchical taxonomy with two complementary axes (Fig.
1
, left).
Steering Outcomes
examines what steering changes, covering target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability.
Method Properties
examines when steering effects hold, covering generalization under cross-lingual prompt shifts and dependence on training data.
2.
Broad method coverage.
We evaluate 23 methods spanning 4 families on 2 models.
These include diverse activation steering methods alongside prompting, LoRA, and SFT baselines.
3.
Efficacy–side-effect trade-off characterization.
We characterize each adjustable method through its efficacy–side-effect trade-offs, revealing how unintended effects change alongside target efficacy.
Our central finding is that
current activation steering methods do not outperform the Prompt Steering baseline in the efficacy–side-effect trade-off on either evaluated model
.
Although some activation steering methods outperform this baseline on existing benchmarks, none achieves higher target efficacy without greater composite side effects under our default aggregation.
On Gemma-2-9B-it, for example, A-PSR improves the Concept Expression score by 1.30 points but incurs an average normalized degradation of 0.12.
Consistent with this, steering efficacy and side effects generally increase together as intervention strength grows.
Nevertheless, activation steering remains useful because its adjustable intervention strength provides access to high-efficacy operating points.
Among activation steering approaches, methods with learned interventions tend to achieve more favorable trade-offs than optimization-free methods.
We further find that target efficacy is often preserved under out-of-distribution prompts. In contrast, side effects tend to become more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and fluency.
Finally, sample efficiency varies substantially across methods, reflecting
different levels of dependence on training-data size.
2
Related Work
Representation-Based Activation Steering.
Representation-based activation steering controls model behavior by intervening on
internal activations at inference time. Early methods often modeled target concepts
with linear directions, motivated in part by the linear representation hypothesis
(
Bolukbasi et al., 2016
;
Elhage et al., 2022
;
Park et al., 2024
;
Nanda et al., 2023
)
. Existing methods span
contrastive directions, subspaces, latent representations,
geometric transformations, hypernetworks, and nonlinear interventions
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Marks & Tegmark, 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024
;
Pham et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Jin et al., 2026
;
You et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. We organize the methods evaluated in this
work by their underlying mechanisms in Section
4
.
Benchmarks for Activation Steering.
Existing benchmarks have begun to standardize the evaluation of activation steering, but each covers only a subset of the relevant evaluation dimensions. AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
evaluates 500 steering targets across activation steering, prompting, and fine-tuning methods, but its off-target evaluation is limited to instruction following and fluency. SteeringSafety
(
Siu et al., 2026
)
studies behavioral entanglement across nine predefined safety perspectives within a curated safety concept set. FaithSteer-BENCH
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
focuses on deployment-time reliability, evaluating clean controllability, capability preservation, and robustness under changing conditions at a single calibrated operating point. SteerEval
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
broadens evaluation across behavioral domains and concept granularities, while CLaS-Bench
(
Gurgurov et al., 2026
)
extends steering evaluation to 32 languages and cross-lingual transfer.
Complementary studies have identified specific steering side effects, including degradation in generation coherence
(
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
, capability–behavior trade-offs
(
Sprejer et al., 2026
)
, and sensitivity to individual samples and prompt conditions
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
.
Overall, existing evaluations cover safety entanglement, deployment reliability, cross-lingual control, and other aspects, but remain fragmented across evaluation dimensions and steering methods.

Data Dependence.
To measure how training-data variations—in both the size of the training set and which examples it contains—affect the Overall steering effect, we evaluate
data dependence
through two metrics, Sample Efficiency and Sample Sensitivity, which characterize dependence on the amount of data and on which examples are sampled, respectively.
Sample Efficiency.
Sample Efficiency measures how much of a method’s full-data Overall improvement
can be recovered from fewer training examples. Existing studies often vary
training-set size as method-specific ablations and report absolute task scores,
making data-efficiency comparisons across methods difficult
(
Ding et al., 2026
;
Jiang et al., 2026
)
. We therefore normalize each
reduced-data improvement by the corresponding full-data improvement, yielding a
comparable measure of how efficiently each method uses training data. The exact
estimator and data settings are given in Appendix
A.3.1
.
Sample Sensitivity.
Beyond data quantity, we measure a method’s dependence on training-data
composition under a fixed data budget. We quantify the variation in
factor-

0

lower values indicate weaker dependence on training-data composition. The exact
estimator and data settings are given in Appendix
A.3.2
.
4
Steering Methods
We evaluate 23 representative methods and baselines, plus a Random control. The methods span diverse steering mechanisms while avoiding redundant variants and enabling both method- and mechanism-level analysis. A broader catalogue is provided in Appendix
B
.
4.1
Optimization-Free Steering Methods
Concept Directions.
These methods construct steering directions from activation patterns associated
with a target concept.
DiffMean
adds the difference between positive
and negative mean representations to model activations at inference
time
(
Marks & Tegmark, 2024
)
;
PCA
extracts the first principal component
from positive-example activations
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, while
LAT
applies PCA to contrastive activation
differences
(
Zou et al., 2023
)
. As a control,
Random
applies
DiffMean after randomly partitioning the training examples, removing
concept-specific label alignment.
Structured Interventions.
These methods introduce geometric, latent-space, or unit-level interventions.
Spherical Steering
performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation toward a target direction, aiming to better respect the geometry of the model’s representation space
(
You et al., 2026
)
.
HiDRA
performs steering in a higher-dimensional feature space, where discriminative structure can be captured
(
Pham et al., 2026
)
.
AUSteer
steers in discriminative LLM components and assigns adaptive strengths
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
.
SAE-Based Methods.
SAE-based methods use decoder directions from a sparse-autoencoder dictionary
(
Huben et al., 2024
)
.
SAE
uses a concept-associated feature, while
SAE-A
selects the feature with highest target-discriminative AUROC
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
4.2
Directly Optimized Steering Methods
Learned Steering Directions.
Several methods learn interventions using supervised training.
Linear Probe
trains a linear discriminator between positive and negative representations and uses the learned weight vector as the steering direction
(
Alain & Bengio, 2017
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
SSV
optimizes an additive vector using a language-modeling loss on training responses
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, and
ReFT-r1
similarly learns a rank-one representation intervention, jointly optimizing concept detection and generation-time steering objectives
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
.
Learned Subspace and Adaptive Interventions.
LoReFT
learns a low-rank intervention subspace over hidden representations
(
Wu et al., 2024
)
.
PSR
combines a learned steering direction with an activation-dependent gate, allowing intervention strength to vary across tokens
(
Heyman & Vandeputte, 2026
)
. We evaluate its all-layer variant (
A-PSR
) and single-layer variant (
S-PSR
).
RePS
learns an intervention through preference optimization
(
Wu et al., 2025b
)
.
ODESteer
constructs a vector field from the gradient of a learned nonlinear barrier function and applies multi-step integration
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
;
StepODESteer
uses the same construction with a single update step.
4.3
Hypernetwork-Based Steering Methods
These methods use shared auxiliary networks to generate steering interventions conditioned on natural-language targets.
HyperSteer
trains a transformer-based hypernetwork that maps a natural-language steering target and the model’s internal activations to a dynamically generated steering vector
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
.
FLAS
instead trains a transformer-style FlowBlock to parameterize a concept-conditioned velocity field over activation space
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
.
4.4
Non-Representation-based Steering Methods
Four baseline methods that do not operate directly on model representations are included: two prompting baselines and two parameter-update baselines.
Prompt Steering
uses an LLM to convert each target concept into a short steering context, whereas
Simple Prompt Steering
uses a fixed concept-conditioned instruction; both prepend the resulting context to the original instruction. The prompt templates are provided in Appendix
C.5
. We further evaluate
Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT)
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
and
Low-Rank Adaptation
(LoRA)
(
Hu et al., 2022
)
as the two parameter-update baselines.
5
Experiments
Training.
Following AxBench
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)

sampled from the GemmaScope SAE concept list on Neuronpedia
(

;

. For each concept, we
use DeepSeek-V3.2
(
DeepSeek-AI, 2025
)
to generate 72 contrastive pairs, where the two responses share the same instruction but differ in whether they express the concept. All methods use the complete CONCEPT500 setting; the exception is SFT, discussed below.
Evaluation.
Metric definitions are given in §
3
. All LM-judge metrics
use instructions from AlpacaEval
(
Li et al., 2023b
)

on all 500 concepts and costlier metrics on a 50-concept subset shared
across methods and factors. Appendix Table
6
lists the concept
and instance counts for each metric group. For compute reasons, SFT is trained and
evaluated on 20 concepts throughout. Generalization is evaluated only on text-type
concepts, since cross-lingual prompt shifts do not apply to code or math concepts.

We evaluate Gemma-2-2B-it and Gemma-2-9B-it
(
Gemma Team et al., 2024
)
. We use residual-stream

, FLAS

.
Factors.
For each method with a strength parameter, we sweep its established factors
(Appendix Table

).
5.1
Efficacy and Side Effects

Reducing side effects remains a key challenge for steering methods.
Across both model scales, methods with an explicit steering factor generally incur
larger composite side effects as target efficacy increases. At its Overall-selected
method-level steering factor, A-PSR improves Concept Expression by 1.20 and 1.30 points on
Gemma-2-2B-it and Gemma-2-9B-it, respectively, while incurring composite side
effects of 0.11 and 0.12. Recent methods such as
A-PSR outperform Prompt Steering on AxBench’s Overall and Concept Expression
metrics. Figure
3
further shows that individual
methods can locally surpass Prompt Steering on particular capability metrics.
Yet when a broader range of side effects is considered, no activation steering
method dominates the Prompt Steering baseline on the efficacy–side-effect
trade-off. We examine the robustness of this aggregate
comparison to alternative metric weightings in
Appendix
D.1.1
. These results suggest that future work on steering should focus on reducing unintended effects.
Optimization-free methods generally exhibit worse efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.
Compared with prompting and methods with learned interventions, optimization-free methods generally exhibit less favorable efficacy–side-effect trade-offs. One possible explanation is that prompting leverages existing instruction-following capabilities, while methods with learned interventions incorporate task-specific feedback through gradient-based training. In contrast, directions extracted from representation statistics or pretrained features do not directly constrain the resulting behavioral changes.
Low-strength steering can improve off-target metrics.
Some low-strength interventions improve off-target performance relative to the
unsteered model. Reversing the steering direction removes or reverses these
gains, suggesting direction-dependent conceptual entanglement rather than a
generic effect of weak perturbations
(Appendix
D.3
).
Beyond the aggregate score, method rankings vary across individual side-effect

6
Conclusion
We introduced
SteerScope
, a comprehensive evaluation suite for LLM steering organized around two axes:
Steering Outcomes
and
Method Properties
. Our
taxonomy organizes steering evaluation into target efficacy, side effects on
language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability, and method
properties under distribution and training-data changes. We further provide a
systematic taxonomy of steering methods and conduct controlled comparisons across
optimization-free, directly optimized, and hypernetwork-based approaches, alongside
prompting, LoRA, and SFT baselines. By comparing strength-dependent
efficacy–side-effect curves across methods and model scales, SteerScope provides
a broader view than comparisons based on selected operating points.
Our evaluation reveals that performance on existing benchmarks does not fully
reflect steering quality. Activation steering methods that outperform the Prompt Steering
baseline on existing benchmarks do not necessarily maintain this advantage
when broader side effects are considered, and stronger steering efficacy is generally
accompanied by larger unintended effects. Activation steering nevertheless remains
valuable for its adjustable access to high-efficacy operating points. Among
activation steering approaches, methods with learned interventions tend to achieve more
favorable trade-offs than optimization-free methods. Improvements at weak
intervention strengths suggest that side effects can reflect conceptual entanglement
rather than uniform degradation. We further find that under out-of-distribution
prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to be
more pronounced. Methods also exhibit substantially different sample-efficiency profiles.
Use of Generative AI
We used generative AI in the experimental workflow. DeepSeek-V3.2-Instruct generated concept-conditioned positive and negative responses for the contrastive training data, as well as concept-specific instructions for Prompt Steering, A-PSR, and S-PSR. GPT-4o-mini was used to score concept expression, instruction relevance, and fluency; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct was used to evaluate JailbreakBench responses. The corresponding prompts, scoring criteria, and settings are reported in the experimental details and appendix. We also used generative AI to polish the manuscript. The authors take responsibility for the LLM-generated materials and LLM-based judgments used in this work.

.

and

Column
Definition
Contrastive Data
Uses contrastive positive and negative examples of a target concept to derive a steering vector.
Scaling
Multiplies selected activation components, directions, or subspaces rather than adding a vector.
Linear Change
Locates a dominant linear direction that best represents a target concept and steers by linear addition.
Subspace Change
Locates a dominant multi-dimensional subspace that best represents a target concept and steers in that subspace.
Geodesic
Steers by geodesic rotation or norm-preserving.
Latent Space
Steers in a transformed representation space, such as SAE, random-feature, kernel, or invertible latent spaces.
Adaptive Strength
Adapts the steering strength based on the input prompt or current activations at inference time or gated.
Multi-Step Dynamics
Applies steering through multiple sequential updates.
SAE-Based
Uses a sparse autoencoder to select or construct steering directions.
Shared Module
Creates a reusable learned steering tool across multiple concepts.

Experimental Details
C.1
Models and Shared Setup
We evaluate all methods on instruction-tuned Gemma-2 models at 2 scales,
google/gemma-2-2b-it
and
google/gemma-2-9b-it
. For methods
defined at a single intervention site, we intervene on the residual stream at
layer 20 in both models, matching the intervention site used during both
training and evaluation of HyperSteer
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
,
FLAS
(
Jin et al., 2026
)
, and S-PSR
(
Heyman & Vandeputte, 2026
)
. Layer 20 corresponds
to approximately 77% and 48% of the
26- and 42-layer model stacks, respectively. The
training data for each concept contain 72 contrastive
response pairs generated by DeepSeek-V3.2-Instruct, giving 144 labeled examples. Unless
otherwise specified, training uses bfloat16 precision and a base random seed of
42, from which method- and concept-specific seeds are derived. Gradient-based
methods use AdamW with a linear learning-rate schedule and no warmup, except for
FLAS as specified below. All methods use the complete CONCEPT500 setting, except
SFT, which is trained and evaluated on 20 concepts.

C.6
Prior Human Validation of AxBench-Style Judges
Our Concept Expression, Instruction Relevance, and Fluency evaluators follow
the AxBench prompts and ternary scoring scheme and use the same judge model,
GPT-4o-mini
(
Wu et al., 2025a
)
. AxBench evaluated these judges against human
ratings using five participants, each of whom scored 30 steered generations
spanning six methods on Gemma-2-9B at layer 20. The reported Pearson correlation
was
0.57
0.57
among human raters and
0.58
0.58
between the LLM judge and human raters,
indicating that, in the AxBench setting, LLM–human agreement was comparable to
inter-human agreement.
The comparable LLM–human and inter-human agreement supports the use of these
AxBench-style evaluators in SteerScope. We further complement the three
LLM-based scores with established task-specific benchmarks and deterministic
evaluators wherever available.

D.2
Ranking Agreement Across Side-Effect Metrics
To examine whether the aggregate score masks metric-specific differences, we
rank methods by their degradation on each side-effect metric at their
Overall-selected method-level steering factors. We then compute Spearman correlations between the
metric-specific rankings.
Figure 8:
Spearman correlations between method rankings produced by different
side-effect metrics on Gemma-2-2B-it (left) and Gemma-2-9B-it (right) at
layer 20. Each method is evaluated at its Overall-selected method-level steering factor.
The metrics do not produce fully consistent method rankings, supporting the
need for multi-dimensional side-effect evaluation.
Ranking agreement is mixed on Gemma-2-2B-it but generally stronger on
Gemma-2-9B-it. JailbreakBench false refusal is a notable exception, showing
weak or negative correlations with most other metrics.
We hypothesize that this difference may reflect the range of evaluation examples each
model can solve. The 9B model may solve more difficult examples whose successful
completion depends on multiple overlapping capabilities; steering-induced
disruption of these shared capabilities may therefore manifest across several
metrics simultaneously. In contrast, floor effects on the 2B model may obscure
such shared degradation.

article.headline: 23种激活引导方法评测：未胜提示基线
article.lede: SteerScope以15项指标评测23种引导方法，发现激活引导在功效与副作用的平衡上仍未超越提示基线。
article.problem: 激活引导只需在推理时干预内部表示即可控制大模型行为，但既往评测各自只覆盖一部分维度：AxBench的副作用只看指令跟随与流畅度，SteeringSafety聚焦安全纠缠，FaithSteer-BENCH只在单一校准工作点评估。因此，「引导到底改变了什么」与「这些改变在输入分布变化、训练数据变化下是否成立」这两个问题一直缺乏系统刻画，功效与副作用之间的权衡关系也没有被完整测量。
article.method: 作者提出SteerScope，把15项指标组织成两条轴：Steering Outcomes测量目标功效（Concept Expression）以及语言质量、任务能力、安全与可靠性三类副作用；Method Properties测量跨语言提示分布偏移下的泛化保持率，以及样本效率与样本敏感性两项数据依赖指标。评测不比较单个工作点，而是沿每个方法的强度因子扫描出功效—副作用曲线；在Gemma-2-2B-it与Gemma-2-9B-it的第20层残差流上，以匹配的模型、任务和评测协议对比23种方法（含提示、LoRA、SFT基线）以及一个Random对照。
article.results: 在各自按Overall选出的方法级强度上，A-PSR在Gemma-2-2B-it与Gemma-2-9B-it上分别把Concept Expression提高1.20与1.30分，同时带来0.11与0.12的平均归一化副作用；在两个模型规模上，没有任何激活引导方法能在不增加复合副作用的前提下取得更高功效，即未能超过Prompt Steering基线。改变11项副作用指标的权重做100万次Dirichlet采样后，Prompt Steering在Gemma-2-2B-it上仍有99.83%（Dirichlet(1)）与88.61%（Dirichlet(0.2)）的抽样中不被支配。跨语言设置下，13个方法里有11个在OOD提示上的指令相关性退化更严重、9个的流畅度退化更严重，而概念增益多数基本保持；样本效率方面，HyperSteer与DiffMean在小数据预算下保留的全数据效应比例明显更高，A-PSR、FLAS、LoRA、ReFT-r1则更依赖数据量。
article.why_it_matters: 它提示现有榜单上的领先并不等于引导质量更高：一旦把语言质量、任务能力与安全可靠性一起计入，激活引导相对提示基线的优势就消失了，后续工作应把重心放在压低非目标副作用上。同时，沿强度扫描而非单点比较的做法，也让「可调强度」这一激活引导的真实价值变得可测量。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖Gemma-2的两个规模与第20层单点干预，SFT因算力限制只在20个概念上训练与评估，泛化实验也只保留ID增益≥0.1的方法计算保持率。此外，方法级强度因子是在完整ID评测集上按Overall选出的，作者承认这可能让工作点校准偏乐观；复合副作用采用11项指标等权平均，虽做了权重扰动检验，但高度稀疏偏好下结论稳健性下降。

TopKLoRA
enables faithful circuit discovery

Abstract
Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable.
We present the full method of
TopKLoRA
, extending the preliminary proposal of
Masiak et al. (2025)
, an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the
k
k
largest adapter latents are active at each token.
Unlike SAEs,
TopKLoRA
is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents.
We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning
gemma-2-2b
,
Qwen2.5-1.5B
, and
Qwen2.5-7B
on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both
necessary
and
sufficient
to implement the backdoor.
Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance.
Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using
TopKLoRA
latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm.
We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code:
https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA

1
Introduction
Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model to a target distribution using data whose provenance often cannot be verified. This makes fine-tuning an attack surface, where a small fraction of poisoned examples suffices to implant a backdoor
(
Wan et al., 2023
)
. Such backdoors, behaviours conditioned on input triggers, have been shown to persist through subsequent safety training
(
Hubinger et al., 2024
)
. High-level defences that act on the data, such as filtering, or those that target outputs, including safety-tuning, leave the low-level mechanism untouched. Furthermore, attempts to localise it in dense weights have proven inconsistent
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
. In our work, we propose a conceptually different approach that makes the fine-tuning update itself auditable, so any behaviour can be attributed to a small set of named components and removed without retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning already confines the update to an adapter, but does not enforce interpretability. Post-hoc dictionaries may provide interpretable latents, yet are optimised to reconstruct activations rather than to cause downstream model behaviour. We therefore propose a circuit discovery framework based on interpretable-by-design adapters.
TopKLoRA
adapters were first proposed in preliminary form by
Masiak et al. (2025)
, who introduced the core mechanism and reported initial results on downstream task performance and autointerpretability, treating its latents as SAE features. In this work, we present the full method, interpreting a
TopKLoRA
adapter instead as a dictionary of conditional steering vectors (Section
3.1
) which, when attached to multiple layers or sub-layer modules, compose into sparse circuits implementing the trained capability. We modify the original architecture formulation by adding a
ReLU
\mathrm{ReLU}
to each adapter’s latent computation. We also develop and adapt several circuit discovery algorithms to the sparse adapter setup, as described in Section
4
. We further report a comprehensive evaluation on the sleeper agents case study and compare with baselines.
Across three base models,
TopKLoRA
concentrates the backdoor into circuits up to an order of magnitude smaller than those of a rank-matched dense LoRA. Ablating the verified circuit removes the backdoor on at least 99.9% of held-out triggered prompts and, whenever the adapter spans several layers, leaves instruction-following close to that of a model that was never poisoned. Dense circuits, by contrast, cover half or more of the adapter and are no more specific than a random latent set of the same size. On organisms with gradient-routed, planted circuits, the same pipeline recovers circuits that lie largely within the planted set, far above chance. This shows that our circuit discovery method includes latents that are known to be responsible for the fine-tuned capability.
Our main contributions
are as follows:
1)
We describe a complete
TopKLoRA
methodology that introduces
compositional
interpretable latents without incurring the reconstruction-loss penalty.
2)
Building on
TopKLoRA
latents, we propose a Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery (CLCD) pipeline that yields highly surgical circuits. We demonstrate it on a real-world sleeper agent case study.
3)
We demonstrate a gradient-routing-based methodology for constructing realistic model organisms with localised circuits.

Circuit discovery.
Circuit discovery aims to identify the part of a model’s computation responsible for a given behaviour
(
Olah et al., 2020
;
Elhage et al., 2021
)
. Many early works defined a circuit as a directed acyclic graph of raw neurons or higher-level network components, such as attention heads. Initially, researchers primarily discovered circuits through iterative, human-guided search via causal interventions such as
activation patching
and
path patching
(
Wang et al., 2022
;
Hanna et al., 2023
)
. These methods were soon complemented by automatic search algorithms
(
Conmy et al., 2023
;
Syed et al., 2023
;
Hanna et al., 2024
;
Bhaskar et al., 2025
)
.
A critical challenge of directly interpreting model internals is polysemanticity in MLP neurons and attention heads
(
Bricken et al., 2023
;
Kissane et al., 2024
)
. Subsequent work therefore shifted the unit of analysis towards more monosemantic, sparse dictionary features, resulting in feature circuits and attribution graphs
(
Marks et al., 2025
;
Dunefsky et al., 2024
;
Ameisen et al., 2025
)
. Nevertheless, feature circuits inherit the training objective of the sparse dictionary learning method they are defined over. SAE latents are optimised for reconstruction rather than for downstream causal effect
(
Braun et al., 2024
)
and localise causal variables at a similar level to raw neurons
(
Mueller et al., 2025
)
. Sparse Feature Circuits (SFC)
(
Marks et al., 2025
)
view the model under study as a computational graph, whose nodes are SAE feature activations and SAE error terms at each token position. As the feature nodes are interpretable, the resulting circuit can itself be interpreted as a graph of named features and edges between them, and the error nodes capture the reconstruction error.
Sleeper agents.
In their work,
Hubinger et al. (2024)
show that LLMs can be trained to exhibit conditionally deceptive behaviour, performing a specific action when exposed to a trigger.
Yu et al. (2025)
run causal tracing on LoRA-trained backdoors and find that by localising and ablating about 3% of attention heads, they can decrease the attack success rate by over 90% in the best case, though this effect is inconsistent, does not replicate across backdoor types, and the authors do not measure model degradation. Finally,
Sheshadri et al. (2025)
apply Latent Adversarial Training to remove backdoors with an unknown trigger, but the method does not localise the backdoor inside the model.

4
CLCD: Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery
We focus on the application of circuit discovery to fine-tunes that introduce a new behaviour.
We treat learnt behaviour presence as a binary property: either correctly learnt and present in a generation string, or absent, and its rate on a dataset split is the fraction of prompts on which it is present.
A behaviour could be, for example, adherence to a chat template, instruction following, or refusal.
The Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery (CLCD) algorithm has two stages: search and verification. Search produces a ranking of the pool, while verification sweeps prefixes of that ranking and determines circuit membership. This formulation allows us to mix and match search algorithms while keeping our verification rules. We compare three search strategies: prefix search over attribution ranking (CLCD-prefix), Sparse Feature Circuits, and single-pass elimination (CLCD-elimination). We call our search contrastive because it scores latents on paired prompts: one elicits the behaviour, and the other one is its control, the same prompt with the eliciting element removed. We assign each latent a score that corresponds to how much it accounts for the difference in the model’s behaviour between the two. The prompt dataset is partitioned into disjoint attribution, elimination, and verification splits.

6.3
Can the backdoor be removed without damaging the model?
Across all three base models, ablating the verified circuit removes the backdoor on at least 99.9% of held-out prompts in every organism, with the remaining leaks studied in Appendix
G.3
.
Simultaneously, in all 30 multi-layer
TopKLoRA
adapters, ablating a circuit does not decrease instruction-following capability, leaving retention close to one (Figure
5
).
Dense LoRA matches this only in the all-layers family, where its circuits often span more than half of the adapter and are no more specific than a random latent set, reflecting adapter redundancy rather than a localised mechanism.
We note that the retention score of single-layer adapters improves with model scale. Ablating a single-layer circuit typically brings gemma-2-2b and Qwen2.5-1.5B close to their base models, whereas every single-layer Qwen2.5-7B organism retains its instruction-following, consistent with its considerably smaller circuits. The retention measure is less precise for Qwen2.5-7B because its adapter improves the base model less, yet every seed’s 95% CI stays above 0.8.
Finally, since poisoning could itself impair the model, we compare gemma-2-2b
TopKLoRA
organisms with clean twins trained with no poisoned examples (Table
4
). First, intact poisoned organisms score the same as their clean twins, indicating that poisoning does not cost instruction-following. Second, after ablating the verified circuit, multi-layer organisms remain close to their clean twins, whereas most single-layer organisms fall well below them. This reinforces our surgicality claims based on the retention score: in adapters spanning several layers, removing the
TopKLoRA
circuit undoes the backdoor while leaving a model close to one that was never poisoned.

Limitations and Conclusion
This work has several limitations. First, we experiment only with models up to 7B. We believe the circuits would be even more surgical in larger models, but this remains future work. Second, our sleeper agent setup relied on a syntactic tag, which limits the complexity of the learnt behaviour. Additionally, our method assumes access to contrastive pairs and knowledge of the trigger to localise the backdoor, which is unrealistic in many cases. We plan to extend our work to semantic and unknown triggers in the future. Third, we do not study the interpretability of individual latents, but rather treat them as uninterpreted nodes in a larger circuit. Finally, we do not analyse the base model’s contribution beyond the SFC experiments, where we model it as an error node. Further investigation is required to find latents that interact with base model features.
We demonstrate that when a model is trained on a poisoned dataset with
TopKLoRA
, we can successfully locate and surgically ablate the part of the fine-tuned model responsible for implementing a backdoor. These circuits are sparse and, when ablated, do not degrade benign fine-tuned task performance. We consider this a step toward interpretable and auditable fine-tuning.

Causal-scrubbing ranking (CLCD-elimination)
CLCD-elimination uses the same attribution score as CLCD-prefix but ranks the pool by absolute score, so latents with negative scores are included and elimination can keep a latent whose removal would strengthen the behaviour. The algorithm runs a single pass over the pool from weakest absolute score to strongest, in a similar manner to ACDC
(
Conmy et al., 2023
)
.
A latent is removed if, with it and all earlier removals taken out of the pool, the surviving latents still pass both verification tests, described in Section
4.2
. Otherwise, it is kept. Each latent is tested once on the disjoint elimination prompt dataset split and its membership decision is fixed at that step. The outcome therefore depends on the visiting order. In practice, the tests are evaluated on nested subsets of the dataset split with early stopping. CLCD-elimination produces a ranking with kept latents in descending attribution order followed by removed latents in reverse removal order.
CLCD-verify then sweeps this ranking on the verification dataset split.

G.1
Does the attribution order matter for CLCD-verify?
CLCD-elimination visits the latent pool from the weakest to the strongest attribution score. To test whether order matters, we rerun it on the single-layer gemma-2-2b organisms with the pool visited in a uniformly random order, three permutations per organism, which uses no attribution at all. Besides the verified circuit, we report the latents elimination keeps (the
kept set
), which isolates the effect of the order, since the verified circuit also depends on the prefix sweep that adds removed latents back and rounds the size up to the grid.
For
TopKLoRA
, the random order enlarges every circuit, as shown in Figure
10
. The kept set triples, from a median of 18 to 54 latents, and the verified circuit grows from 22% to 61% of the adapter. Dense circuits, by contrast, change far less. Their kept set grows from 165 to 211 latents, and the verified circuit, which must span about 90% of the adapter under either order, keeps its size in 12 of 15 runs. Every random-order circuit still passes verification, with at most one held-out backdoor response in 4,000, so attribution makes
TopKLoRA
circuits small rather than valid. Circuits are also not unique:
TopKLoRA
kept sets from different orders overlap by only 7–23% (Jaccard index), several times chance, around a shared core of 3–9 latents, so a verified circuit is a minimal circuit rather than the unique one.

article.headline: 稀疏LoRA把后门压缩成小回路，可精准切除
article.lede: TopKLoRA 每 token 只激活 k 个隐变量，配合对比回路发现，在三款模型上把后门回路缩小至密集 LoRA 的
article.problem: 微调数据来源往往无法核验，少量投毒样本就足以植入后门，而且这类条件触发行为能挺过后续安全训练。参数高效微调虽然把更新限制在适配器内，但 LoRA 瓶颈对可逆线性变换不变、缺乏特权基，原始隐变量本身不可辨识；SAE 等事后字典又以重建激活为目标，而非优化下游因果效应，因此难以把恶意能力定位到具体单元。
article.method: TopKLoRA 在 LoRA 瓶颈上加 ReLU 与 TopK：先算 z=ReLU(Ax)，每个 token 只保留 k 个最大的隐变量，再用 B 上投影，因此每个隐变量可读作一对「条件方向 + 操纵方向」的条件化 steering vector，多层、多模块的适配器组合成稀疏回路。作者提出对比隐变量回路发现（CLCD）：在成对 prompt（触发与去触发）上用积分梯度给全部隐变量排序（另与 Sparse Feature Circuits、单遍消融排序比较），再用固定网格扫描前缀，要求候选回路满足必要性（零消融后验证集行为率恰为 0）与充分性（只保留该回路时行为率相对完整模型的下降在 2 个标准误内）。
article.results: 在 gemma-2-2b、Qwen2.5-1.5B、Qwen2.5-7B 的 sleeper agent 案例中，训练集为 10,000 条 alpaca-cleaned 指令加 500 条投毒样本（毒化率 4.76%），各 organism 在 1,000 条留出触发 prompt 上 ASR 至少 94%，干净 prompt 上至多 5/1,000 触发。验证后的 TopKLoRA 回路在全部 30 组同种子配对中都小于 rank 匹配的密集 LoRA，且差距随适配层数增大：gemma-2-2b 单层中位回路占适配器 22.3%（密集 89.3%）、9 层 band 7.4%（69.4%）、全层 3.4%（41.2%）；Qwen2.5-1.5B 9 层 band 为 22.7%（90.7%）、全层 9.7%（58.3%）。消融验证回路后，每个 organism 在至少 99.9% 的留出触发 prompt 上不再出现后门，且 30 个 multi-layer TopKLoRA 适配器的指令跟随保留率接近 1；作为对照，同尺寸随机隐变量集合消融在六个家族中的五个仍留下后门（中位 ASR 0.92–1.00），而五个密集家族中随机消融即可移除后门（中位 ASR 0.00）。必要性比充分性更省：只消融排名最前的 1.2–6.8% 隐变量就能把 ASR 降到 0，密集 LoRA 需要 20.6–38.9%。在梯度路由植入已知回路的 organism 上，验证回路大部分落在植入集内（如 d=8 时中位 98%，随机概率 12.5%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「可审计的微调」做成可操作流程：恶意能力能被归因到少量具名隐变量并直接切除，无需重训练，也不必牺牲正常指令跟随能力，为 interpretable-by-design 的适配器架构提供了实证支撑。
article.limitations: 实验只做到 7B 模型，触发器是语法标签（|TRIGGER|/|RUN|），且方法假设已知触发器并需要对比 prompt 对，真实投毒场景通常不具备这些条件；作者只把隐变量当作未解释的图节点，未分析基座模型的贡献。附录还显示，用随机访问顺序做消融仍能通过验证（回路从占适配器 22.3% 升到 61.4%），不同顺序保留集合的 Jaccard 重叠仅 7–23%，说明找到的是极小回路而非唯一回路。
article.figure_caption_zh: 在单层 gemma-2-2b 上，按归因分数顺序访问隐变量做 CLCD 消融，比随机顺序更能压缩 TopKLoRA 的验证回路（左）与保留集合（右），而密集 LoRA 回路几乎不受访问顺序影响。

Sensorimotor Alignment:
A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
Yunfei Xie
Affiliation:
Rice University
Howard H. Qian
Affiliation:
Rice University
Shiyi Lan
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Kaiyu Hang

Rice University
Chen Wei
Abstract
Robot foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, motivating low-cost offline proxies for model capability.
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
21
]
suggests that as representations improve, modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion?
To test this, we propose
Sensorimotor Alignment
(
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model’s sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion.
We find that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones
before
costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs).
Beyond this correlation,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs).
With
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
, we extend PRH to robotics and make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.
†

1
Introduction
Robot foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models
[
4
,
3
]
, video models
[
50
]
, and world action models
[
15
,
28
,
5
]
. Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation
[
30
,
33
]
or the real world
[
1
,
9
]
, where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for policy capability.
A natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs
[
31
,
57
]
or pixel-level video quality for world models
[
18
,
52
,
23
]
. However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether a representation is organized for action
[
59
,
24
,
47
,
35
]
. Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, a model must produce different motions across tasks even in similar scenes. This requires aligning the sensory representation with the motor representation.
This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
21
]
, which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to a shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces.
For example, images and text are two projections of the same underlying world.
As vision and language models scale,
they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points.
We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical robot motion be viewed as another projection of that same world, such that more capable embodied models better align their vision and language representations with the structure of motion trajectories?
We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space.
We formalize this as
Sensorimotor Alignment
(
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free metric, illustrated in
Figure
1
. For each episode in a robot dataset, a model’s image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episode’s nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment.
In
Section
3
, we show that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the task success of the resulting VLAs, more strongly than their visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs),
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
likewise correlates more strongly with task success than video-quality metrics such as FID
[
18
]
, SSIM
[
52
]
, and PSNR
[
19
]
, and for real-robot policies,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed offline correlates with physical-robot task success on a shared set of tasks. Across these settings, sensorimotor alignment correlates with task success more closely than VQA or video-quality metrics.
Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closed-loop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
to supply that explanation, as shown in
Section
4
. For example, fine-tuned VLAs often ignore the language instruction and act mainly on what they see; we find that their task success correlates with the
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
of their vision features, not their text features.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose a new view of embodiment: more capable embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with the structure of motion trajectories. To test this, we introduce
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
, a training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations.
•
Across model families, in simulation and on real robots,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with task success, making it a low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation.
•
Furthermore, we use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
to explain, at the representation level, several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs that were previously observed only through closed-loop results, making it a diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models.
We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
21

argues that as models of different modalities become more capable, their representations converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We test the prediction that models whose image–text representations align more closely with end-effector trajectories should achieve higher downstream task success.
We quantify this alignment using Sensorimotor Alignment (
